debounce.logic: After a high-frequency event (typing, resize, scroll) fires, wait N ms before running; if it fires again in the meantime, the timer resets, so the handler only runs once the user has "stopped" for more than N ms. Implemented with a timer variable plus clearTimeout/setTimeout. Typical uses: search-box suggestions, form validation.
debounce.prompt: Implement "Debounce" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] While the user keeps typing, don't fire a request on every keystroke; run once after a short pause so the UI stops refreshing constantly. [When it triggers] After a high-frequency event such as input, resize or scroll fires, start a timer; any new event within the wait resets it, and the handler runs once after the quiet period expires. [Implementation] Keep a timer in a closure; on each call, clearTimeout first, then setTimeout. In React, store the timer in useRef so re-renders don't lose it, and call clearTimeout in the useEffect cleanup so it can't fire after unmount. If the first call needs an immediate response, add leading: run once when the timer is empty; trailing controls whether to run one last time after the quiet period; turning both off disables the function. [Key parameters] wait=300ms (300ms for search suggestions, 150ms for resize); leading=false (run immediately on the first call?); trailing=true (run the last call after the quiet period). [Pitfalls] If the debounced function is defined inside the component body, every render creates a new timer, which means no debouncing at all; pin it with useRef. Don't debounce a submit button: users will think the click didn't register; disable the button there instead. [Dependencies] None.

throttle.logic: No matter how densely events fire, run at most once every N ms, giving a steady output rate. Difference from debounce: debounce runs "once the user stops", throttle runs "continuously at a steady pace". Typical uses: scroll loading, dragging, mouse following.
throttle.prompt: Implement "Throttle" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] For high-frequency actions such as scrolling, dragging and mouse following, run the handler at a fixed, even rhythm so the UI tracks the input smoothly and never runs hundreds of times per second. [When it triggers] The first event runs immediately; further events inside the cooldown window are dropped, and the next one is let through only when the window ends. Unlike debounce ("run once the user stops"), throttle keeps a steady output even while events keep coming. [Implementation] Keep a lastTime in a closure; on each call check whether Date.now() - lastTime exceeds wait, and only then run and update lastTime. To avoid losing the final call, add a trailing timer that runs it afterwards. For purely visual updates such as scroll and resize, prefer requestAnimationFrame throttling: at most one run per frame, naturally aligned with the refresh rate. In React, keep lastTime and the timer in useRef and clearTimeout in the useEffect cleanup. [Key parameters] wait=100ms (100-200ms for scroll loading, one frame, i.e. 16ms, for mouse following); leading=true (run immediately on the first call?); trailing=true (run one last time when the cooldown ends?). [Pitfalls] If the throttled function is defined inside the component body, every render creates a new closure and resets lastTime to its initial value, so nothing is throttled; pin it with useRef or useMemo. Also don't set wait above 300ms for finger-following animation: the position visibly jumps and lags behind the finger. [Dependencies] None.

skeleton.logic: While data loads, first render a set of gray placeholder blocks that match the real content's layout (often with a shimmer animation), then swap in the real content when the data arrives. It reduces waiting anxiety and layout shift (CLS) better than a spinner.
skeleton.prompt: Implement "Skeleton Screen" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Before data returns, the page already shows gray placeholder blocks with the same layout as the real content, so users see content taking shape instead of a blank page with a spinner. [When it triggers] Render the skeleton as soon as the request is sent, for both the first screen and list pagination; switch it away the moment the response arrives or fails. [Implementation] Copy the real component's structure into a placeholder version: the same number of rows, round avatars, text line heights, using divs with a background color to form blocks, with fixed width and height matching the real content. For the shimmer, use one linear-gradient background with a CSS animation on background-position sweeping across horizontally; don't drive it frame by frame in JS. Toggle between skeleton and real component with a loading-state ternary; in Next.js it can go straight into loading.tsx. [Key parameters] shimmer period=1.5s (linear, infinite loop); placeholder radius=4px; minimum display time=300ms (prevents a flash when the response is instant); last text line placeholder width=60%. [Pitfalls] If the skeleton height doesn't match the real content, the whole page jumps down on swap and CLS actually gets worse; measure the real card height first, then hardcode the placeholder size. Put aria-busy="true" on the container and aria-hidden on the skeleton, otherwise screen readers announce a pile of empty blocks. [Dependencies] None.

virtual-list.logic: A long list renders only the few items visible in the viewport (plus a buffer above and below), using a tall spacer container and computed offsets to simulate the full scrollbar. It cuts DOM nodes from tens of thousands to a few dozen, fixing jank in large lists.
virtual-list.prompt: Implement "Virtual List" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A list with tens of thousands of rows still scrolls smoothly, the scrollbar length and position match the real data size, and users can't tell that only a few dozen nodes are actually rendered. [When it triggers] Enable it when the list exceeds about 200 items; when scrolling changes the visible range, recompute and re-render that slice. [Implementation] Give the outer container a fixed height with overflow:auto, and put an inner spacer element with height = itemCount x rowHeight to produce the scrollbar. Listen to scrollTop and compute startIndex=floor(scrollTop/rowHeight) and visibleCount=ceil(containerHeight/rowHeight), rendering a few extra rows above and below as a buffer; put that slice into an absolutely positioned layer offset by transform:translateY(startIndex*rowHeight). For variable row heights, measure after render, cache each item's height, maintain a prefix sum of heights, and use binary search to locate startIndex. In React projects, @tanstack/react-virtual or react-window is more reliable. [Key parameters] rowHeight=48px (with fixed row height it must match the actual CSS value exactly); overscan=5 items (buffer above and below, 3-10); measure the container height with ResizeObserver, don't hardcode it. [Pitfalls] If list items have margin or padding that isn't counted in rowHeight, the offset accumulates and leaves large blank areas at the bottom; using the array index as key makes the framework reuse the wrong nodes while scrolling, so text typed in an input leaks into other rows: the key must be the data's own id. [Dependencies] Can be hand-written with no dependencies; for React, @tanstack/react-virtual is recommended.

easing.logic: Animation speed isn't constant; it follows a time-to-progress curve (controlled by cubic-bezier). ease-out starts fast and ends slow, feeling crisp; ease-in-out is slow at both ends and fast in the middle, the most natural. Easing is what makes motion feel "alive".
easing.prompt: Apply "Easing" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Elements that move, expand or fade in no longer go at a constant speed; they accelerate and decelerate at the start and end, so they feel like objects with weight instead of being dragged along by a program. [When it triggers] At every moment a transition or animation takes effect; enter, exit, hover feedback and panel expansion must all specify easing explicitly, never leaving the browser's default ease. [Implementation] Set it with transition-timing-function or animation-timing-function, or pass it to the easing field of element.animate. The division of labor: enter and fly-in use ease-out, fast start and slow end (for crisper, cubic-bezier(0.16,1,0.3,1)); exit and collapse use ease-in; position changes where both ends are on screen use ease-in-out; for a bounce, raise the second control point's y above 1, e.g. cubic-bezier(0.34,1.56,0.64,1). Save the few commonly used curves as CSS variables and reuse them site-wide. [Key parameters] duration=200ms (micro-feedback) / 300ms (panels) / 500ms (large movements); bounce control point y=1.56 (the larger, the stronger the bounce). [Pitfalls] Using only ease or linear site-wide: linear should only be used for endlessly rotating spinners, and on UI elements it looks stiff; also don't give exits ease-out, or the element seems to linger. [Dependencies] None.

keyframes.logic: Use @keyframes to define style snapshots at time points such as 0%, 50% and 100%; the browser interpolates between keyframes automatically. Suited to looping, multi-stage motion (breathing lights, loading spinners, translate + scale combos).
keyframes.prompt: Implement "Keyframes" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The element performs continuous multi-stage motion on its own: a breathing light pulsing in brightness, a loading icon spinning at constant speed, an entrance that scales up then settles back, all running without any user action. [When it triggers] Starts when the element gets a class carrying an animation; for entrance effects, use IntersectionObserver to add the class when it enters the viewport; looping effects stay on until the state ends, then the class is removed. [Implementation] First define style snapshots at 0%, 50% and 100% with @keyframes, then write animation: name 1.2s ease-in-out infinite on the element. To hold the end state, add fill-mode: forwards; for back-and-forth swinging, use direction: alternate; multiple animations are listed comma-separated, each timed independently. To clean up the class or chain follow-up logic after the animation ends, listen to the animationend event instead of estimating with setTimeout. [Key parameters] duration=1.2s (breathing light 2s, loading spinner 0.8s, entrance 300ms); timing-function=ease-in-out (a constant-speed spinner must use linear); iteration-count=infinite; delay=index x 60ms (staggered list entrance). [Pitfalls] Animating top/left/width in keyframes reflows on every frame; switch to transform and opacity. Don't write @keyframes for just a start and end state; a transition is simpler. Forgetting to disable looping animations under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce makes motion-sensitive users uncomfortable. [Dependencies] None.

stagger.logic: When a group of elements (list items, cards) enters, each one appears a short delay after the previous one, creating a wave-like rhythm. It has more depth and polish than everything appearing at once. Implement by incrementing animation-delay by index, or with an animation library's stagger option.
stagger.prompt: Implement "Stagger" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] List items and cards don't all pop in at once; they enter one after another like a wave, giving the rhythm more depth. [When it triggers] On the first render of the list, on re-render after a filter change, or the moment the whole group scrolls into the viewport. [Implementation] Pure CSS: give every item the same animation (opacity from 0 to 1, translateY(16px) back to 0), write the index into an inline custom property --i when rendering, then use animation-delay: calc(var(--i) * 60ms); setting el.style.animationDelay while iterating in JS also works. With libraries: in framer-motion set transition.staggerChildren to 0.06 in the parent's variants; in GSAP use gsap.to(items,{stagger:0.06}). [Key parameters] gap between neighbors=50-80ms (over 120ms drags); per-item duration=400ms; total group duration cap ≈ 600ms. [Pitfalls] Blindly incrementing delay across dozens or hundreds of items makes the last one appear seconds later: cap the delay beyond 10 items, or only stagger the batch visible on the first screen; also, with an initial state of display:none the animation never runs, so use opacity:0. [Dependencies] None.

parallax.logic: When scrolling, different layers move at different speeds (background slow, foreground fast), mimicking the real-world effect that near things move faster than far ones and creating spatial depth. Implement by listening to scroll and setting each layer's translateY by a factor, or with CSS transform + perspective.
parallax.prompt: Implement "Parallax" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] While scrolling, the background layer moves slower than the foreground content, giving the picture front-to-back depth so the page is no longer a flat sheet. [When it triggers] After the element enters the viewport it updates continuously with scrolling, and stops computing as soon as it leaves the viewport. [Implementation] Prefer pure CSS: give the scroll container perspective: 1px and overflow-y: auto, and the background layer transform: translateZ(-2px) scale(3); the browser drives everything natively, with zero JS and no dropped frames. When finer control is needed, use IntersectionObserver to attach a scroll listener only while the element is visible (with passive: true); the callback only sets a flag, and the real computation goes into requestAnimationFrame: write transform: translate3d(0, Ypx, 0) by (viewport center - element center) x factor, with a different factor per layer. [Key parameters] speed=0.3 (background 0.2-0.4, foreground 0.6-0.8, 1 means moving with the page); maxOffset=80px (larger exposes the image edge); leave 20% extra height on the background image. [Pitfalls] Reading getBoundingClientRect while writing styles inside the scroll callback interleaves reads and writes, forcing synchronous layout and turning scrolling into a slideshow: cache measurements and only write inside rAF. Don't do full-page parallax on mobile: Safari doesn't dispatch events during scrolling, so the effect jumps. [Dependencies] None.

glassmorphism.logic: A semi-transparent panel plus backdrop-filter: blur() blurs the content behind it, producing a frosted-glass look, combined with a thin border and a subtle highlight. Commonly used for modals, nav bars and cards. Mind performance: large blurred areas are GPU-heavy.
glassmorphism.prompt: Implement "Glassmorphism" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The panel sits over the page like a sheet of frosted glass: the content behind is blurred but still shows through in color and shape, with a thin bright edge around it, feeling light and layered. [When it triggers] A permanent style, in effect whenever a modal opens, the nav bar sticks or a card floats up; it doesn't depend on interaction. [Implementation] Give the panel a semi-transparent background: rgba(255,255,255,0.12), add backdrop-filter: blur(16px) saturate(180%), plus a -webkit-backdrop-filter with the same value for Safari; then add border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.18) as the glass edge and box-shadow: 0 8px 32px rgba(0,0,0,0.25) to lift the layer. There must be something visible behind it (an image or color gradient); blurring a solid background looks like nothing was done. Wrap it in @supports (backdrop-filter: blur(1px)) and fall back to an opaque background when unsupported. [Key parameters] blur=16px (nav bar 12px, large panels 24px); background opacity=0.12 (dark background) / 0.65 (light background); saturate=180% (restores saturation lost to blurring); border=1px. [Pitfalls] Laying blur over the full screen or a long scroll container makes the GPU recompute the whole region every frame, dropping frames on mid-range devices; when a parent has overflow:hidden, corners leak square edges, so put the border-radius on the glass element itself. [Dependencies] None.

neumorphism.logic: The element has the same color as the background, and two opposite-direction box-shadows, one light and one dark, simulate a soft 3D look of being "extruded from / pressed into" the background, like soft plastic. Visually gentle but low in contrast; use with caution for buttons that need clear boundaries.
neumorphism.prompt: Implement "Neumorphism" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Buttons and cards share the background's color, looking extruded from or pressed into the same block of soft plastic, with no outline, only soft light-and-shade transitions. [When it triggers] A permanent style; on press (:active) it flips from raised to inset, giving a pressed-down feedback. [Implementation] The container and the element share one background color (for the light theme use a mid-light gray like #e0e5ec, not pure white or black); give the element two box-shadows: one offset to the bottom-right in a color about 10% darker than the background, one offset to the top-left in a color about 10% lighter; for the inset state, add the inset keyword to both. Use a uniformly large border-radius; the larger, the more it looks like soft plastic. [Key parameters] offset=6px (larger for bigger elements); blur=12px (about 2x the offset); light/dark difference=±10% (use color-mix or adjust the L of hsl); border-radius=16px. [Pitfalls] Using it for primary buttons and inputs: same-color low contrast makes it hard to see what is clickable, and fails the 4.5:1 contrast ratio; keep CTAs as solid fills and use neumorphism only for secondary controls and decorative cards. [Dependencies] None.

gradient.logic: Color transitions smoothly along a direction: linear, radial or conic. Used for backgrounds, buttons and text (background-clip:text). Advanced: multiple color stops, stacked gradients, animated angles for a flowing-light effect.
gradient.prompt: Implement "Gradient" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The background or button color transitions smoothly along one direction with no visible banding, giving more depth than a flat color. [When it triggers] A permanent background style; on hover or on a timed loop, switch the angle or shift the color stops for a flowing-light effect. [Implementation] Linear: background: linear-gradient(135deg, #6366f1 0%, #ec4899 100%); radiating from a point: radial-gradient(circle at 30% 20%, ...); color wheel: conic-gradient. Multiple gradients can be stacked with commas, earlier ones covering later ones, with rgba transparent stops for soft layering. For animation, don't animate background-position (it doesn't run on the compositor); instead place an oversized gradient layer beyond the container and translate it with transform, or register --angle as an angle type with @property and transition the conic-gradient's angle. Same-hue light-to-dark transitions tend to band; add "in oklab" to the interpolation or add an intermediate stop. [Key parameters] angle=135deg (top-left to bottom-right is the most common); stops=2 to 3 (more than 4 gets muddy); lightness difference between ends=15% to 25%; flow period=8s to 15s. [Pitfalls] Writing a transition directly on background-image doesn't animate, since gradients aren't interpolable by default; use transform or @property instead. Also, a gradient background with 100vh height jumps on mobile when the address bar collapses; use 100dvh. [Dependencies] None.

elevation.logic: Use shadow blur radius and offset to express how "high above the page" an element is: the higher, the larger and softer the shadow, building a clear hierarchy (card < floating button < modal). A unified elevation scale makes the interface feel more orderly.
elevation.prompt: Implement "Elevation" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Cards, floating buttons and modals are distinguishable at a glance in front-to-back order; the higher the element, the larger and softer its shadow, so the interface has order instead of a pile of flat color blocks. [When it triggers] Permanent; on hover or drag, temporarily go up one level, and drop back on release. [Implementation] First define a scale of CSS variables --shadow-1 to --shadow-5, each level made of two box-shadows: a small-offset, small-blur dark contact shadow, and a large-offset, large-blur faint shadow for diffusion; as the level rises, increase both the y offset and blur and lower the opacity. Components only reference semantic levels like var(--shadow-2) and never hand-write values in business code. In dark themes, express height by raising surface brightness instead, and lighten the shadows themselves. [Key parameters] level-1=0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,.08); level-3=0 4px 12px rgba(0,0,0,.12); level-5=0 12px 32px rgba(0,0,0,.18); hover transition: box-shadow 150ms ease-out. [Pitfalls] Each component writing its own shadow values leaves seven or eight different shadows on one screen and scrambles the hierarchy; they must be collected into variables. Also don't use pure black without transparency, which looks dirty. [Dependencies] None.

autosave.logic: Listen to the form's or editor's change event and, with a debounce timer, trigger a save after the user stops typing; typically use setTimeout/useDebouncedCallback to PUT the draft to the backend or write it to localStorage/IndexedDB, and use a saving/saved/error state machine to show progress in the UI. To avoid data loss, flush the last unsaved change on beforeunload or before a route change.
autosave.prompt: Implement "Autosave" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Users don't need to click a save button; content is saved shortly after they stop typing, a corner indicator shows saving or saved, and the content is still there after a refresh or crash. [When it triggers] After each change, start a debounce timer and save once when the quiet period ends; flush unsaved changes immediately on route change, when going to the background, and before closing. [Implementation] Drive the indicator with an idle/saving/saved/error state machine, and wrap the save function in a debounce. Write drafts to localStorage, or IndexedDB for large documents; the remote PUT overwrites the same draftId and carries updatedAt, and the server returns a conflict if it detects the client is behind. For the final save before the page closes, use navigator.sendBeacon or fetch with keepalive:true; a plain fetch is cut off when the page unloads. [Key parameters] debounce=800ms (1000ms for plain text, 500ms for short forms); max forced-save interval=30s (persist at least once even while typing continuously); "saved" indicator stays for 2s. [Pitfalls] Writing the whole content back into the editor after a successful save makes the caret and scroll position jump; on mobile, beforeunload often doesn't fire at all when switching away, so use visibilitychange as a fallback. [Dependencies] None.

optimistic-ui.logic: When a mutation starts, immediately update the local cache/state with the predicted result and render the success state without waiting for the server; on success, reconcile with the real data; on failure, roll back to the snapshot from before the mutation and show a notice. The typical pattern in React Query is cancelQueries + setQueryData in onMutate, saving the rollback context.
optimistic-ui.prompt: Implement "Optimistic UI" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] After liking, renaming or checking off a todo, the UI shows the success state instantly with no spinner; if the server fails, quietly revert and show a notice, so the whole thing feels like a local operation. [When it triggers] Change local state the moment the write request is sent, without waiting for the response; when the response returns, reconcile with the real data; on error, roll back to the snapshot from before the operation. [Implementation] With React Query, do it in useMutation's onMutate: first cancelQueries for the same key so an in-flight old response can't wash out the optimistic value; save a snapshot with getQueryData and put it in the returned context; then setQueryData with the predicted result. In onError, take the snapshot from context and restore it with setQueryData; in onSettled, invalidateQueries so server data has the final say. Without a library it's the same idea: store the old value in a variable before changing state, and restore it in catch. Where the server generates the id, use a temporary id as placeholder and replace it with the real id on success. [Key parameters] snapshot granularity=the whole data of the query key (don't store only the changed field); failure notice duration=4000ms; enable only for high-success, reversible operations (like, favorite, reorder), not for payment or deletion. request-cancellation.logic: Create a signal with AbortController and pass it to fetch/axios; when the input changes or the component unmounts, call controller.abort() to terminate the in-flight request, preventing a stale response from overwriting the new result or triggering setState warnings on an unmounted component. Usually abort in the useEffect cleanup, or use axios CancelToken or react-query's automatic cancellation.
request-cancellation.prompt: Apply "Request Cancellation" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] When users switch pages quickly or type search terms in rapid succession, the results of stale requests never suddenly overwrite the current content, and the console no longer shows setState-after-unmount warnings. [When it triggers] Cancel the previous request of the same kind before sending a new one; cancel all in-flight requests when the component unmounts; also call it when the user clicks a "Cancel" button. [Implementation] Before each request, new AbortController() and pass controller.signal as the second argument of fetch (axios also supports a signal option); send the request inside useEffect and call controller.abort() in the cleanup, with the search term and other variables in the dependency array, so the previous request is cancelled automatically whenever the value changes. In catch, if err.name === 'AbortError', just return; don't treat it as a real error and show a notice. For multiple concurrent requests, keep controllers in a Map by key, and abort the old one with the same key before sending a new one. [Key parameters] create a new controller every time, an aborted one can't be reused; for timeout cancellation use AbortSignal.timeout(8000); works best combined with a 300ms debounce. [Pitfalls] Only aborting without a race fallback: if the underlying implementation doesn't cancel completely, the old response still comes back; the safe approach is to also keep an incrementing request sequence number and discard the callback if it isn't the latest. Another common mistake is showing AbortError as a network error, so users see a baffling error each time they switch pages. [Dependencies] None.

stale-while-revalidate.logic: On a cache hit, immediately return the old data (stale) so the UI opens instantly, while re-requesting the latest data in the background and silently replacing it and re-rendering when it arrives. SWR/React Query use a key as the cache index, with revalidation on focus/reconnect, a dedup time window, and the cache-control: stale-while-revalidate header.

[When it triggers] On mount, a cache hit returns the old value and sends a background request; also revalidate on window refocus, network reconnect, and once staleTime has passed. [Implementation] Use TanStack Query or SWR: index the cache with an array key, and the key must include every parameter that affects the result (page, filter, sort); staleTime decides how long data counts as stale, gcTime decides how long the cache is kept, refetchOnWindowFocus enables revalidation on focus, and concurrent requests for the same key are deduplicated automatically. After a data mutation, use invalidateQueries to invalidate the related keys. [Key parameters] staleTime=30s (0 for high real-time needs, 5min for config data); gcTime=5min; dedupingInterval=2s; retry=1. [Pitfalls] Leaving pagination or filter parameters out of the key makes page changes hit the same cache entry and show the previous page's data; also setting staleTime to Infinity while expecting automatic updates means it never revalidates again. [Dependencies] @tanstack/react-query or swr.

request-deduplication.logic: Concurrent requests for the same key within a short time send only one real network request; the other callers reuse the same in-flight Promise. Implemented by maintaining a Map<key, Promise>: on call, if one is already pending, return the cached Promise, and clear it after it resolves. Also called request coalescing, often combined with batching to merge multiple calls into one batch request.
request-deduplication.prompt: Apply "Request Deduplication" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] When several components need the same data at once, only one network request is sent, the network panel no longer shows a string of identical API calls, and the first screen is faster. [When it triggers] Concurrent calls with the same key within the dedup window; the most typical case is several components mounting at page initialization and requesting the same endpoint. [Implementation] Keep a module-level Map, with the key built from "method + URL + serialized params" and the value being that request's Promise. The request function checks the Map first: on a hit, return that in-flight Promise directly; on a miss, actually send the request, store the Promise, and delete the key in finally. To also get a short-lived cache, don't delete immediately; use setTimeout to delete at the end of the window. For batching, collect the ids gathered within the window and merge them into one batch API call after one microtask. If you already use SWR or React Query, they deduplicate by key by default; just tune dedupingInterval. [Key parameters] dedupingInterval=2000ms; batch merge window=10ms or one microtask; key serialization must sort object param keys stably, otherwise {a,b} and {b,a} count as two keys. [Pitfalls] Forgetting to delete the key in finally caches a failed Promise forever, so every later call gets the same error and can never send a request again; also putting a timestamp or random number into the key means the key never repeats and deduplication is useless. [Dependencies] None; built in if you already use SWR / @tanstack/react-query.

retry-backoff.logic: After a request fails, don't retry immediately; wait with an increasing delay = base * 2^attempt, and add random jitter to avoid a thundering herd; give up when the max retry count is reached or a non-retryable 4xx error occurs. Usually done with a recursive setTimeout or a library's retry/retryDelay config, retrying only idempotent requests and network/5xx errors.
retry-backoff.prompt: Implement "Retry with Exponential Backoff" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] On network jitter or a transient server 5xx, users see no error; the request quietly retries itself and succeeds, and a notice appears only when it truly can't. [When it triggers] Retry only on network errors, timeouts, 5xx and 429; never retry 400, 401, 403, 404 or a user-initiated cancel. [Implementation] Write a recursive async wrapper: after catching a retryable error, await sleep(delay) and call itself again, with delay growing as base times 2 to the power of attempt, then multiplied by a random factor of 0.5 to 1.5 as jitter to spread requests out; when attempt exceeds the limit, throw the original error. If the response carries a Retry-After header, wait according to it first, and give each attempt its own timeout with AbortController. [Key parameters] base=300ms; factor=2; maxRetries=3 (about 2s total); maxDelay=10s; jitter=plus or minus 50%. [Pitfalls] Blindly retrying a non-idempotent POST such as placing an order causes duplicate submissions; only auto-retry GET/PUT/DELETE or requests carrying an idempotency key. Also, retrying in a fixed-interval loop knocks the service over again the moment it recovers, as all clients hit it at the same time. [Dependencies] None.

cursor-pagination.logic: Instead of offset/limit (slow for deep pages and prone to gaps and duplicates), use a stable cursor (id or timestamp) of the last record on the previous page as the next cursor; the backend fetches the next batch with WHERE id > cursor ORDER BY id LIMIT n, and the response carries nextCursor/hasMore, which the frontend uses as the next request's parameter. Suited to infinite scroll and live-inserted data streams.
cursor-pagination.prompt: Implement "Cursor Pagination" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Paging to page several hundred still opens instantly, and when new data is inserted the list never shows an item twice or skips a whole stretch. [When it triggers] The first-screen request carries no cursor; after that, each click on "Load more" or scroll to the bottom sends the nextCursor returned by the previous page. [Implementation] The API takes request params limit and cursor and returns items, nextCursor and hasMore. The backend fetches by a stable, unique sort key, like WHERE (created_at, id) < (cursor_time, cursor_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT n+1; the extra row is used both to determine hasMore and to provide the next cursor. The cursor joins the sort field and id and is base64-encoded into an opaque string; the frontend only passes it back as is and never parses it. The frontend stores nextCursor in list state and, when hasMore is false, stops requesting and shows an end-of-list notice; with React Query, having useInfiniteQuery's getNextPageParam return nextCursor is the easiest. [Key parameters] limit=20 items (20-50 for infinite scroll, smaller on mobile); the sort must include a unique id as a tiebreaker; fetch 1 extra row to determine hasMore. [Pitfalls] Using a single possibly-duplicated timestamp column as the cursor makes rows written in the same millisecond get skipped as a block; also having the frontend parse or assemble the cursor contents breaks everything when the backend changes its implementation: the cursor must be treated as an opaque string. race-condition-guard.prompt: Apply "Race Condition Guard" to the code mentioned above. [Implementation] In useEffect, declare let ignore = false, check ignore before setState when the response arrives, and set it to true in the cleanup. Or use AbortController: create one inside the effect, pass the signal to fetch, call abort() in the cleanup, and in catch recognize AbortError and simply ignore it. Outside React, use an incrementing requestId and compare to see whether it is the latest one. [Key parameters] decision value=an incrementing requestId or the ignore flag inside the closure (not a value but an identity carried by every request); effective concurrency=1, a new request invalidates the old one as soon as it is sent. polling.logic: The frontend uses setInterval or a recursive setTimeout to periodically pull the latest data from the server to simulate real time; to avoid pile-ups, it usually schedules the next one only after the previous response returns (recursive setTimeout), and pauses polling when the page is hidden (visibilitychange) or unfocused to save traffic. React Query's refetchInterval is the declarative implementation.

[Goal] Status on the page (task progress, order status, unread count) updates itself without users refreshing manually; when switched to another tab it stops, so it doesn't waste traffic and battery. [When it triggers] Start on component mount; schedule the next one after each response returns; pause when the page is hidden or the window loses focus, and on returning to the foreground pull once immediately, then resume; stop as soon as a terminal state (success or failure) is reached. [Implementation] Don't use setInterval; use a recursive setTimeout: schedule the next one only after this request has been awaited, so slow responses don't cause requests to pile up. Keep the timer id and a stopped flag in refs; on unmount, clearTimeout and set the flag so it can't keep running afterwards. Listen to document's visibilitychange: clearTimeout when hidden, run once immediately when visible. On request failure, double the interval with exponential backoff and reset it after success. With React Query, set refetchInterval and leave refetchIntervalInBackground at its default false. [Key parameters] interval=5000ms (1000-2000ms for progress bars, 30000ms for ordinary lists); backoff cap=60000ms; stop and notify after 5 consecutive failures. [Pitfalls] With setInterval and an endpoint that occasionally takes eight seconds, requests stack up and the server gets knocked over by your own clients; also, not checking on response whether the component has unmounted or the params have changed lets old results overwrite the new page's data. react-suspense.logic: When data or code isn't ready, a component throws a Promise; the nearest <Suspense fallback> boundary catches it and renders a placeholder, and when the Promise resolves it automatically retries rendering the real content. Combined with React.lazy for code splitting, or Suspense-enabled data sources (use hook / RSC), it gives declarative loading states and avoids hand-written isLoading branches.
react-suspense.prompt: Implement "Suspense" at the place mentioned above. [When it triggers] When a component in the wrapped subtree suspends because data or code isn't ready, the nearest Suspense boundary renders the fallback immediately; when the suspended Promise completes, rendering is retried automatically. [Implementation] Wrap the subtree that may suspend in <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton/>}>; for code splitting use React.lazy with dynamic import, one boundary each at the route level and around heavy components. On the data side, choose a Suspense-capable solution: React 19's use(promise), React Query's useSuspenseQuery, or a direct await in a server component. Draw boundaries by "what can appear together as a block"; don't wrap the whole page in a single one. Wrap an ErrorBoundary outside as well: Suspense only handles loading states, not errors. For updates like tab switches where you don't want the fallback to flash, wrap them in useTransition to keep the old content and show isPending. [Key parameters] make the fallback's height close to the real content's to avoid layout jump when it appears; boundary levels=one at the route level plus one per heavy component; transition updates always go through useTransition. [Pitfalls] Creating a new Promise or sending a request directly during render gives a different Promise each render and causes an infinite suspend loop: the promise must be returned stably by a cache layer; also, writing Suspense without an ErrorBoundary blanks the whole page as soon as a request fails. memoization.logic: Cache a pure function's result or a component's render output, skipping repeated computation when inputs are unchanged; in React, useMemo caches expensive computations, useCallback caches function references, and React.memo skips child re-renders via shallow comparison. [Implementation] First find the truly slow parts with the Profiler. Wrap expensive pure computations (sorting, filtering large arrays) in useMemo with all dependencies listed; pin callbacks passed to memoized children with useCallback; wrap the child component itself in React.memo. layout-thrashing.logic: Alternating between reads (offsetHeight/getBoundingClientRect) and writes of DOM styles in a loop repeatedly triggers forced synchronous reflow, and performance collapses; the fix is to batch all reads first and writes after, or separate the read and write phases with requestAnimationFrame / FastDOM.
layout-thrashing.prompt: Apply "Layout Thrashing" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Batch DOM operations cause no repeated reflows, and performance goes from stuttering back to smooth. [Implementation] Separate the read and write phases: first collect all dimensions into an array, then compute new styles, and finally apply the changes together; or separate with requestAnimationFrame; or use FastDOM to sequence automatically. [Key parameters] batch=50-100 elements; polling=once per frame. [Pitfalls] Moving to requestAnimationFrame without actually separating reads from writes; changing position with transform doesn't trigger reflow, but changing width/height requires a read; some libraries implicitly cause lots of reflows. hydration.logic: The static HTML sent by SSR needs hydrateRoot on the client to attach event listeners and restore component state, turning dead markup into an interactive app; the client's first render must match the server HTML exactly, otherwise a hydration mismatch is reported. The first screen is visible early, but interactivity (TTI) has to wait for the JS to download and execute.
hydration.prompt: Apply "Hydration" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] The server-rendered first screen is not only visible but clickable; during client takeover the page doesn't flicker or reflow, and the console shows no content-mismatch errors. [When it triggers] When the client JS loads and runs, it takes over existing HTML once; this only happens on SSR/SSG output, pure client-side rendering has no such step. [Implementation] Use hydrateRoot(container, <App/>) as the entry instead of createRoot().render(). The core is making sure the server and client first renders output exactly the same: move values that only exist on the client, such as Date.now(), Math.random(), localStorage, window size and browser language, into useEffect and setState after mount, with the first render using the same placeholder as the server. For components that can only run on the client, use dynamic import with SSR turned off (dynamic with ssr:false in Next.js), or gate them with a mounted state. To shorten time to interactive, split bundles by route and defer non-first-screen components. [Key parameters] first-screen JS size target under 170KB (gzipped); time-to-interactive target under 3.5s (mid-range device on 4G); suppressHydrationWarning may only be added to a single text node such as a timestamp. [Pitfalls] Writing a typeof window !== 'undefined' branch directly in render makes the two sides' first renders necessarily differ, and after a mismatch the whole subtree is discarded and re-rendered; another common trap is invalid HTML nesting (a div inside a p), where the browser auto-corrects and the DOM structure no longer matches what the framework expects. [Goal] Most of the page stays static HTML and only interactive components download JS, giving a small bundle and a fast first screen. [When it triggers] At build time, components that need hydration are identified by directive markers. [Implementation] Use Astro's client: directives (client:load immediately, client:visible on entering the viewport, client:idle when idle, client:only client-side only); bundle JS only for those components and leave the rest as HTML; the initial load pulls only the shell, and interactive components are lazy loaded on demand. [Key parameters] hydration condition=by interaction importance; chunk granularity=by feature module. [Pitfalls] Marking too many client:load makes it an SPA; sharing data between islands causes hydration-order problems; dynamic styles in prerendered output can break. [Dependencies] Astro framework.

resumability.logic: An alternative to hydration proposed by Qwik: the server serializes component state and event listener locations into the HTML, and at startup the client doesn't re-execute component code but resumes from the paused point; only when a real interaction happens is the corresponding small piece of code lazy loaded on demand. It achieves near-zero startup JS, decoupling TTI from page size.
resumability.prompt: Apply "Resumability" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] The page is interactive immediately after loading, without re-executing component code. [When it triggers] The server serializes state and event locations into the HTML. [Implementation] Qwik supports this natively: use $(symbol) pointers to reference interactive points; at startup the client registers event delegation, and handlers are lazy loaded only when an event fires; serialization uses QRL to store code locations and props. [Key parameters] serialization granularity=function level; chunk loading=user interaction or requestIdleCallback; pointer density=needs balancing. [Pitfalls] Circular references fail to serialize; user actions pile up before the event handlers load; React patterns can't be directly converted to Qwik. [Dependencies] Qwik framework.

code-splitting.logic: Use dynamic import() to split the bundle into multiple chunks by route or component, so the first screen loads only necessary code and the rest is fetched asynchronously when needed; React.lazy + Suspense or framework route-level splitting is common practice, and webpack/vite automatically produce the split bundles and on-demand prefetching accordingly.
code-splitting.prompt: Apply "Code Splitting" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] The first screen downloads only the JS the current page needs, so entering the site is faster; large pieces such as editors, charts and maps load only when the user really opens them. [When it triggers] On route change, fetch that route's chunk on demand; load heavy components on their first render, and prefetch ahead of time when the mouse hovers over their entry point. [Implementation] Use dynamic import() as the split point: in React, write const Chart = lazy(() => import('./Chart')), wrap it in Suspense for a fallback, and use an ErrorBoundary to catch chunk load failures. For hover prefetch, call the same import() once in onMouseEnter. On the build side, use Vite's manualChunks to split the framework and chart libraries into a vendor chunk. [Key parameters] per-chunk limit=150KB (gzipped); first-screen JS budget=200KB (gzipped); hover prefetch delay=200ms. [Pitfalls] Writing the import() path as a concatenated variable prevents static analysis by the bundler, so it either produces no chunk or bundles the whole directory; also splitting too finely makes the first screen serially request dozens of small files, which is actually slower. [Dependencies] None.

infinite-scroll.logic: When scrolling nears the bottom (or a sentinel element + IntersectionObserver fires), automatically request the next page and append it to the list, using cursor pagination and loading/last-page flags to avoid duplicate triggers. Long lists also need virtualization to recycle the DOM, otherwise nodes pile up endlessly and memory and performance collapse.
infinite-scroll.prompt: Implement "Infinite Scroll" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When the user scrolls near the bottom, the next page is attached automatically, with a loading skeleton in between and a "No more items" message at the end, with no button clicks needed. [When it triggers] Request the next page when the sentinel element at the end of the list enters the viewport (with a lead margin); don't trigger while loading or when there is no more data. [Implementation] Put a 1px-high sentinel div at the end of the list and observe it with IntersectionObserver; the callback must satisfy isIntersecting, not currently loading, and more data available before sending a request, using rootMargin to preload a few hundred pixels early. Paginate with a cursor rather than offset to avoid duplicates when new data is inserted. After the request returns, append the new data to the list and update the cursor and hasMore. Call observer.disconnect() on unmount. In React, useInfiniteQuery manages pagination state most easily. When the list may exceed a few hundred items, you must add virtualization to recycle the DOM, plus a "Back to top" button and scroll position restoration. [Key parameters] rootMargin='0px 0px 400px 0px' (preload 400px early); threshold=0; limit=20 per page; after 2 automatic retries on failure, switch to manual click-to-retry. [Pitfalls] Checking only for entering the viewport and not whether a load is in progress sends several page requests from one hit of the bottom and puts duplicates in the list; also letting nodes pile up without recycling makes memory balloon after thousands of items, scrolling drops frames, and the tab may even crash. [Dependencies] None; for React, @tanstack/react-query is optional.

pull-to-refresh.logic: Listen to touchstart/touchmove at the top of a list; when the list is already scrolled to the top and the user keeps pulling down, show a stretchable refresh indicator that follows the finger's displacement, and on release past a threshold trigger a refresh request and spring back. You need to handle overscroll, threshold detection and locking while refreshing; native overscroll-behavior can also help.
pull-to-refresh.prompt: Implement "Pull-to-Refresh" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When the finger pulls down at the top of the list, a refresh indicator follows it downward; releasing after pulling far enough shows a spinner while fresh data loads, then springs back into place when done. [When it triggers] Enter the pulling state only when the container's scrollTop is 0 and the finger moves downward; refresh triggers on release only if the displacement exceeds the threshold, otherwise it springs back immediately. [Implementation] Listen to touchstart to record the start Y, compute the displacement in touchmove, and when the conditions hold call preventDefault to block native scrolling and set the container's translateY to the damped displacement. On touchend, if past the threshold, lock at the refresh height and call the refresh function; when done, add a transition to spring back to 0. touchmove must be registered with { passive: false }, otherwise preventDefault silently fails. [Key parameters] trigger threshold=60px; refreshing-state resting height=50px; damping factor=0.5; spring-back animation=300ms ease-out; minimum spin time=500ms. [Pitfalls] Intercepting touchmove without checking scrollTop makes the page drag even when scrolled to the middle, ruining scrolling entirely; on iOS also add overscroll-behavior: contain to the container. [Dependencies] None.

intersection-observer.logic: Use IntersectionObserver to asynchronously watch the intersection ratio between a target element and the viewport (or a specified root); when it enters the viewport, the callback triggers image loading, lazy rendering, exposure tracking or infinite scroll, replacing inefficient scroll + getBoundingClientRect polling. rootMargin enables early preloading and threshold controls the trigger ratio.
intersection-observer.prompt: Apply "Intersection Observer" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Elements do work only when they enter or leave the viewport (loading images, playing entrance animations, reporting exposure); scrolling itself doesn't drop frames and there's no need to repeatedly measure positions in scroll callbacks. [When it triggers] The callback fires asynchronously when the observed element's intersection ratio with the viewport (or a specified root container) crosses the set threshold; at the moment an element is observed, it also calls back once immediately with its current state. [Implementation] After new IntersectionObserver(callback, { root, rootMargin, threshold }), call observe(el) for each target. The callback receives an entries array; iterate and check entry.isIntersecting, using entry.target to get the specific element; for one-shot tasks such as lazy loading, entrance animations and exposure tracking, call unobserve(entry.target) right after handling to avoid repeated triggers. Call disconnect() on unmount. To detect inside a scroll container, pass that container as root; if omitted, the browser viewport is the default. In React, create it in useEffect, disconnect in the cleanup, and keep the instance in useRef. [Key parameters] threshold=0 (any peek counts), 0.5 (must be over half visible), or an array [0,0.25,0.5,1] to get continuous ratios; rootMargin='200px' (triggers 200px early; a negative value shrinks the detection area instead); exposure tracking usually uses threshold=0.5 and counts once only after 1000ms of dwell. [Pitfalls] Creating a new observer on every render without disconnecting multiplies callbacks and reports tracking events repeatedly; also a target with display:none or zero height never triggers, so measure its box first when debugging. [Dependencies] None.

lazy-loading.logic: Defer loading of resources until they're really needed: for images/iframes, use the native loading="lazy" attribute to let the browser schedule by viewport, or use IntersectionObserver to swap data-src into src. The core is to load only visible resources on the first screen, reducing initial bandwidth use and main-thread blocking.
lazy-loading.prompt: Apply "Lazy Loading" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] The first screen downloads only the images and resources that are visible, so the page opens faster and uses less data; while scrolling down, the content further below is loaded slightly ahead of time. [When it triggers] Start loading when an element approaches the viewport (by some pixels of lead); resources within the first screen don't participate in lazy loading and load immediately. [Implementation] For images and iframes, prefer the native attribute loading="lazy" and let the browser schedule them uniformly. When you need earlier prefetch or a fade-in effect, use IntersectionObserver: put the real URL in data-src, and in the callback when entry.isIntersecting is true assign it to src and unobserve, with a positive rootMargin so it triggers early. Every image must have fixed width/height or aspect-ratio to reserve its space. [Key parameters] rootMargin=200px (400px for long lists); threshold=0.01; images within the first two screens use loading="eager" with fetchpriority="high". [Pitfalls] Adding loading="lazy" to the large first-screen image, i.e. the LCP element, directly worsens LCP; also lazy loading without reserving dimensions makes the whole page jump down when the image arrives, sending CLS soaring. [Dependencies] None.

scroll-restoration.logic: On forward/back navigation or returning to a list page, restore the previous scroll position to improve browsing continuity; set history.scrollRestoration='manual' to turn off the browser default, store scrollTop in history.state or sessionStorage yourself on route changes, and scrollTo on return. SPAs especially need to handle this manually.
scroll-restoration.prompt: Implement "Scroll Restoration" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When going from a list into a detail page and then back, the page is still at the position of that item instead of being thrown to the top to scroll down again. [When it triggers] Record the current scroll position before leaving the route; restore it after returning to the page via back navigation once the content has finished rendering; on normal forward navigation to a new page, scroll to the top. [Implementation] First set history.scrollRestoration = 'manual' to turn off the browser's default restoration so it doesn't fight your logic. On leaving the route, store window.scrollY (or the inner container's scrollTop if scrolling happens in an inner container) in sessionStorage keyed by the route path, and read it back on return. The key is to scroll only after the content has actually expanded the height: if data is fetched asynchronously, call window.scrollTo in a useLayoutEffect after the data arrives, or wait one frame with requestAnimationFrame; also cache the list data, otherwise the list is empty on return and there's nowhere to scroll to. [Key parameters] storage uses sessionStorage (isolated per tab, key 'scroll:' plus the route path); restore timing=useLayoutEffect or rAF after data has rendered; use behavior 'auto' rather than 'smooth', otherwise users see an obvious scrolling animation. [Pitfalls] Calling scrollTo before the data returns, when the page isn't tall enough, only scrolls to the current maximum height and stops halfway; also forgetting to turn off the browser's built-in restoration makes two sets of logic fight over scrolling, so the view jumps once and then jumps back. [Dependencies] None.

resource-hints.logic: Use <link rel> to establish connections or fetch resources ahead of time: preconnect/dns-prefetch warm up cross-origin connections, preload fetches the current page's critical resources (fonts, first-screen images) at high priority, and prefetch fetches resources the next page may need at low priority into the cache. The browser decides priority and timing from the rel type.
resource-hints.prompt: Apply "Resource Hints" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Critical resources have connections established or are preloaded ahead of time, reducing later latency. [When it triggers] Triggered when <link rel> tags are declared in the <head>. [Implementation] dns-prefetch resolves DNS; preconnect establishes TCP/TLS; preload fetches current-page resources (fonts, scripts) at high priority; prefetch fetches the next page at low priority. [Key parameters] number of preconnects=3-4; preload along the FCP path; prefetch is run by the browser automatically when idle. [Pitfalls] A preloaded resource that is never consumed is wasted; forgetting crossorigin makes the cache miss; over-preloading crowds out bandwidth. [Dependencies] None (native HTML).

intent-prefetch.logic: Predict the user's next action and fetch data or code ahead of time: on mouse hover, mousedown, entering the viewport or touch start, prefetch the target page's resources so they're ready by the time of the real click. Next.js's <Link> automatically prefetching in the viewport, and quicklink/instant.page, are typical implementations, trading probability for first-screen speed.
intent-prefetch.prompt: Implement "Intent-based Prefetching" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Resources are preloaded before the user clicks, so the click opens instantly. [When it triggers] Hover, mousedown, entering the viewport, or predicting the next step from an input box. [Implementation] After listening for hover/mousedown, fetch or insert <link rel="prefetch">; use libraries such as quicklink (automatic via IntersectionObserver) or instant.page (mousedown); Next.js <Link> prefetches automatically. [Key parameters] hover delay=50-200ms; concurrency=2-3; prediction accuracy>=30%. [Pitfalls] Prefetching everything wastes data and battery; repeated prefetching of already-used pages; dynamically rendered link targets go stale. [Dependencies] quicklink/instant.page libraries (optional).

speculation-rules.logic: Declaratively tell Chromium via <script type="speculationrules"> which URLs to prefetch or prerender in the background, with eagerness (conservative/moderate/eager) controlling the trigger timing (e.g. hover for 200ms, entering the viewport); on a matching navigation it opens almost instantly. Unsupported browsers ignore it, so it is progressive enhancement.
speculation-rules.prompt: Apply "Speculation Rules API" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] At click time the target page is already fully prerendered and navigation has no delay. [When it triggers] <script type="speculationrules"> is declared in the HTML. [Implementation] Configure rules declaring the URLs to prerender and eagerness (conservative/moderate/eager); Chromium loads the page in the background and brings it to the foreground when the navigation matches. [Key parameters] eagerness=conservative is safest, moderate balanced, eager suited to high-conversion pages; number of URLs=3-5. [Pitfalls] A prerendered page that depends on user-specific state becomes invalid; beforeunload fires during prerendering; non-Chromium browsers ignore it. [Dependencies] None (W3C standard).

bfcache.logic: The browser freezes the entire page (including the JS heap and DOM) into memory and restores it instantly on back/forward instead of reloading; to keep it eligible, don't use the unload event and don't set Cache-Control: no-store; use pagehide/pageshow instead and check event.persisted to tell whether the page was restored from bfcache.
bfcache.prompt: Apply "Back-Forward Cache" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] The page is restored instantly on back/forward, with an experience close to a native app. [When it triggers] When the browser's back/forward button is clicked. [Implementation] Avoid unload and beforeunload (use pagehide and pageshow); don't set Cache-Control:no-store; clean up resources in pagehide and check event.persisted; re-initialize in pageshow. [Key parameters] when persisted=true, minimize initialization; pageshow delay=0ms. [Pitfalls] Pages that have used unload have bfcache disabled, and it may stay disabled even after removal; large SPAs that clear state on unload end up inconsistent. [Dependencies] None (native browser).

normalized-cache.logic: Split the nested data returned by APIs by __typename+id into a flat entity table, so different queries reference the same copy of the same entity; after a mutation updates that entity anywhere, all views referencing it sync automatically. Apollo Client/urql's normalized cache relies on this to avoid inconsistent data and duplicate storage.
normalized-cache.prompt: Apply "Normalized Cache" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] The same entity stays in sync across places, and an update in one place is automatically reflected in every reference. [When it triggers] Apollo Client/urql automatically decomposes GraphQL responses as they are received. [Implementation] Configure Apollo Client's InMemoryCache, declare typePolicies using __typename+id as the primary key; every object needs __typename and a unique id; when modifying, call client.cache.modify or go through a mutation, and all references sync automatically. [Key parameters] keyFields=['__typename','id']; merge strategy=a merge function; evict for cleanup. [Pitfalls] Forgetting __typename; a mutation returning an object without a full id; forgetting to trigger a re-render after modification; wrong insertion-position logic for paginated lists. [Dependencies] Apollo Client/urql.

offline-first.logic: The app reads and writes local storage (IndexedDB/Cache Storage) first to guarantee offline availability, then syncs changes to the server asynchronously; a Service Worker intercepts requests using a cache-first or network-falling-back-to-cache strategy and reconciles when the network returns. Users can browse and operate even when offline.
offline-first.prompt: Apply "Offline-First" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] The app can still be browsed and operated offline, and syncs automatically when the network returns. [When it triggers] The Service Worker intercepts fetch and decides whether to read local or network per strategy. [Implementation] Store static resources in Cache Storage; store user data and the pending-sync queue in IndexedDB; use a cache-first (static) or network-first (API) strategy; when offline, write to the queue and wait for recovery with the Background Sync API. [Key parameters] version number=incremented with each release; timeout=30s; strategy by resource type. [Pitfalls] Using cache-first for APIs causes stale data; concurrent write conflicts in IndexedDB; conflicts from sharing across multiple tabs. [Dependencies] Workbox library or a native Service Worker.

background-sync.logic: When offline, queue the user's actions (usually in IndexedDB) and register a sync event through the Service Worker's Background Sync API. Once the network is back, the browser wakes the SW automatically to replay the queued requests to the server, even if the page has been closed. Suited to eventually consistent scenarios such as sending messages or submitting forms.
background-sync.prompt: Implement "Background Sync" for the code mentioned above. [Goal] Offline actions are saved to a queue and replayed automatically when the network returns, succeeding even if the page is closed. [When it triggers] Register with registration.sync.register(tag) while offline. [Implementation] The page stores the action in IndexedDB; register a sync event; the SW's sync listener walks the queue and sends requests one by one; delete an item on success, keep it for retry on failure; set a retry count and backoff. [Key parameters] tag = identifier for the action type; maxAttempts=3; retryDelay=1000ms; timeout=30s. [Pitfalls] The queue has no versioning, so a schema change makes old items unparseable; multiple syncs with the same tag are coalesced; edit conflicts. [Dependencies] workbox-background-sync or the native Service Worker API.

service-worker-cache.logic: A Service Worker intercepts network requests in the fetch event and answers them from Cache Storage according to a strategy: cache-first (static assets), network-first (APIs), stale-while-revalidate, and so on. It precaches the app shell during install and purges old-version caches during activate. This is the core of PWA offline support and instant loading.
service-worker-cache.prompt: Implement "Service Worker Caching" for the code mentioned above. [Goal] Static assets load instantly, APIs degrade gracefully, and the app works offline. [When it triggers] install precaches the app shell; the fetch event picks a strategy by URL; activate cleans up old caches. [Implementation] On install, caches.open(VERSION) and addAll the assets; in fetch, match the URL pattern (/api uses network-first, /static uses cache-first); with network-first, fall back to caches.match when the network fails; stale-while-revalidate returns the cache first and updates in the background. [Key parameters] VERSION = changes with each release; strategy chosen by resource type; precache < 50MB. [Pitfalls] Not deleting old caches across versions keeps new assets from taking effect; dynamic routes should not be cache-first; navigator.onLine is unreliable. [Dependencies] Workbox or the native Service Worker API.

lqip.logic: Load a tiny (a few hundred bytes) blurred thumbnail or inline base64 placeholder first, which holds the layout and gives a color outline; once the full image finishes loading, fade it in to replace the placeholder. This avoids layout shift and blank flashes. The low-res version is pre-generated at build time and often paired with an aspect-ratio placeholder.
lqip.prompt: Implement "Low-Quality Image Placeholder" (LQIP) at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Show a tiny blurred thumbnail before the image loads to hold the layout, then fade in the real image when it finishes. [When it triggers] Show the placeholder as soon as the image tag mounts; fade in once the full image is done. [Implementation] Generate a 20x12 low-res thumbnail or base64 at build time; ; use loading="lazy"; after onload, swap with a CSS transition fade. [Key parameters] Placeholder size = 20-50 bytes; placeholder dimensions = 20x12px; fade duration = 300-500ms; fetchPriority="high". [Pitfalls] Placeholder colors that look jarring; forgetting aspect-ratio makes the page jump; onload never fires if loading fails; large base64 files. [Dependencies] None (blurhash/thumbhash libraries can automate it).

blurhash.logic: Encode an image into a compact 20-30 character string (stored in the API JSON). The client decodes it into a blurred gradient placeholder shown before the full image loads, saving bandwidth compared with sending a thumbnail. It extracts a few frequency components via DCT; on the front end, the blurhash library decodes to a canvas that you draw.
blurhash.prompt: Implement "BlurHash blurred placeholder" (BlurHash) for the code mentioned above. [Goal] A 20-30 character string encodes color and shape, decodes quickly into a placeholder, and saves 90% of the bandwidth. [When it triggers] The server encodes; the client decodes after receiving. [Implementation] The server encodes the image into a string with the blurhash library; send it to the client (in JSON or a data attribute); the client calls decode(hash, w, h, punch) to get ImageData and draws it to a canvas; replace the src once the full image is done. [Key parameters] Resolution = 4x3; punch=1.0 (saturation); transition = 300ms. [Pitfalls] Too high a punch distorts colors; URL-unsafe characters need escaping; converting canvas to img has a cost; some images look poor. [Dependencies] The blurhash npm package.

thumbhash.logic: An improved BlurHash: at the same byte count it keeps more detail and reproduces color more accurately, supports an alpha channel, and can infer the aspect ratio automatically. It encodes an image into a very short binary (stored as base64), which the front-end thumbhash library decodes into a data URL or canvas placeholder. Well suited to list thumbnail previews.
thumbhash.prompt: Implement "ThumbHash compact placeholder" (ThumbHash) for the code mentioned above. [Goal] Smaller and sharper than BlurHash, with alpha support and an inferable aspect ratio. [When it triggers] The server encodes; the client decodes and displays. [Implementation] The server calls encode(pixels, w, h) to produce binary and converts it to a base64 string; the client calls decode(hash) to get {w, h, rgba}; use thumbhashToDataURL(hash) to get a data URL directly; replace it once the full image is done. [Key parameters] hash = 10-20 bytes as base64; aspect-ratio recovery accuracy = ±10%; transition = 300ms. [Pitfalls] Escape URL-unsafe characters; RGBA needs /255 normalization; some images look oversaturated; pair the recovered aspect ratio with CSS aspect-ratio. [Dependencies] The thumbhash npm package.

progressive-image.logic: Use progressive JPEG or interlaced PNG so the image appears over multiple scan passes from blurry to sharp, instead of being painted line by line from the top; the browser repaints repeatedly while downloading. It also broadly refers to the blur-up strategy of showing a small image first and the large one later, giving a recognizable picture sooner on weak networks.
progressive-image.prompt: Implement "Progressive Image Loading" for the code mentioned above. [Goal] Images appear from blurry to sharp, so users see recognizable content sooner on weak networks. [When it triggers] Takes effect automatically when the image itself is progressively encoded. [Implementation] Produce progressive JPEG (multi-pass scans) or interlaced PNG with MozJPEG or libvips; the browser repaints while downloading; or do blur-up manually: load a 20x12 base64 thumbnail first, load the high-res image at the same time, and swap when it completes. [Key parameters] JPEG scan count = 3-5; optimizeScans = enabled; thumbnail = 20x12px. [Pitfalls] Not every tool generates progressive output by default (explicit flags needed); some older browsers have bugs; keep the fallback chain clear when mixing in WebP. [Dependencies] None (imagemin-mozjpeg can automate it).

drag-and-drop.logic: The native HTML5 approach sets draggable="true" on an element and writes data into dataTransfer on dragstart; the drop target must call preventDefault in dragover to allow dropping, and reads the data back on drop. Modern libraries (dnd-kit, react-dnd) simulate it with pointer events, maintaining their own drag layer and collision detection for smoother animation and touch support.
drag-and-drop.prompt: Implement "Drag and Drop" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Users can press and hold a card to pick it up; while dragging there is a follow-the-cursor overlay and a drop indicator; on release it lands in the new position and the order is saved. [When it triggers] Dragging starts only after the pointer is pressed and moves a short distance, to avoid conflicting with clicks; it ends on release or Esc. [Implementation] For list sorting use dnd-kit: wrap the scope in DndContext, call useSortable on each item, update the order with arrayMove in onDragEnd, and render the follow-the-cursor overlay with DragOverlay. For file drops use native HTML5: set draggable="true" on the element, write data to dataTransfer on dragstart, the drop target must call preventDefault in dragover to allow dropping, and read dataTransfer.files in drop. [Key parameters] Activation distance = 8px (use a 200ms long press on touch screens); auto-scroll edge margin = 50px; drop animation = 200ms. [Pitfalls] Forgetting preventDefault on dragover: the symptom is that the item can be picked up but not dropped, with no error at all; also, changing the DOM order directly without updating state. [Dependencies] @dnd-kit/core and @dnd-kit/sortable (none needed for pure file drops).

swipe-gesture.logic: Record the start coordinates on touchstart/pointerdown, compute deltaX/deltaY in touchmove to get displacement and direction, and on touchend combine a distance threshold and velocity to decide whether a left/right swipe fires. To distinguish it from scrolling, the main axis is usually locked: only when horizontal movement exceeds vertical is it treated as a swipe.
swipe-gesture.prompt: Implement "Swipe Gesture" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Users can flick across an element to switch cards, turn pages, or trigger actions, with native-app feel and no interference with normal vertical scrolling. [When it triggers] pointerdown records the start, pointermove accumulates displacement, and on pointerup, if displacement or velocity exceeds the threshold, it counts as a swipe and dispatches the callback for that direction. [Implementation] Use Pointer Events throughout (pointerdown/move/up/cancel) so one codebase covers mouse, touch, and pen. On press, record startX, startY, and startTime, and call setPointerCapture so events are still received when the pointer leaves the element. On move, compute dx and dy; the first time either exceeds about 10px, lock the main axis: if horizontal displacement is larger than vertical, treat it as a swipe gesture and call preventDefault on subsequent moves to block page scrolling; otherwise treat it as vertical scrolling and abandon the gesture. On release, compute velocity = |dx| / (now - startTime); enough distance or enough velocity counts as success. Add touch-action: pan-y to the container to hand vertical scrolling back to the browser, and remember to handle pointercancel. [Key parameters] Distance threshold = 50px or 25% of container width; velocity threshold = 0.3px/ms (a fast flick counts even if the distance is short); axis-lock threshold = 10px; container touch-action: pan-y. [Pitfalls] Calling preventDefault without locking the axis traps users who want to scroll the page up and down, the most hated issue on mobile; also, listening only to touch events leaves desktop mouse and pen users with no support. [Dependencies] None.

long-press.logic: On pointerdown/touchstart, start a setTimeout of about 500ms; if pointerup, movement beyond a tolerance, or pointercancel happens in the meantime, clearTimeout to cancel. If the timer fires as expected, it counts as a long press, usually opening a context menu or entering multi-select mode.
long-press.prompt: Implement "Long Press" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Holding an element for about half a second opens a context menu or enters multi-select mode with a slight vibration; a slight slide or a quick release is treated as a normal click. [When it triggers] pointerdown starts the timer; pointerup, pointercancel, or movement beyond tolerance cancels it; when it runs out, it counts as a long press. [Implementation] On pointerdown, record the start point and start a setTimeout; clearTimeout on pointermove beyond the tolerance, on pointerup, and on pointercancel. Use a fired flag to preventDefault in the subsequent click so the click doesn't run again. On mobile, add touch-action: manipulation to the element and preventDefault in contextmenu, otherwise the system long-press menu takes over first. [Key parameters] duration=500ms (about 600ms on iOS); movement tolerance=10px; navigator.vibrate(10) for 10ms of haptics. [Pitfalls] Canceling only on pointerup and not handling pointercancel when the page scrolls makes the menu pop up at odd moments. [Dependencies] None.

pinch-zoom.logic: Listen to touchmove with two fingers, compute the distance between the two touch points with Math.hypot, and divide the current distance by the initial distance to get a scale applied via transform:scale(). Set touch-action:none to block the browser's default zoom, and use the midpoint of the two fingers as the transform-origin.
pinch-zoom.prompt: Implement "Pinch to Zoom" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] During a two-finger gesture, the target element scales around the midpoint of the fingers, with intuitive feedback. [When it triggers] touchmove fires continuously. [Implementation] touchstart records the two touch coordinates; touchmove computes the current distance (Math.hypot) divided by the initial distance to get scale; apply transform:scale(); use the two-finger midpoint (x1+x2)/2,(y1+y2)/2 as transform-origin; set touch-action:none; optionally spring back on touchend. [Key parameters] scale=0.5-3.0; transform-origin = two-finger midpoint; sensitivity factor; spring-back time=300ms. [Pitfalls] Without touch-action:none the system zoom conflicts; wrong midpoint coordinate conversion; a finger lost at touchend causes a jump; fails inside cross-origin iframes. [Dependencies] None (plain JS and CSS).

swipe-to-dismiss.logic: A card or notification follows the finger via translateX; on release, check whether the displacement or velocity passes the halfway point or a threshold: if so, it animates off and is removed from the list; if not, it springs back. Commonly used to swipe a list item left to reveal a delete button, or to swipe a whole sheet down to close an overlay.
swipe-to-dismiss.prompt: Implement "Swipe to Dismiss" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The user presses a list item and drags horizontally; the card follows the finger and reveals a delete button behind it; if released past halfway it flies off and disappears from the list, otherwise it springs back. [When it triggers] pointerdown on the card starts tracking; during pointermove the displacement updates in real time; on release, displacement ratio or velocity decides between fly-off and spring-back. [Implementation] The card follows the finger with transform: translateX; disable transition while dragging for zero latency, and place an absolutely positioned action-button layer behind it. On release, check whether horizontal displacement exceeds half the container width or the velocity exceeds the threshold: if so, enable transition, animate translateX to ±100%, then collapse the height to 0 for a collapse animation, and only remove it from the data after the animation ends; otherwise animate back to 0. After deletion, immediately show a lightweight toast with undo. Also lock the main axis and set touch-action: pan-y on the container. Keyboard users need an equivalent delete button. [Key parameters] Fly-off threshold = 50% of container width (the half-open state that reveals the button sits at 25%); velocity threshold = 0.5px/ms; fly-off animation 200ms ease-out, height collapse 150ms; undo window 5000ms. [Pitfalls] Changing left or margin instead of transform while following the finger triggers reflow every frame, making mid-to-low-end phones slideshow-slow; also, with no spring-back animation after release the card stalls half-open and users think it's broken. [Dependencies] None; for complex gestures, framer-motion's drag is optional.
