bottom-sheet.logic: A panel that rises from the bottom of the screen and supports multiple snap points (collapsed/half/full). While dragging the handle it changes translateY to follow the finger, and on release snaps to the nearest snap point. There is a scrim behind it, dragging down past a threshold closes it, and background scrolling is usually locked while it's open.
bottom-sheet.prompt: Implement "Bottom Sheet" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A panel rises from the bottom of the screen covering part of the content; the handle at the top can be dragged, it can rest at half and full heights, and dragging down far enough closes it. [When it triggers] Click the entry point to open with a rise animation; while dragging the handle it follows in real time; on release it snaps to the nearest snap point; tapping the scrim or dragging down past the threshold closes it. [Implementation] Container is position: fixed; bottom: 0, positioned with transform: translateY(), and the closed state is translateY(100%). While dragging, change translateY directly in pointermove and temporarily disable transition to keep it following the finger; on pointerup restore transition and pick the nearest snap point by position and release velocity. When open, lock background scrolling and install a focus trap. [Key parameters] snapPoints=[0.5, 0.9] (fraction of viewport height); close threshold = dragged down more than 25% of panel height; animation = 300ms. [Pitfalls] Setting panel height to 100vh gets it clipped when the mobile address bar collapses; use 100dvh instead; also, an inner list fighting the panel for gestures: only move the panel on a downward drag when the inner scrollTop is 0. [Dependencies] None (vaul is also an option).

hover-intent.logic: Don't respond immediately on mouseenter; instead delay (e.g. 150ms) before expanding the menu, and cancel if mouseleave happens in the meantime, so a mouse merely passing over doesn't trigger it by mistake. An advanced version compares pointer speed: only when the pointer slows down and moves toward the target is it judged as real intent.
hover-intent.prompt: Implement "Hover Intent" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The menu doesn't fire by accident; it expands only when the pointer dwells or heads toward it. [When it triggers] A delayed decision after mouseenter. [Implementation] On mouseenter, start a delayed timer (150ms) instead of opening immediately; mousemove computes speed/direction and cancels if the pointer sweeps past quickly; if the delay expires without cancellation, expand; mouseout clears the timer; the advanced version computes the slope of the line to the target to judge direction. [Key parameters] Delay=150ms; speed threshold=0.5-1px/ms; menu lookahead=10px; looping = wrap from last back to first. [Pitfalls] Too long a delay feels sluggish; too short causes false triggers; reset the delay when entering the menu; touch screens have no hover; wrong coordinate system in the speed calculation. [Dependencies] None (the hoverIntent plugin or native code).

marquee-selection.logic: On mousedown in an empty area, record the start point; on mousemove, draw an absolutely positioned semi-transparent selection rectangle from the start point to the current point. In real time, use getBoundingClientRect for rectangle intersection tests, mark hit elements as selected, and end the selection on mouseup.
marquee-selection.prompt: Implement "Marquee Selection" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Dragging in an empty area shows a semi-transparent rectangle, and elements within its range are highlighted. [When it triggers] mousedown, mousemove, mouseup. [Implementation] mousedown records the start point; mousemove computes the rectangle's top-left corner and size and draws it on an overlay; in real time, use getBoundingClientRect() to detect intersecting elements and add a selected class; mouseup removes the overlay. [Key parameters] overlay = position:fixed, border, background:rgba(0,0,255,0.2); intersection test = rectangle overlap; modifiers = Shift/Ctrl. [Pitfalls] A start point on an element triggers click; scroll coordinates go wrong in long lists; nested elements make it impossible to select children. [Dependencies] None (plain JS and CSS).

hit-area.logic: A visually small button reaches the 44x44 touch standard by enlarging its clickable area, commonly with a transparent ::before pseudo-element or negative margin that extends the click range without changing the visual size. React Native achieves the same with the hitSlop prop.
hit-area.prompt: Implement "Hit Area" for the code mentioned above. [Goal] Small buttons get a clickable area enlarged to 44x44px, meeting the touch standard. [When it triggers] Designed and implemented at build time. [Implementation] Extend with a ::before pseudo-element (position:absolute, negative margin); or add padding together with background-clip:content-box; or padding + box-sizing; use hitSlop in React Native. [Key parameters] Minimum size=44x44px; visual size=24-32px; pseudo-element z-index=1. [Pitfalls] Forgetting position:absolute on the pseudo-element disturbs document flow; wrong margin direction; odd underlines on Safari a tags; buttons placed close together make their hit areas overlap. [Dependencies] None (pure CSS).

context-menu.logic: Listen for the contextmenu event and call preventDefault to suppress the system menu, then position a custom overlay at the mouse coordinates. You need to handle edge flipping (expand upward/leftward when space is insufficient), closing on outside click and Esc, and give menu items role="menuitem" to support keyboard up/down selection.
context-menu.prompt: Implement "Context Menu" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Right-clicking the target element pops up a custom menu at the mouse position; near the screen edge it flips back automatically so it isn't clipped; clicking blank space or pressing Esc closes it. [When it triggers] The target element's contextmenu event (a long press on mobile also fires it); it closes on clicking a menu item, clicking outside the menu, pressing Esc, window resize, or page scroll. [Implementation] Listen for contextmenu and preventDefault to suppress the system menu, store e.clientX/clientY in state, and open the menu. The menu is positioned at those coordinates with position: fixed and rendered into a portal under body, so ancestors' overflow:hidden can't clip it. After opening, measure the menu size; if it doesn't fit on the right, use x minus the menu width instead, and likewise vertically, i.e. edge flipping. For accessibility, give the container role="menu" and each item role="menuitem"; on open move focus to the first item, support up/down keys to move, Enter to activate, and Esc to close and return focus. For outside clicks, use a pointerdown on document to check whether the target lies within the menu. [Key parameters] Safe distance from viewport edge=8px; menu min width=160px; z-index unified with other overlays (e.g. 1000); self-implemented long-press duration=500ms. [Pitfalls] Using absolute positioning with an ancestor that has a transform puts the menu far from the mouse; fixed positioning plus a portal is what holds up; also, supporting only mouse interaction leaves keyboard and screen-reader users unable to open it, so provide a "more" button that opens the same menu. [Dependencies] None; in React, Radix UI's Context Menu is optional.

resizable.logic: Place a resize handle on the element's edge; after mousedown on the handle, listen to mousemove on the document, change width and height by the pointer displacement delta, and clamp between min/max. Simple cases can use CSS resize:both plus overflow:auto directly; complex cases require your own calculation.
resizable.prompt: Implement "Resizable" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Moving the mouse to a panel edge changes the cursor to a double-headed arrow; press and drag to change width and height in real time; after release the size is kept and is the same next time it opens. [When it triggers] pointerdown on the handle enters the drag state, pointermove keeps resizing, and pointerup ends it and persists the size. [Implementation] Place an absolutely positioned handle on the edge, visually thin but with a generous hit area. On pointerdown call setPointerCapture to lock subsequent events to that element, and record the starting pointer position and starting size; in pointermove compute starting size plus the displacement delta, clamp it between the limits with Math.min and Math.max, and assign it to a CSS variable rather than calling setState every frame. Set user-select: none on body while dragging. [Key parameters] Handle hit width=6px; minWidth=200px; maxWidth=60% of the parent container; double-clicking the handle resets to the default width=280px. [Pitfalls] Listening only to the handle's own mousemove means a fast drag leaves the element and breaks; you must use setPointerCapture or attach the listener to document. [Dependencies] None.

sortable.logic: While a list item is dragged, the other items shift with transform to open a gap, and the new insertion index is computed in real time from the pointer position. On release, the data array is reordered with arrayMove and a transition animation runs, often combined with the FLIP technique so positions connect smoothly before and after the reorder.
sortable.prompt: Implement "Sortable" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Pressing and dragging a list item makes it follow the pointer, while other items smoothly make way to reveal the insertion gap; on release it lands in the new position and the order is kept, with no abrupt jumps throughout. [When it triggers] Pressing on the drag handle and moving past the start threshold enters dragging; the insertion index is computed in real time during movement; on release it drops into place and commits the new order. [Implementation] Prefer dnd-kit: wrap the container in DndContext, pass the current id array to SortableContext, have each item use useSortable to get attributes, listeners, and transform, and in onDragEnd update the data with arrayMove and persist it. When hand-rolling, the dragged item follows the pointer with transform, and the other items shift with transform based on where the pointer lands, with a transition; at the moment of reorder use the FLIP approach: record each item's getBoundingClientRect first, measure again after changing the order, use transform to add the difference back, then transition to 0, so positions connect smoothly. After dropping, use an optimistic update and roll the order back if the API fails. [Key parameters] Start threshold = 5px of movement or a 250ms long press (avoids conflicts with click and scroll); make-way animation 200ms ease-out; auto-scroll trigger zone at the container edge=60px, speed about 10px/frame. [Pitfalls] Changing the data array order mid-drag makes the framework rebuild nodes and unmount the element being dragged, so the feel suddenly breaks; change only the visual transform during dragging and change the data on release; also, mouse-only support prevents keyboard users from sorting, and dnd-kit's KeyboardSensor fills that gap. [Dependencies] @dnd-kit/core and @dnd-kit/sortable recommended; SortableJS for simple cases.

focus-trap.logic: When a modal opens, confine Tab focus inside the container: find all focusable elements in it, listen for Tab/Shift+Tab, wrap to the first when Tab is pressed on the last, and jump to the last when Shift+Tab is pressed on the first. On close, return focus to the element that triggered it.
focus-trap.prompt: Implement "Focus Trap" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] After a dialog opens, Tab cycles only inside it and focus never escapes to the page behind; on close, focus automatically returns to the original button. [When it triggers] Install when the modal opens and move focus into the container; intercept Tab and Shift+Tab while open; remove it and restore focus on close or unmount. [Implementation] On open, first save document.activeElement, use querySelectorAll to collect the focusable elements in the container (button, a[href], input, select, textarea, etc.) and filter out disabled ones. In keydown, Tab on the last one calls preventDefault and focuses the first; Shift+Tab does the reverse. An easier way is to add the inert attribute to the background content, so the browser blocks all focus and clicks behind it at once. [Key parameters] Container tabindex=-1 (can focus() but is not in the Tab sequence); initial focus = the first interactive element, or the cancel button for destructive actions; background blocking = inert. [Pitfalls] Collecting the focusable list only once at open means asynchronously rendered new elements never join the cycle; also, giving focus to the container div without tabindex="-1" makes focus() silently do nothing. [Dependencies] None.

roving-tabindex.logic: In a group of like controls (toolbar, menu), only the current item gets tabindex="0" and the rest get tabindex="-1", so Tab enters the whole group in one stop rather than passing through item by item. Inside the group, arrow keys move focus instead; on switching, update each item's tabindex and call focus() on the new item.
roving-tabindex.prompt: Implement "Roving Tabindex" for the code mentioned above. [Goal] Tab enters the whole group in one stop, and arrow keys move focus within the group. [When it triggers] The user presses the Tab key. [Implementation] All buttons start with tabindex="-1", except the current one, which is "0"; a keydown listener handles the arrow keys, computes the next button, sets that item's tabindex="0" and the old one's to "-1", and calls focus(); for screen readers use aria-activedescendant. [Key parameters] Initial="-1"; current="0"; arrow keys = ArrowRight/Left (horizontal), Down/Up (vertical); looping. [Pitfalls] Forgetting to update tabindex; some libraries already build this in and conflict; aria-activedescendant pointing at a non-existent element; wrong indices for dynamic elements. [Dependencies] None (plain JavaScript).

keyboard-shortcut.logic: Listen globally for keydown, combine metaKey/ctrlKey/shiftKey with e.key, and when a registered combination matches, preventDefault and run the command. You need cross-platform normalization (Mac's ⌘ corresponds to Ctrl), ignoring triggers inside input fields, and a mapping table maintained to avoid conflicts.
keyboard-shortcut.prompt: Implement "Keyboard Shortcut" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Experienced users can trigger common commands without touching the mouse, the shortcut list is discoverable in the UI, and typing in input fields never triggers them by accident. [When it triggers] A document-level keydown; a match with a registered combination calls preventDefault and runs the command; when focus is inside input, textarea, or contenteditable, everything passes through except global combinations (such as Cmd+K). [Implementation] Maintain a registry whose keys are normalized combination strings (such as 'mod+k', 'shift+/') and whose values are the handler and a description for the help panel. Listen to keydown, lowercase e.key, concatenate metaKey, ctrlKey, altKey, shiftKey in a fixed order to generate a string in the same format, and look it up in the table. For cross-platform, use 'mod' to stand for Command on Mac and Ctrl elsewhere, and render it as ⌘ or Ctrl by platform when displaying. In React, register once in a top-level useEffect and call removeEventListener in the cleanup function. For sequence shortcuts (press g then i), use a buffer with a timeout that clears it. Also build a shortcut help panel opened with ?. [Key parameters] Listen to keydown rather than the deprecated keypress; sequence timeout=1000ms; use e.key to judge characters and e.code to judge physical key positions (things like WASD need code); inside input fields let through only Escape and mod combinations. [Pitfalls] Using e.keyCode breaks everything on non-QWERTY layouts or with a Chinese IME active; also, forgetting to exclude input fields makes the UI jump around while the user is mid-typing. [Dependencies] None; hotkeys-js is optional for complex sequences.

command-palette.logic: Ctrl/Cmd+K summons an overlay with a search box; typing fuzzy-matches against the command list and highlights matches, arrow keys up/down select, and Enter executes. Commands are registered as objects with a title/icon/callback, and libraries such as cmdk and kbar are commonly used for grouping and list virtualization.
command-palette.prompt: Implement "Command Palette" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Pressing Cmd/Ctrl+K floats a search box up in the upper-middle of the page; typing instantly filters the executable commands and navigable pages, up/down keys select, and Enter executes. [When it triggers] Summoned by a global shortcut; filters in real time as input changes, and remote search is debounced first; after Enter executes, it closes automatically and clears the input. [Implementation] Listen to keydown on document; when metaKey or ctrlKey is held and e.key lowercased is k, call preventDefault. Register commands as an array of objects containing id, title, group, and a run callback; filter with subsequence matching, finding each input character's position in the title in order and using it for highlighting. The input uses role="combobox" and the list uses role="listbox", and the highlighted item is indicated via aria-activedescendant. [Key parameters] Shortcut=Cmd+K / Ctrl+K; remote-search debounce=200ms; max items shown per group=8; panel width=640px, distance from top=15vh. [Pitfalls] Missing preventDefault makes the browser jump to its own search bar; also, failing to intercept up/down keys in the input makes the cursor wander inside the text instead of switching options. [Dependencies] cmdk (none if you implement it yourself).

Once activated, focus jumps to the main-content anchor, sparing keyboard and screen-reader users from tabbing through the nav bar item by item.
skip-link.prompt: Implement "Skip Link" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Keyboard and screen-reader users jump to the main content with a single Tab, without passing through the navigation. [When it triggers] Present on page load; appears when Tab is pressed. [Implementation] Put a hidden link at the start of : Skip to main content; sr-only hides it normally (visibility:hidden or clip-path) and shows it on :focus; mark the main content with id="main-content". focus-visible.logic: Use the :focus-visible pseudo-class to show the focus ring only during keyboard navigation and not on mouse clicks, balancing accessibility with visual tidiness. Avoid removing focus styles wholesale with outline:none; instead, define a prominent ring under :focus-visible.
focus-visible.prompt: Implement "Focus Visible" for the code mentioned above. [Goal] Keyboard users see a focus ring, mouse clicks show none, and each mode gets what suits it. [When it triggers] During keyboard navigation (Tab). [Implementation] Set the focus style (outline, box-shadow, etc.) with the :focus-visible pseudo-class; :focus (mouse) can optionally have no style; ensure contrast >= 3:1. [Key parameters] Width=2-4px; color=contrast >= 3:1; radius=match the element; outline-offset=2px. [Pitfalls] Blindly using outline:none leaves keyboard users lost; some older browsers don't support it; libraries setting styles implicitly override the focus ring. scroll-snap.logic: Set scroll-snap-type:x mandatory on the container and scroll-snap-align:start/center on children; after scrolling ends, the view snaps to the nearest alignment point. Carousels or paged scrolling can be done in pure CSS, with scroll-padding handling the snap offset.
scroll-snap.prompt: Implement "Scroll Snap" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] After a horizontal card list or full-screen paged scroll is released, it automatically aligns to the boundary of one item and never stops between two items showing half a card, with a feel close to native paging. [When it triggers] The browser snaps automatically when the user's scroll or swipe ends and inertia decays; calling scrollTo or scrollIntoView also lands on a snap point. [Implementation] Pure CSS is enough: the scroll container gets overflow-x:auto, scroll-snap-type: x mandatory, display:flex, and children get scroll-snap-align: start (use center for centered carousels) with a fixed or percentage width. With a sticky nav, use scroll-padding-top to shift snap points down so content isn't covered; for individual children that need fine-tuning use scroll-margin. To know which item it currently rests on, observe the children with IntersectionObserver at threshold 0.6; the one that hits is the current item, and use it to sync the indicator dots. When clicking a dot to jump, pair it with scroll-behavior: smooth for a smooth transition. For full-screen paging, change the snap axis to y mandatory and set child height to 100dvh. [Key parameters] scroll-snap-type: x mandatory (forced snapping) or proximity (snaps only when close, friendlier for long content); scroll-padding-top = sticky bar height (e.g. 56px); child width 85% so the next card's edge peeks out as a swipe hint. [Pitfalls] Using mandatory on content taller than the viewport means users can never scroll to the middle and get forcibly bounced away; such content must use proximity; also, using snap while also writing your own JS inertia scrolling makes the two systems fight and jump back and forth. [Dependencies] None.

scroll-spy.logic: While the page scrolls, highlight the nav item corresponding to the section currently in view. Use IntersectionObserver to watch each section enter and leave the viewport, or compare each section's offsetTop with scrollTop during scroll, and mark the one that most recently entered the viewport as active.
scroll-spy.prompt: Implement "Scroll Spy" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] As the page scrolls down, the table-of-contents item for the current section highlights automatically so the user always knows which part they're viewing; clicking a TOC item smooth-scrolls there. [When it triggers] The highlight updates whenever a section enters or leaves the viewport; on clicking a TOC item, scroll first and resume automatic following after scrolling ends. [Implementation] Observe all sections with IntersectionObserver, using rootMargin to squeeze the detection zone into a narrow band in the upper part of the viewport, so basically only one section hits at a time; in the callback set its id as active; when several intersect at once, take the one whose boundingClientRect.top is smallest and greater than 0. Click navigation uses scrollIntoView for smooth scrolling, and anchors get scroll-margin-top to clear the fixed header. [Key parameters] rootMargin="-20% 0px -70% 0px"; threshold=0; scroll-margin-top=80px; pause automatic updates after a click=600ms. [Pitfalls] Switching to a scroll event that loops over every offsetTop and compares them drops frames because it computes every frame while scrolling; also, a section shorter than the detection band gets skipped entirely, so its heading never highlights. [Dependencies] None.

sticky-header.logic: Use position:sticky;top:0 so an element pins when scrolled to the edge, and releases only when it exceeds its ancestor container. To detect the "stuck" state (e.g. to add a shadow), place a sentinel element at the top and use IntersectionObserver to see whether it has left the viewport.
sticky-header.prompt: Implement "Sticky Header" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] As the page scrolls down, the header (or table head, or group title) stays pinned at the top while content passes underneath; once stuck, add a shadow or darken the background so the change in layering is visible. [When it triggers] The element enters the stuck state automatically when scrolled to the distance from the container top specified by top; it releases automatically once it scrolls out of its parent's range, which is exactly where the push-out effect of group titles comes from. [Implementation] Give the element position: sticky, top: 0, and a z-index, and make sure the background is opaque, otherwise content underneath shows through. Detect "stuck" with the sentinel technique: place a 1px-tall sentinel before the sticky element and observe it with IntersectionObserver; when the sentinel leaves the viewport the header is stuck, so add an is-stuck class to the header to toggle the shadow; this is far cheaper than recomputing positions in scroll. For multiple stuck layers (page header plus table head), give different layers accumulated top values and separate them with z-index. [Key parameters] top=0 (with a global nav, use the nav height, e.g. 56px); z-index=10 (kept separate from dialogs' 1000); stuck shadow 0 1px 3px rgba(0,0,0,.12), toggle transition 150ms. [Pitfalls] If any ancestor has overflow: hidden/auto, sticky fails completely or works only within that container; this is the most common reason for "why isn't it sticking", so check overflow level by level going up; another pitfall is a parent whose height exactly equals the content height, leaving sticky no room to move, so it looks like it isn't working. [Dependencies] None.

scroll-lock.logic: When an overlay opens, lock background scrolling. The simplest way is overflow:hidden on body, but the vanishing scrollbar shifts the layout, so padding-right must compensate. On iOS you also need position:fixed with top=-scrollY or overscroll-behavior:contain to prevent scroll chaining.
scroll-lock.prompt: Implement "Scroll Lock" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] While an overlay is open the background page doesn't budge at all, and the wheel and fingers act only inside the overlay; after closing, it returns to the original scroll position with no horizontal page jump. [When it triggers] Lock when the overlay mounts or opens; unlock on unmount, close, or route leave; when several overlays are open at once, unlock by reference count. [Implementation] Set overflow: hidden on body, and add padding-right equal to the scrollbar width (innerWidth minus documentElement.clientWidth) to cancel the horizontal jump caused by the scrollbar disappearing. This doesn't work on iOS Safari; you need to record scrollY, set position: fixed on body with a negative top, and on unlock clear the styles and scrollTo back. [Key parameters] Scrollbar compensation = measured value (usually 15px, don't hardcode); scroll containers inside the overlay get overscroll-behavior: contain; unlock only when the lock count drops to 0. [Pitfalls] Writing only overflow: hidden without compensating padding makes the whole page shift right a bit when the overlay opens; on iOS, setting position: fixed without saving scrollY makes the page snap back to the top after closing. [Dependencies] None.

svg.弹层打开时锁住背景滚动 · 不然背后跟着一起动: Lock background scroll · or it moves too

modal-dialog.logic: The native <dialog>'s showModal() brings a focus trap, Esc-to-close, and a ::backdrop scrim for free. A custom implementation needs role="dialog" aria-modal="true", locking focus and background scroll on open, closing on Esc and scrim click, and returning focus to the trigger element after closing.
modal-dialog.prompt: Implement "Modal Dialog" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The dialog floats over a semi-transparent scrim; on open, focus moves into the dialog automatically and Tab cycles only inside it, the background can neither scroll nor be clicked, Esc or a scrim click closes it, and after closing focus returns to the original button. [When it triggers] Opens when the trigger button is clicked; closes on Esc, scrim click, or the close or cancel button; a form dialog with unsaved content asks for confirmation before closing. [Implementation] Prefer the native dialog element: call showModal() to open; the browser provides top-layer stacking, a focus trap, Esc-to-close, and the ::backdrop scrim; call close() to close and listen for the close event to wrap up. If implementing it yourself: render into a portal under body; give the container role="dialog" aria-modal="true" and aria-labelledby pointing at the title; on open record document.activeElement, move focus to the first focusable element in the dialog, intercept Tab in keydown to cycle focus between first and last, and close on Esc; add overflow:hidden to body to lock background scrolling and also add padding-right equal to the scrollbar width to prevent horizontal page shake; after closing, return focus. [Key parameters] Scrim rgba(0,0,0,.5), enter/exit animation 150-200ms; unified z-index layer (e.g. 1000); max height 90dvh with the content area scrolling on its own. [Pitfalls] Adding only a scrim without a focus trap lets focus escape to the page behind on Tab, and screen-reader users never know the dialog exists; also, applying position:fixed directly to body to lock scrolling resets the scroll position to the top on iOS. [Dependencies] None; in React, Radix UI Dialog is optional.

svg.的 showModal() 自带焦点陷阱、Esc 关闭、::backdrop: 's showModal() has a built-in focus trap, Esc close, ::backdrop
svg.压住背景 · 焦点关在里面 · Esc 就能退: Blocks bg · traps focus · Esc exits

drawer.logic: A panel that slides in from one side of the screen; normally it's moved out of the viewport with transform:translateX(-100%), and when opened it's set to 0 and a scrim is shown. It supports closing on scrim click or Esc; on mobile an edge-swipe drag that follows the finger is often added, together with a focus trap and background scroll lock.
drawer.prompt: Implement "Drawer" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A panel slides in from one side of the screen covering part of the page, with a semi-transparent scrim behind it; clicking the scrim or pressing Esc slides it back. [When it triggers] Opens on clicking the entry button; closes on scrim click, Esc, the inner close button, or a route change; a slide animation plays once on open and once on close. [Implementation] The panel is position: fixed spanning one side, defaulting to transform: translateX(-100%) and changing to translateX(0) when opened; animating only transform and opacity uses the compositor layer and triggers no reflow. After closing, finish with conditional rendering; don't leave it in the DOM where it can still be focused by Tab. On open, lock background scroll, install a focus trap, and move focus into the drawer at the same time; on close, return focus to the trigger button. [Key parameters] Width=320px (85vw on mobile); animation=250ms cubic-bezier(0.4,0,0.2,1); scrim=rgba(0,0,0,0.4). [Pitfalls] Using left or margin-left for the displacement reflows continuously during the animation, visibly janky on low-end devices; also, reducing only opacity to 0 after closing leaves the element in the DOM and focusable, so Tab jumps into an invisible drawer. [Dependencies] None.

svg.平时 translateX(-100%) 移出视口 · 不是 display:n: Normally translateX(-100%) off the viewport · not display:none

popover.logic: A floating layer positioned relative to its trigger element, with positioning computed by Floating UI/Popper, which handles flip and shift automatically to avoid overflowing the viewport. The newer native Popover API uses the popovertarget attribute and the top layer, stacking on top naturally and providing light dismiss.
popover.prompt: Implement "Popover" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Clicking or hovering the trigger element pops up a small floating layer next to it that always sticks to the trigger; near the viewport edge it automatically flips to the other side or shifts, so it is never clipped and never covers the trigger. [When it triggers] Opens on click or hover of the trigger; closes on clicking outside the popover, pressing Esc, or the trigger scrolling out of the viewport; position is recomputed on page scroll and window resize. [Implementation] Leave positioning to Floating UI: computePosition(trigger, floating, { placement, middleware: [offset(8), flip(), shift({ padding: 8 }), arrow({ element })] }), then use autoUpdate to follow automatically on scroll and size changes. Render the popover into a portal under body to avoid ancestor overflow clipping and z-index fights. You can also use the native Popover API: add the popover attribute to the floating element and popovertarget to the button; the browser handles top-layer stacking and closing on outside click, and you add the positioning on top. For accessibility, give the trigger aria-expanded and aria-controls; for menu-type popovers move focus into the popover on open, and close with Esc and return focus. [Key parameters] offset=8px (gap between popover and trigger); placement='bottom-start'; shift padding=8px (margin from the viewport edge); hover-type close delay=150ms, leaving time for the mouse to move into the popover. [Pitfalls] Computing the position once by hand with getBoundingClientRect without listening to scroll leaves the popover floating in place when the page scrolls; also, with hover-open, the popover closes immediately when the mouse crosses the gap between button and popover, so add a delay or a transparent safe zone. [Dependencies] @floating-ui/dom (@floating-ui/react for React); the native Popover API works for simple cases.

svg.定位靠 Floating UI 算 · 放不下会自动翻边、贴边: Positioned by Floating UI · flips and shifts when it doesn't fit

tooltip.logic: Show a short description when the trigger element is hovered or focused, linking a role="tooltip" bubble via aria-describedby so screen readers announce it. It must respond to both hover and focus (to be keyboard-reachable), show with a delay to prevent accidental triggers, be dismissible with Esc, and be positioned by Floating UI just like a popover.
tooltip.prompt: Implement "Tooltip" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Hovering the mouse over or keyboard-focusing an icon or button floats a short description beside it that disappears when you move away; near the screen edge it flips to the other side automatically. [When it triggers] Shows after a delay following mouseenter or focus; hides immediately on mouseleave, blur, Esc, and click. [Implementation] Use Floating UI's computePosition with the offset, flip, and shift middleware, which handle spacing, flipping when there isn't enough room, and shifting at the edge respectively. Give the bubble role="tooltip" and a unique id, and have the trigger point to it with aria-describedby so screen readers read it. Render into body via a portal to avoid being clipped by ancestors' overflow: hidden. [Key parameters] Show delay=400ms (drops to 0 during consecutive hovers within the same group); hide delay=100ms; offset=8px; max width=240px. [Pitfalls] Binding only hover and not focus means keyboard users never see it; touch devices have no hover, so don't put critical information only here; using the native title attribute instead gives uncontrollable styling and doesn't work on mobile. [Dependencies] @floating-ui/dom.

accordion.logic: Multiple collapsible sections, where the heading button toggles aria-expanded and shows or hides the corresponding content region. Height animation commonly uses a max-height transition or grid-template-rows:0fr→1fr; the native <details>/<summary> works with zero JS, and in single-open mode expanding one collapses the others.
accordion.prompt: Implement "Accordion" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A group of heading bars; clicking a heading expands its content with a height transition, and clicking again collapses it; in single-open mode expanding one automatically collapses the rest, so long content no longer stretches the page beyond usability. [When it triggers] Clicking a heading button, or pressing Enter/Space on it, toggles the expanded state; the up/down arrow keys move focus between headings. [Implementation] For zero JS use details and summary; giving the same name attribute to a group yields single-open behavior. For fine animation and controlled state, write it yourself: headings use real buttons bound to aria-expanded and aria-controls, and the content region has a matching id plus role="region" and aria-labelledby. For height animation, prefer wrapping the content in an outer display:grid with grid-template-rows: 0fr, transitioning to 1fr on expand (the inner element needs overflow:hidden), so you never need to know the actual height; use a max-height transition only as a fallback. In single-open mode store the id of the currently expanded item in state, and expanding a new one simply overwrites it. [Key parameters] Transition 200-250ms, easing ease-out; allowMultiple controls single vs. multiple open; when collapsed the content is either not rendered or set to visibility:hidden so Tab doesn't wander into an invisible region. [Pitfalls] Using max-height with a value far larger than the real height (e.g. 9999px) makes the first half of the expand animation run idle, looking like a hitch; keep the value close to the real height or switch to the grid-template-rows approach; also, binding onClick to a div, not using a button and not writing aria-expanded makes it unusable for keyboard and screen readers. [Dependencies] None.

tabs.logic: A group of role="tab" buttons controls showing and hiding the corresponding role="tabpanel", with the current item having aria-selected="true". The keyboard moves between tabs with arrow keys (paired with roving tabindex), and tabs and panels are linked to each other with aria-controls/aria-labelledby.
tabs.prompt: Implement "Tabs" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A row of tabs shows only the content of the currently selected one; clicking a tab switches instantly and the current item has a clear underline; arrow keys move between tabs. [When it triggers] Switches on clicking a tab or pressing the left/right arrow keys; Home/End jump to the first/last; the initial selection is the default item or the one specified by a URL parameter. [Implementation] Wrap a row of role="tab" buttons in role="tablist"; each tab gets aria-selected and aria-controls pointing at its role="tabpanel". For the keyboard use roving tabindex: only the selected tab has tabindex="0" and the rest have -1, and focus moves in sync when arrow keys switch. Unselected panels use the hidden attribute so they are genuinely removed from the Tab sequence. The indicator bar is an absolutely positioned element with a transform translate transition. [Key parameters] Switch animation=200ms; indicator height=2px; minimum tab hit area=44x44px; default selection = the first one or the tab parameter in the URL. [Pitfalls] Faking tabs with div plus onClick means they can be neither focused nor used by keyboard; also, unmounting and remounting the panel on every switch wipes out half-filled form content. [Dependencies] None.

carousel.logic: A horizontally arranged slideshow whose switching relies on transform:translateX displacement or scroll-snap scrolling, with indicator dots and left/right arrows. Key points: autoplay should pause on hover/focus, touch dragging should be supported, infinite looping uses cloned first and last frames, and aria-roledescription is added for screen readers.
carousel.prompt: Implement "Carousel" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A group of images or cards switches horizontally, supporting left/right arrows, indicator dots, touch dragging, and arrow keys; during autoplay, mouse hover or keyboard focus pauses it so users aren't switched away mid-read. [When it triggers] Switches on arrow or dot click, drag release, or arrow keys; autoplay advances at a fixed interval and pauses on hover, focus, and when the page is hidden. [Implementation] The most responsive and simplest approach is scroll-snap: the container gets overflow-x:auto plus scroll-snap-type: x mandatory, and children get scroll-snap-align: center, leaving touch dragging and inertia entirely to the browser; arrows call scrollBy or scrollIntoView({behavior:'smooth'}); the current page is synced to the indicator dots by observing children with IntersectionObserver; hide the scrollbar with scrollbar-width: none. When you need infinite looping or complex linkage, switch to embla-carousel. For accessibility, give the container role="region" and aria-roledescription="carousel", make the dots real buttons with aria-current on the current one, and respect prefers-reduced-motion by turning off autoplay when it matches. [Key parameters] Autoplay interval=5000ms (cards with text shouldn't go below 5000ms); switch animation 300ms ease-out; drag-to-switch threshold = 25% of container width or velocity 0.3px/ms. [Pitfalls] Autoplay that neither pauses nor offers a pause button is the most frequently complained-about accessibility issue; also, computing displacement frame by frame in JS to simulate inertia never matches the feel of native scrolling and easily fights with vertical page scrolling. [Dependencies] None; use embla-carousel for complex requirements.

stepper-wizard.logic: Split a long flow into several steps, maintain a currentStep state controlling which section is shown, and provide previous/next navigation. Each step is validated locally before letting the user pass, the step bar at the top marks the current position with aria-current="step", and completed steps allow jumping back.
stepper-wizard.prompt: Implement "Stepper / Wizard" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A long form is split into 3 to 5 steps; the step bar at the top shows which step out of how many and checkmarks for completed ones; errors are flagged on the current step, not dumped all at once at the end. [When it triggers] Clicking Next runs the current step's validation first and advances only if it passes; completed steps on the step bar can be clicked to jump back; only clicking submit on the last step actually sends a request. [Implementation] Use a currentStep state to index a step array, where each step defines a key, title, schema, and component. The whole wizard shares one form data object, and each step reads and writes only its own fields, so content is still there when jumping back. For validation use zod to define a schema per step, and on Next only parse the current step's fields. Sync currentStep to a URL query parameter so a refresh doesn't lose progress. Give the current step bar item aria-current="step", and after switching move focus to the new step's heading. [Key parameters] Steps=3 to 5 (beyond 6 consider splitting into multiple flows); no more than 5 fields per step; disable the button after submit until the response returns. [Pitfalls] Using a separate form instance per step wipes the later data when you go back a step and then forward again; also, validating only at the final submit sends users back to step one without knowing what's wrong. [Dependencies] None (zod can be used for validation).

svg.维护一个 currentStep · 控制显示哪一段: Keep a currentStep · controls which section shows

toast-snackbar.logic: A briefly appearing, non-blocking notice pushed into a queue/stack for rendering, and removed automatically when a timer fires (timing pauses on hover). Placed in an aria-live="polite" or role="status" region so screen readers announce it, it supports stacking multiple messages and manual dismissal.
toast-snackbar.prompt: Implement "Toast / Snackbar" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] After an action, a short notice floats up in a screen corner and disappears by itself after a few seconds without interrupting the current task; when several arrive at once they stack in order instead of overwriting each other. [When it triggers] Called when feedback is needed but no decision is required, such as after success or failure of an action; removed automatically when the set duration elapses, timing pauses on hover or focus and resumes after moving away. [Implementation] Put a fixed-position portal container under body (top right or bottom center) and maintain an array inside it, each entry with a unique id, type, and text. On call, push an entry and use setTimeout to remove it by id when time is up; on hover clearTimeout, and on leave resume with the remaining time. Give the container aria-live="polite" and role="status" (assertive for errors) so screen readers announce it. Animate enter/exit with transform and opacity, show at most 3 at a time, and queue the rest. Toasts with action buttons stay longer, and the buttons must be reachable by Tab. [Key parameters] duration=4000ms (success 3000ms, with button 5000-7000ms, errors may not auto-dismiss); at most 3 visible at once; enter/exit animation 200ms; container 16px from the screen edge. [Pitfalls] Putting information that needs a user decision or must be seen (delete confirmation, payment failure reason) into a toast means it's missed in a blink; such things belong in a dialog or inline error text; also, placing the container inside a frequently re-rendering component rebuilds it on every render, unmounting old toasts and breaking the animation. [Dependencies] None; in React, sonner or react-hot-toast is optional.

inline-edit.logic: Clicking text switches it in place to an input, focused with the original value selected; blur or Enter submits, and Esc cancels and rolls back. Submission is often paired with an optimistic update, and the "display/edit state" swap is implemented either with contenteditable or by toggling between span and input.
inline-edit.prompt: Implement "Inline Edit" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Clicking heading text turns it into an input in place with the original value fully selected; pressing Enter or clicking elsewhere after editing saves it, and pressing Esc restores the original, with no layout jump of the text. [When it triggers] A single click enters edit mode (use double-click in dense tables to avoid accidental triggers); blur or Enter submits; Escape cancels and rolls back. [Implementation] Use an isEditing state to switch between a span and an input; don't use contenteditable, since pasting brings styles and the caret is hard to control. On entering edit mode, call focus() and select() in an effect. Give the input and span the same font, padding, and line-height so the switch doesn't jump. In keydown, Enter submits and Escape restores the value to the snapshot and then exits. Submission uses an optimistic update, and on failure it rolls back and shows a notice. [Key parameters] Entry = single click (double-click for table-like contexts); max input length = per field, e.g. 100 characters for a title; failure notice stays for 3s; give the trigger element tabindex="0". [Pitfalls] On Esc cancel, the blur submit logic fires first and the undo has no effect; set a cancelled flag in keydown and make blur skip. [Dependencies] None.

svg.常配合乐观更新：先改界面，失败再退回来: Optimistic: update UI, revert on fail
svg.点一下就地变输入框并选中原值 · 不跳页: Click → input, value selected · no jump

multi-select.logic: Maintain a set (Set) of selected ids: a plain click selects one, Cmd/Ctrl+click toggles adding/removing, and Shift+click does range selection from the previous anchor. It commonly offers a select-all checkbox with an indeterminate state and a bulk-action bar that appears once items are selected.
multi-select.prompt: Implement "Multi-select" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Users can click to select several items, Shift-click to select a range, and Cmd/Ctrl-click to add or remove a single item; the top shows "N selected" and a bulk-action bar, and the select-all checkbox shows an indeterminate state on partial selection. [When it triggers] Clicking a row or checkbox updates the selection set; Shift+click does range selection from the last anchor; Cmd/Ctrl+click toggles a single item; pressing Esc or clicking blank space clears the selection. [Implementation] Store selected ids in a Set, and keep a separate anchor id for range selection. The click handler has three branches: with shiftKey, take the index range between the current item and the anchor in the current sorted array and add all ids in that range to the set; with metaKey or ctrlKey, toggle the single item and update the anchor; with neither, clear, select only the current item, and set the anchor. indeterminate is a DOM property, not an HTML attribute, so it must be assigned in an effect via a ref: set true when the selected count is greater than 0 and less than the total. After paging or changing filters, decide explicitly whether cross-page selection is kept or cleared. [Key parameters] Use a Set for the selection, not an array (avoids an includes per row); the anchor updates only on non-Shift clicks; range selection takes the range in the current sorted and filtered order; the action bar appears when there is a selection. [Pitfalls] Storing the selection in an array and checking with includes in render makes every click stutter with thousands of rows; also, taking the range in original data order means that after the user sorts, a completely different batch gets selected. [Dependencies] None.

svg.普通点单选 · Cmd 点加减 · Shift 点选一整段: Click: one · Cmd: toggle · Shift: range

combobox-autocomplete.logic: An input that requests or filters candidates as you type, presenting the dropdown as role="listbox"; arrow keys move the highlighted item via aria-activedescendant pointing at it rather than actually moving focus. It needs debounced requests, Enter to select, Esc to collapse, and handling of no-result and loading states.
combobox-autocomplete.prompt: Implement "Combobox / Autocomplete" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] As the user types in the input, matching candidates appear below in real time with the matched part highlighted; up/down keys select and Enter confirms; there are hints for both no results and loading. [When it triggers] Requests or filters after debouncing input changes; on focus it can first show recently used items; the list collapses on selection, Esc, or click outside. [Implementation] Give the input role="combobox" and aria-autocomplete="list", the dropdown container role="listbox", and each item role="option" with a unique id; during keyboard movement focus always stays in the input, with aria-activedescendant pointing at the highlighted item. Remote requests must be debounced and protected against races, honoring only the last response. Position the dropdown with Floating UI's flip and shift middleware. [Key parameters] Debounce=300ms; minimum characters to trigger search=2; at most 8 items shown (scroll beyond); max list height=320px. [Pitfalls] Making candidates Tab-focusable buttons means keyboard users need a dozen presses to get out of the dropdown; also, out-of-order responses can show the results for the first letter after two letters have been typed. [Dependencies] @floating-ui/dom (none needed for a purely static list).

svg.role=\"listbox\" + aria-activedescendant: role="listbox" + aria-activedescendant · arrows move the highlight

affordance.logic: Visual cues signal that an element is interactive and how to interact with it, such as a button's raised shadow, cursor:pointer, the grab cursor on a draggable area, and an input's border. Good affordances let users know "clickable/draggable" without explanation, and hover and active states are important feedback signals.
affordance.prompt: Implement "Affordance" for the code mentioned above. [Goal] Users see at a glance that an element is interactive and how; the mouse turns into a hand or grab pointer, and clicks give feedback. [When it triggers] Set at page load, shown when the mouse enters. [Implementation] cursor:pointer (clickable), cursor:grab (draggable), cursor:move (movable), cursor:not-allowed (disabled); hover changes the style (brightness +10-20%); active shows the press (reduced depth); buttons use box-shadow to look raised; draggable areas use a dashed border. [Key parameters] hover change = brightness +10-20%; active change = reduced depth; cursor = pointer/grab/move/not-allowed. [Pitfalls] A global cursor:pointer makes all text look clickable; forgetting not-allowed on disabled; an exaggerated active state is tiring; cursor has no effect on mobile devices. [Dependencies] None (pure CSS).

empty-state.logic: When a list or search has no data, don't leave a blank screen; render a placeholder view with an illustration, explanatory copy, and a call to action (CTA). Distinguish the semantics of "first-time no data (guide to create)", "search with no results (suggest changing terms)", and "load error", rather than a single generic "No data".
empty-state.prompt: Implement "Empty State" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When there is no data, don't show a blank page but a centered placeholder: one sentence explaining why it's empty and one clear next-step button, so users know what to do. [When it triggers] Render when the request succeeds but the list length is 0; the check must come after loading ends: show a skeleton screen while loading and an error state on failure. [Implementation] Split the UI state into four branches (loading, error, empty, has data) and dispatch on them; don't lump everything under data.length. Then distinguish empty-state semantics: first-time no data (explain the value plus a primary "Create your first..." button), search or filter with no results (echo the keyword with a "Clear filters" button), and no permission (explain why and whom to ask). The structure is an illustration or icon plus a one-line title, one or two lines of description, and one primary CTA, vertically centered in the content area. Use inline SVG for the illustration and change its colors in sync in dark mode. Give the container role="status" so screen readers announce it. [Key parameters] Illustration 96px; title 16-18px, description 14px in the secondary text color; copy block max width 320px, centered; only one primary button, with secondary actions as text links. [Pitfalls] Using one generic "No data" for every scenario leaves users with no results unable to tell it's a keyword problem or find the way to clear filters; also, drawing a failed request as an empty state leaves users waiting for a list that never comes. [Dependencies] None.

svg.三种空是三件事 · 文案和引导都不一样: Three empties · different copy and CTA

loading-state.logic: Give feedback during asynchronous requests so the UI doesn't look frozen: a spinner or progress bar for lightweight cases and placeholder skeletons for lists. Manage it with an idle/loading/success/error state machine, disable a button once it enters loading after a click to prevent duplicate submissions, and add aria-busy="true" to the container so screen readers know.
loading-state.prompt: Implement "Loading State" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Whenever an asynchronous operation occurs, the UI gives immediate feedback: the button shows a spinner and is disabled, lists show placeholders, and failures show a retryable error. [When it triggers] Enter loading the instant the request is sent; success, failure, and timeout each transition to the corresponding state; requests that return very quickly don't flash an animation. [Implementation] Use an explicit state machine instead of scattered booleans: status takes idle/loading/success/error, with data and error fields, and the UI renders by branching on status. For an inline spinner in a button, keep the width unchanged (replace the text with the spinner rather than removing it), and set disabled and aria-busy="true". Use skeleton screens for the first list load, a small spinner at the bottom when paging, and reduce opacity instead of clearing the whole block on partial refresh. [Key parameters] Spinner display delay=200ms (don't show it if the response is faster); minimum display time=500ms; request timeout=10s; error notice stays until the user acts. [Pitfalls] A single global loading boolean means when two requests run concurrently, whichever returns first turns the overlay off; also, unmounting the whole block while loading loses scroll position and already-typed input. [Dependencies] None.

cubic-bezier.logic: cubic-bezier(x1,y1,x2,y2) defines two control points P1 and P2 (P0 and P3 are fixed at (0,0) and (1,1)); the horizontal axis is normalized time and the vertical axis is progress. The control points' y may exceed 1 or fall below 0, producing overshoot effects such as bounce-back and anticipation (a wind-up dip). The browser uses it to map time from 0 to 1 onto a nonlinear rate of property change.
cubic-bezier.prompt: Implement "Cubic Bézier Curve" for the code mentioned above. [Goal] The distribution of animation speed can be tuned precisely, producing a crisp finish, a slight bounce-back, or an anticipation dip before starting, instead of being limited to the few system keywords. [When it triggers] Anywhere you write transition-timing-function or animation-timing-function, or the easing field of element.animate. [Implementation] Write it as cubic-bezier(x1,y1,x2,y2): P0(0,0) and P3(1,1) are fixed and you supply only the two middle control points; the horizontal axis is normalized time and the vertical axis is progress. x must lie between 0 and 1, otherwise the whole declaration is invalid; y may go out of range to produce an effect that overshoots the endpoint and comes back. Common starting points: crisp finish cubic-bezier(0.16,1,0.3,1), standard two-way cubic-bezier(0.65,0,0.35,1), bounce-back cubic-bezier(0.34,1.56,0.64,1), reverse anticipation first cubic-bezier(0.36,-0.4,0.6,1). Once tuned, save it as a CSS variable for reuse. [Key parameters] x1/x2 range = 0-1 (out of range invalidates the whole thing); how far y exceeds 1 = bounce strength, 1.56 overshoots by about 10%; matching duration = 300-500ms. [Pitfalls] Pairing a bounce curve with properties that have no notion of position, like opacity or color, makes the out-of-range intermediate values get clamped, which looks like a flash; use bounce only on transform. [Dependencies] None.

In UI, entering elements often use ease-out (fast in, slow to a stop) and exiting ones use ease-in, so the motion matches physical intuition. steps-easing.logic: steps(n, jump-term) slices the 0→1 progress into n discrete steps with no interpolation in between. It is commonly used for frame-by-frame sprite sheet playback (each frame jumps the background position by one cell). jump-start/jump-end/jump-both/jump-none decide whether the first and last steps are held. Compared with continuous easing, it produces a snapping, stop-motion, one-cell-at-a-time effect.

Sample a spring equation at a few dozen time steps and paste the values in, and you get realistic bounce/damping in pure CSS; values above 1 produce overshoot. It is the alternative when cubic-bezier cannot express multiple oscillations.

Each sample point is the output value at that moment of progress, and adjacent points are linearly interpolated. spring-physics.logic: Instead of a fixed duration, it simulates a virtual spring using Hooke's law F=-kx plus a damping force, integrating each frame's next position from the current displacement and velocity. Three parameters, stiffness, damping and mass, determine the feel, and the animation ends automatically once it falls below a rest threshold. Framer Motion and react-spring use this in place of the duration + easing approach.
spring-physics.prompt: Implement "Spring Physics" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The element no longer runs mechanically for a fixed duration; it is pulled toward the target as if it had weight, overshoots slightly at the end and then settles, and changing the target midway continues smoothly. [When it triggers] Starts on a state change: drag release, toggle switch, card expansion; if the target changes before the animation finishes, continue from the current velocity instead of restarting. [Implementation] In React, use Framer Motion's transition: { type: 'spring', stiffness, damping, mass } directly, or react-spring's useSpring, replacing the old duration plus easing entirely. To hand-roll it, integrate numerically in rAF: each frame compute a = (-stiffness * (x - target) - damping * v) / mass, then v += a * dt and x += v * dt, and write x into transform; once both the displacement error and velocity stay below the threshold for several consecutive frames, finish and snap the value to the target. Take dt as the difference between two frame timestamps, clamped to 33ms. [Key parameters] stiffness=300 (200–400 is typical for UI, higher is faster); damping=30 (25–40 gives basically no overshoot); mass=1; restDelta=0.01. [Pitfalls] If you also give a spring a duration, most libraries fall back to a tween and all the elasticity is lost; a damping below 10 looks fun, but a button that wobbles three times makes users think it is frozen; hard-coding dt to 16ms in rAF makes the spring run slow or even diverge when frames drop. [Dependencies] framer-motion or react-spring (none if you hand-roll the integration).

A damping ratio of about 1 is critical damping (no overshoot and the fastest settling); below 1 is underdamped and oscillates back and forth; above 1 is overdamped and sluggish with no bounce. Tuning UI feel is a matter of balancing damping against stiffness.

Framer Motion takes a plain number, 1-100. [Key parameters] damping=10 (settles quickly); damping=2-5 (3-5 bounces, lively); damping>20 (sluggish). momentum-scroll.logic: When the finger lifts, record the instantaneous release velocity, then each frame decay that velocity by a friction coefficient (v*=friction) while continuing to move until it drops below a threshold and stops, simulating a real glide. interpolation.logic: Computes an intermediate value between a start and end value from progress t (0~1); the most basic form is linear interpolation lerp = a + (b-a)*t. Easing is really just bending the time t through an easing function first, then feeding it to lerp. Colors, transform matrices and paths each have their own interpolation methods (e.g. colors must be interpolated in a specific color space).

Common web approximations: stack semi-transparent afterimage layers along the velocity direction, or use SVG feGaussianBlur / CSS blur() for a directional blur along the motion axis. The higher the speed, the stronger the blur, which hides the stepping caused by low frame rates and strengthens the sense of speed. When driven by properties, filter can change in real time with velocity.

flip-technique.logic: First-Last-Invert-Play: record the position and size before the change (First) and after it (Last), use transform to invert the element back to its original position so it looks like nothing moved (Invert), then clear the transform and play the animation (Play). Because only transform/opacity are animated throughout, it turns an expensive layout change into a cheap compositor animation. React layout animations and View Transitions use this idea under the hood.
flip-technique.prompt: Apply "FLIP Technique" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] When a list is reordered, a card expands or an element changes container, it glides smoothly from the old position to the new one instead of jumping there instantly. [When it triggers] Measure once before and once after any DOM operation that changes layout: sorting, filtering, adding/removing items, switching between grid and list views. [Implementation] Four steps. First: before the change, call getBoundingClientRect() on every participating element and store top/left/width/height. Last: change the DOM or state as usual so the layout lands in its new position, then measure again. Invert: compute dx/dy and the scale ratios, and immediately write transform: translate(dx,dy) scale(sx,sy) to push the element back to its original position; at this moment nothing has visually moved. Play: on the next frame (inside requestAnimationFrame) add transition: transform 300ms and clear the transform, and the element slides over by itself. In React, do the measuring and Invert in useLayoutEffect so the user never sees the intermediate state. [Key parameters] duration=300ms; easing=cubic-bezier(0.2,0,0,1); stagger=20ms/item (don't stagger beyond 20 items). [Pitfalls] If you clear the transform right after Invert without waiting a frame, the browser coalesces the two writes, the element appears directly at the end position and the animation never happens; if an element has a leftover transform before measuring, clear it first, otherwise the positions drift further and further off. [Dependencies] None (in React you can also use framer-motion's layout prop).

will-change.logic: Tells the browser in advance that a property (such as transform or opacity) is about to change frequently, so it can promote the element to its own compositor layer and prepare optimizations ahead of time. Add it before the animation starts and remove it after it ends; leaving it on many elements permanently eats memory and slows the page. It is a hint, not a guarantee, and overuse backfires.
will-change.prompt: Apply "will-change" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] The animation is smooth from its very first frame, with no blurry or jittery first few frames and no momentary blur on text. [When it triggers] Add it a short time before the animation starts (mouseenter, a panel about to expand, an element just entering the viewport), and remove it immediately after the animation ends (transitionend or animationend); never leave it on permanently. [Implementation] Declare only the property that actually moves: will-change: transform, or will-change: transform, opacity. Managing the lifecycle in JS is the most reliable: set el.style.willChange = 'transform' when entering the interactive state, and set it back to 'auto' in the end callback. For pure CSS, attach it to the parent's hover instead of the element itself, e.g. .card:hover .inner { will-change: transform }, so no compositor layer is held while idle. Keep the number of elements hinted at the same time in the single digits. [Key parameters] Lead time=100–200ms; simultaneously hinted elements ≤10; list only 1–2 properties, never write will-change: all. [Pitfalls] Putting a permanent will-change on every item of a long list forces hundreds of compositor layers into existence, memory balloons and scrolling gets worse than without it; writing all makes the browser give up optimizing; promoting a layer can change font anti-aliasing, so adding it to static text makes the glyphs look blurry. compositor-layer.logic: The browser paints certain elements into their own bitmap texture and hands it to the GPU; when animating, the compositor thread only needs to translate/scale/blend those textures, bypassing the main thread's layout and paint. transform and opacity changes take this path, so animations stay smooth even when the main thread is blocked. Layers are created by triggers such as will-change, 3D transforms and video.
compositor-layer.prompt: Apply "Compositor Layer" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Hand the animation to the GPU compositor thread so the picture stays smooth even while the main thread is busy running JS, instead of freezing on a long task. [When it triggers] Promote the layer before the animation starts and drop it after it ends; promote elements like dragged cards, fixed headers and fullscreen overlays when they enter the interactive state. [Implementation] Animate only transform and opacity; changes to these properties need no re-layout or repaint and can be completed directly on the compositor thread. When you need to promote a layer in advance, add will-change: transform (or the old transform: translateZ(0)) before the animation starts, and remove will-change in transitionend / animationend rather than hard-coding it in the stylesheet. Use the DevTools Rendering panel's Layer borders, or the Layers panel, to confirm the layers were actually created and the count hasn't run away. [Key parameters] Keep same-screen layers under 20; memory per layer ≈ width × height × 4 bytes (a fullscreen layer is about 8MB); will-change duration = only the few hundred milliseconds around the interaction. [Pitfalls] Writing will-change: transform on every list item exhausts memory and makes things worse, and on low-end devices whole areas go blank; also, promoting a layer but still animating width or left triggers reflow anyway, so the layer was wasted. [Dependencies] None.

compositor-only-properties.logic: Only transform and opacity (and some filters) can be handled on the compositor thread alone without triggering layout and paint, making them the cheapest properties to animate. Using translate instead of top/left and scale instead of width/height keeps 60fps running steadily on the GPU. Animating left, height, box-shadow and the like causes reflow and repaint every frame and drops frames easily.
compositor-only-properties.prompt: Apply "Compositor-Only Properties" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Animations run steadily at 60fps, with no dropped frames during scrolling and interaction, and no stutter or blur on low-end devices. [When it triggers] Whenever you write any animation that changes frame by frame, choose properties under this constraint: transitions, @keyframes, rAF loops and drag-following all count. [Implementation] Narrow animated properties down to transform and opacity: use translate3d(x,y,0) instead of top/left/margin for movement; scale() instead of width/height/font-size for resizing; opacity together with visibility instead of toggling display directly; scaleX with transform-origin: left instead of animating width for progress bars. For shadow and background color changes, overlay an absolutely positioned pseudo-element and animate only its opacity. After the change, record a trace in the DevTools Performance panel and confirm that no frame shows Layout or Paint bars, only compositing. [Key parameters] Per-frame budget ≤16.7ms (60Hz); main-thread script ≤8ms/frame; keep the number of compositor layers within a few dozen. [Pitfalls] Assuming transform always goes through the compositor: filter: blur() still repaints every frame, and an ancestor's overflow: hidden with rounded corners can drag it back to the main thread; sweeping shine effects done with background-position are paint-level and drop frames once the element is large, so animate a gradient layer's transform instead. reflow-repaint.logic: Changing geometric properties (width/height, position, font) triggers a reflow (relayout): the browser recomputes the layout of every affected element. Changing only appearance such as color or background triggers a repaint. Both run on the main thread, are expensive and cascade. Animations should avoid them as much as possible and animate only transform/opacity to stay on the compositor path.
reflow-repaint.prompt: Apply "Reflow & Repaint" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Interactions and animations no longer drop frames because of repeatedly measuring sizes and changing layout; scrolling and dragging follow the pointer, and operations on long lists stop stuttering. [When it triggers] Every time you read offsetTop, offsetWidth, getBoundingClientRect, scrollTop or getComputedStyle, or write width/height, position, font or display; alternating reads and writes inside a loop is especially deadly. [Implementation] Animate only transform and opacity, not left/top/width/height. When you must change layout, separate reads from writes: read all the geometry values you need in one pass into an array, then write them all back together, avoiding a read right after a write that forces a synchronous layout. Insert nodes in bulk by mounting a DocumentFragment once. Don't measure by hand what ResizeObserver or IntersectionObserver can give you; if you must measure, do it at the start of a requestAnimationFrame callback. [Key parameters] Per-frame budget=16.7ms (60Hz), with a Layout phase target of <4ms; in the Performance panel, at most 1 purple Layout block per frame. [Pitfalls] Setting el.style.height in a loop and immediately reading offsetHeight forces a synchronous layout on every iteration, 1000 items means 1000 reflows; this is layout thrashing, fixed by reading first and writing after. [Dependencies] None.

request-animation-frame.logic: Registers a callback that runs just before the browser's next repaint, synchronized with the display refresh (about every 16.7ms); update animation state inside it and call itself recursively to form a frame loop. The callback receives a high-resolution timestamp, which you use to compute displacement from the real elapsed time (delta), so speed doesn't distort when frames drop. It pauses automatically in background tabs, making it more power-efficient and accurate than setInterval.
request-animation-frame.prompt: Implement "requestAnimationFrame" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The picture updates continuously at the display's refresh rate, with no frame skipping or tearing, and stops automatically when the page goes to the background so it doesn't burn power. [When it triggers] Start when per-frame computation is needed: JS numeric tweens, drag-following, canvas drawing, scroll-position throttling; cancel when the goal is reached or the component unmounts. [Implementation] Write a loop(now): first compute delta = now - last (on the first frame, initialize last to now), advance state by delta rather than by frame count, then write styles or redraw, and at the end recurse with id = requestAnimationFrame(loop); start with a single requestAnimationFrame(loop) call and stop with cancelAnimationFrame(id). In React, keep id and last in useRef and cancel in the useEffect cleanup function. For scroll throttling, use a boolean ticking flag that is reset to false inside the rAF callback, guaranteeing only one computation per frame. [Key parameters] Expected frame interval=16.7ms (60Hz); delta cap=50ms (clamp anything larger to 50ms to prevent a jump the moment the tab returns to the foreground); throttle granularity=once per frame. [Pitfalls] Forgetting cancelAnimationFrame, so the loop keeps running after unmount and manipulates removed nodes; hard-coding delta to 16.7ms, which makes the animation twice as fast on a 120Hz screen; reading getBoundingClientRect in the callback and writing styles right after, which also triggers a forced synchronous layout. [Dependencies] None.

frame-budget.logic: To sustain 60fps, each frame from input to paint must complete in about 16.7ms (about 8.3ms on a 120Hz screen), and part of that is reserved for browser compositing, leaving roughly 10ms for script. Once JS + style + layout + paint overrun within a single frame, the frame is dropped. Optimization means slicing long tasks and moving work off the main thread to stay within this budget.
frame-budget.prompt: Apply "Frame Budget" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Stay within each frame's time budget to keep the frame rate smooth: about 16.7ms/frame at 60fps, about 8.3ms/frame at 120fps. Overrunning drops the frame immediately and users perceive it as stutter. [When it triggers] Long tasks and heavy layout/paint recomputation need to be sliced. [Implementation] Schedule precisely with requestAnimationFrame; work that takes more than 10ms (about 10ms is available to JS, and browser compositing takes about 6ms) must be split across multiple frames, using MessageChannel/setTimeout to schedule a task queue, or offloading to a background thread with a Web Worker. Virtualizing long lists and debouncing resize are also ways to stay within budget. [Key parameters] 60fps=16.7ms/frame, 120fps=8.3ms/frame, script time available ~10ms, long-task threshold 50ms (must be sliced). [Pitfalls] Chrome DevTools' CPU throttling differs a lot from real hardware, and DevTools itself also eats budget (close the Performance tab and measure again); if a single frame can't finish the computation, it absolutely must be split across frames. [Dependencies] None.

jank.logic: An unstable frame rate: some frames miss their deadline because the main thread is busy, so the picture stalls or jumps. Common causes are long tasks, layout thrashing and animating non-compositor properties. Use the DevTools Performance panel to look at red long tasks and dropped-frame markers to locate it; the goal is to keep every frame steadily within the frame budget.
jank.prompt: Apply "Jank" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Scrolling, animation and input response stay smooth and steady throughout, with no sudden stalls or jumps and a consistent feel. [When it triggers] During scrolling, while animations play, and during first-screen rendering and large batch data rendering; when a user says it "hitches", troubleshoot with this routine. [Implementation] Measure first, then change: record an interaction in the DevTools Performance panel, look at the dropped-frame markers on the Frames track and the long tasks over 50ms on the Main track, and locate the specific function before touching anything. Three common kinds of fix: slice long tasks (split big loops into batches with setTimeout or requestIdleCallback, move pure computation into a Web Worker); keep animations to transform and opacity only; switch long lists to virtual scrolling that renders only the visible area. In scroll and pointermove callbacks only store values, and put the actual DOM writes into requestAnimationFrame; add passive:true to listeners. [Key parameters] Frame budget=16.7ms (60Hz) or 8.3ms (120Hz); long-task threshold=50ms (slice anything longer); per-frame JS target <8ms. [Pitfalls] Sprinkling will-change and debounce everywhere on a hunch without measuring, when the real culprit is often a single synchronous huge JSON parse or a forced synchronous layout; also drawing conclusions from testing only on a 60Hz screen, where high-refresh screens have only half the budget. [Dependencies] None.

hardware-acceleration.logic: Historically, transform:translateZ(0) or translate3d(0,0,0) was used to trick the browser into treating an element as 3D content and forcibly promoting it to a GPU compositor layer for smoothness (the so-called 3D hack). Today the semantically clear will-change:transform is preferred. Overuse creates too many layers and balloons GPU memory, which slows things down instead.
hardware-acceleration.prompt: Apply "Hardware Acceleration Hack" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Promote to a GPU compositor layer to speed up animation, but overuse blows up GPU memory and slows things down instead. [Implementation] Historically transform:translateZ(0) or translate3d() was used; the modern recommendation is will-change:transform or contain:layout, which are semantically clear; transform/opacity animations are already compositor-friendly and need no hack. backface-visibility.logic: Controls whether an element's back face is shown when it is rotated to face away from the screen; with hidden, it becomes invisible after rotating past 90°. For a card-flip effect, stack the front and back faces, set backface-visibility:hidden on each, and when rotating with rotateY only the face pointing forward shows. The old syntax also had the side effect of triggering a compositor layer.
