web-animations-api.logic: Use element.animate(keyframes, options) to create an animation directly in JS, passing a keyframe array and options such as duration/easing/fill, and get back an Animation object you can control with play/pause/reverse/finished. It reuses the browser's native compositor engine, so performance matches CSS animation while being programmable and awaitable via finished. It suits dynamically generated or finely controlled scenarios.
web-animations-api.prompt: Implement "Web Animations API" (WAAPI) at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The animation's keyframes are computed by JS at runtime and can be precisely paused, reversed and seeked, with performance identical to CSS animation, and the code can wait for it to finish before doing the next step. [When it triggers] When keyframe values are only known at runtime (FLIP displacement, randomized entrance offsets), when you need to control playback midway, or when logic must run after the animation ends. [Implementation] Call el.animate(keyframes array, options): each item in the keyframes array is a style object, for example from { transform: 'translateY(20px)', opacity: 0 } to { transform: 'none', opacity: 1 }; in options give duration, easing, fill and iterations. It returns an Animation object with play, pause, reverse, cancel and finish methods; currentTime can be assigned directly to make a scrubbing handle, playbackRate changes speed, and await anim.finished waits for it to complete. Before triggering again, use el.getAnimations() to get all animations on that element and cancel them one by one. [Key parameters] duration=300ms (micro-interactions 150–250ms, page-level 300–400ms); easing='cubic-bezier(0.2,0,0,1)'; fill='both'; iterations=1 or Infinity. [Pitfalls] Calling animate again without cancelling the old animation makes several animations compete for the same property, so the element flashes back or stops at odd positions; fill defaults to 'none', so after playing, the property immediately snaps back to its original value, which is often mistaken for the animation not working. transform-origin.logic: Defines the reference point of a transform: rotation turns around it and scaling shrinks toward it; the default is the element center (50% 50%). Setting it to top left makes the element rotate around its top-left corner, opening and closing like a door. It doesn't change the element's own layout, only how the transform is applied, and with 3D transforms you can also set a third-dimension z value.
transform-origin.prompt: Apply "Transform Origin" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Rotation and scaling happen around the right point: dropdown menus expand from the corner of the trigger button, toggles flip around their axis, a needle turns around the dial's center, instead of the whole block swelling from the middle. [When it triggers] Specify it explicitly anywhere you write rotate, scale or skew; when the popup direction or element size changes, re-check that the origin is still right. [Implementation] Use transform-origin to set the reference point; values can be keywords (top left, bottom center), percentages (relative to the element's own box) or lengths (measured from the top-left corner), and it only affects how the transform is applied, not the element's own layout. [Key parameters] Default=50% 50% (element center); common for menu expansion=top left; matching scale start=0.95; transform-box=fill-box (required for SVG). perspective.logic: Sets the distance from the viewer to the z=0 plane for 3D transforms: the smaller the value, the more exaggerated the perspective (near-large, far-small becomes more pronounced); the larger, the closer to orthographic with no perspective. Put it on the parent element (the perspective property) so all children share one vanishing point, or write transform:perspective() into a child's own transform to act on it alone. Without it, rotateY and the like just look flattened and lack depth.
perspective.prompt: Implement "Perspective" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Define the viewer position for 3D transforms to create a near-large, far-small depth effect; smaller values exaggerate the perspective. [When it triggers] Must be paired with 3D transforms such as rotateY/X. [Implementation] perspective:1000px on the parent element so all children share a vanishing point; or on the child's own transform:perspective(1000px) rotateY(45deg); the smaller the distance, the stronger the perspective. [Key parameters] perspective:1000px (standard); perspective:500px (exaggerated); perspective-origin:50% 50%. [Pitfalls] Forgetting perspective leaves 3D with no depth; too large a value approaches orthographic; perspective-origin has no effect on the child element; without preserve-3d, layering breaks. [Dependencies] None.

transform-3d.logic: Translation and rotation along the X/Y/Z axes: translateZ moves an element toward or away from the viewer, and rotateX/rotateY flip it around the horizontal or vertical axis for a 3D page-turn. It needs the parent's perspective to have depth, and these transforms automatically trigger a GPU compositor layer. It is the basis of card flips, cubes and depth parallax.
transform-3d.prompt: Implement "3D Transform" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Elements have real depth: a card can flip along an axis to reveal its back, layers are pulled apart front to back, and when rotating the nearer side gets bigger and the farther side smaller. [When it triggers] Flip on hover or click, enter in 3D when the element scrolls into the viewport, tilt in real time following the pointer. [Implementation] Write perspective: 800px on the parent container to set the viewpoint, and to let children keep their own 3D space give them transform-style: preserve-3d. The standard card flip: outer wrapper with preserve-3d, front and back faces absolutely positioned on top of each other, the back with transform: rotateY(180deg), both faces with backface-visibility: hidden, and on the wrapper's hover rotateY(180deg) as a whole with a transition. Use translateZ for depth: positive values move toward the viewer, negative away. Multiple transforms go in one transform property and apply from right to left; generally write translate before rotate. [Key parameters] perspective=800px (smaller means stronger perspective; use 800–1200px for cards); rotateX/rotateY=±12deg (subtle hover tilt) or 180deg (flip); translateZ=20px; duration=400ms. matrix-transform.logic: matrix(a,b,c,d,e,f) and matrix3d(16 values) are the underlying unified representation of all translate/scale/rotate/skew: every named transform is compiled by the browser into a matrix, and multiple transforms are multiplied together. Reading transform via getComputedStyle gives you the matrix form. Writing matrices by hand enables compound affine transforms, such as skews, that the named functions can't cover.

[Implementation] matrix(a,b,c,d,e,f) represents a 2D affine transform and matrix3d(16 values) a 3D one. Multiple transforms are merged automatically by matrix multiplication. Hand-written matrices can do transforms the named functions can't cover (such as skew plus scale), but math errors are easy to make. Parameters are in column-major order (not row-major), and getComputedStyle returns the final composite matrix, not the original values. [Pitfalls] Parameter order is column-major, not row-major (easy to hand-write wrong); getComputedStyle returns the final matrix rather than the original declaration (you can't reverse out the rotate angle); math errors in a hand-written matrix cause "distortion". [Dependencies] None.

preserve-3d.logic: transform-style:preserve-3d makes child elements stay in the same 3D space established by the parent, with each child's z depth genuinely taking part in the layout; the default flat flattens children and projects them onto the parent's plane. When building cubes and polyhedra you must set preserve-3d on the container, otherwise the faces can't interleave front to back correctly in three dimensions.

[Implementation] Interpolate the d attribute of the two SVG paths vertex by vertex; the start and end paths must have exactly the same number of vertices, otherwise use a library such as flubber to align the points. Simple shapes (circle to square) can be approximated with clip-path or border-radius. GSAP MorphSVGPlugin can handle point-count differences automatically. [Key parameters] Duration 300-600ms, easing=easeInOut, point alignment (automatic in flubber), consistent path direction (to avoid reverse rotation). scroll-triggered-animation.logic: Use IntersectionObserver to watch an element intersecting the viewport, and in the callback add a class that triggers the animation or call GSAP/AOS; threshold and rootMargin control the trigger point. Unlike scroll-driven animation, it fires once and plays the whole animation, rather than following scroll progress frame by frame.

[Goal] When a section scrolls into the viewport it automatically plays an entrance animation, ends in its final state, and doesn't replay when scrolling back. [When it triggers] Fires once at the moment the element's intersection ratio with the viewport reaches the threshold; only reset when it leaves the viewport if you need it to replay back and forth. [Implementation] Use IntersectionObserver: pass { threshold: 0.2, rootMargin: '0px 0px -10% 0px' } when constructing it; in the callback, if entry.isIntersecting is true, add an in-view class to the element and then unobserve it; in CSS, write the final state under .in-view with a transition. To replay repeatedly, replace the unobserve with an else branch that removes the class. Only reach for GSAP ScrollTrigger when you need scroll pinning with multi-step sequences; a plain entrance doesn't need a library. [Key parameters] threshold=0.2 (fires when 20% is visible); rootMargin bottom -10% (the element must go up a bit more before triggering, avoiding playing right at the edge); transition duration=500ms. [Pitfalls] Switching to calling getBoundingClientRect in a scroll event forces synchronous layout every frame, which is both janky and power-hungry; also, if the initial state is opacity:0 and the script errors out, the whole block is invisible forever, so provide a fallback style for failure. view-transitions-api.logic: Call document.startViewTransition(callback): the browser first screenshots the old view, runs the callback to update the DOM, then screenshots the new view, and automatically generates ::view-transition-old/new pseudo-elements for a default cross-fade. You can customize the transition by overriding those pseudo-elements' keyframes in CSS; for MPAs, use @view-transition{navigation:auto} to enable cross-document transitions.
view-transitions-api.prompt: Implement "View Transitions API" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When switching views, the old and new pictures cross-fade automatically, and designated elements also grow smoothly from their old position to the new one, with no white flash or hard cut. [When it triggers] Any update that replaces a large chunk of DOM: route changes, list to detail, filter changes, theme switching. [Implementation] Wrap the DOM-changing code entirely in document.startViewTransition(() => { update DOM }); in React use flushSync to make sure the callback completes synchronously. To make an element morph through the transition, give the same element the same view-transition-name in the old and new views; the name must be unique across the whole page. Override the animation with ::view-transition-old(root) and ::view-transition-new(root) for duration and curve. For multi-page sites, write @view-transition { navigation: auto } in CSS to enable cross-document transitions. Feature-detect before calling: if startViewTransition doesn't exist, change the DOM directly and return. [Key parameters] duration=300ms (same-page 200–300ms, cross-document 400ms); easing=ease-out; view-transition-name unique across the page. [Pitfalls] Giving every list item the same name: duplicate names make the whole transition get skipped; firing an async request in the callback without returning the Promise means the DOM hasn't changed when the screenshot is taken, so effectively no transition; during the transition the picture is a frozen screenshot, so don't expect to click during those few hundred milliseconds. [Dependencies] None.

ripple-effect.logic: At the click coordinates, generate an absolutely positioned circular span centered on that point, animate it from transform:scale(0) up to cover the whole container while fading opacity, and let the parent's overflow:hidden clip the overflow. Use the pointer event's offsetX/offsetY to place the center; it is the signature of Material touch feedback.

[Goal] When a button is pressed, a translucent ripple spreads out from the touch point, fills the button and fades away, giving tactile feedback that the press registered. [When it triggers] Create it at the instant of pointerdown, not on click, otherwise the feedback lags half a beat; remove the node as soon as the animation ends. [Implementation] Set the container to position:relative and overflow:hidden. In the pointerdown callback, use getBoundingClientRect() to compute the touch point's coordinates relative to the container (e.clientX minus rect.left), create a new span absolutely positioned at that point, with width and height set to a diameter that covers the farthest corner, style it with border-radius:50% and transform:translate(-50%,-50%) scale(0), then use span.animate() to animate to scale(1) with opacity from 0.35 to 0, and call span.remove() in its finished callback to clean up. [Key parameters] duration=500~600ms; starting opacity=0.35 (use translucent white on dark backgrounds); diameter=2x the maximum distance from the touch point to the four corners; easing=cubic-bezier(0,0,0.2,1). [Pitfalls] Forgetting overflow:hidden lets the ripple overflow as a big circle covering its surroundings; not cleaning up old spans on rapid clicks piles up DOM nodes; also, expecting the span's own rounding to match the button's corners, when only the parent's overflow:hidden clips cleanly. count-up.logic: Uses requestAnimationFrame to interpolate from a start value to the target over a set duration with an easing curve, writing Math.round of the current value into the element's text every frame; large numbers are then formatted with thousands separators. Typically done with countup.js or a hand-rolled tween, for animated KPI numbers on dashboards.
count-up.prompt: Implement "Count-Up" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A KPI number rolls quickly from 0 to its final value and decelerates to a stop at the end, drawing the eye to that figure. [When it triggers] Run once when the number first scrolls into the viewport (IntersectionObserver, threshold 0.4, unobserve immediately after firing); when data refreshes, roll from the old value to the new one instead of restarting from 0. [Implementation] A hand-written rAF tween is enough: store the start time plus from and to; each frame compute progress p = Math.min((now - start) / duration, 1), apply an easing that decelerates at the end (e.g. 1 - Math.pow(2, -10 * p)) to get e, current value = from + (to - from) * e, format with toLocaleString() for thousands separators and write it to textContent; when p reaches 1, write the final value directly so floating-point error doesn't leave you at 9999. Fix decimal places with toFixed, and add font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums to the container so every digit has the same width. [Key parameters] duration=1500ms (1.2-2s, never over 2.5s); easing=easeOutExpo (decelerates at the end); decimals=0; threshold=0.4. [Pitfalls] Without tabular digits the whole row jitters left and right when the digit count changes; rebuilding innerHTML every frame drops frames, so only touch textContent; dozens of counters each running their own rAF loop also stutter, so merge them into one loop that advances them all. [Dependencies] None (countup.js also works).

When the value changes, transform: translateY scrolls the target digit into an overflow:hidden viewport, producing a mechanical odometer-style roll digit by digit. [Implementation] Advance with recursive setTimeout (not setInterval): increment the index each time and write el.textContent = full.slice(0, i), adding a little random jitter to each delay around a base value to feel more human; always split characters with Array.from(str) or Intl.Segmenter, never by index. [Key parameters] speed=60ms/char (English 40-60ms, Chinese 80-120ms); extra 300ms pause after punctuation; 1500ms hold at the end of a sentence; cursor blink period 1s. svg-path-drawing.logic: Set the SVG path's stroke-dasharray equal to the total path length (obtained via path.getTotalLength()), then animate stroke-dashoffset from the total length to 0; the whole dash pattern shifts so the stroke looks as if it is being drawn. Commonly used for signatures, icon outlining and growing connector lines as a draw-on effect.
svg-path-drawing.prompt: Implement "SVG Path Drawing" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Lines look like they are drawn live by a pen, extending from start to end, for signatures, icon outlining and growing flowchart connectors. [When it triggers] Once, when the element scrolls into the viewport or when some state is reached (e.g. draw a checkmark on submit success). [Implementation] First give the path fill:none and a stroke. Get the total length len with path.getTotalLength(), set path.style.strokeDasharray to len and strokeDashoffset also to len, so the line is completely hidden; then use a transition or element.animate to animate strokeDashoffset to 0, and the whole dash shift becomes the draw-on effect. For fixed-length icons you can skip JS: hardcode stroke-dasharray and stroke-dashoffset in CSS and animate to zero with @keyframes. To draw multiple lines in sequence, give each an incrementing animation-delay; for a reverse erase, animate the offset from 0 to len. [Key parameters] duration=1-2s (estimate as path length divided by about 300px/s); easing=ease-in-out; stroke-linecap=round; gap between segments=200ms. [Pitfalls] getTotalLength() must be called when the element is in the document and visible; inside display:none it returns 0 and the animation looks like it is fully drawn from the start; also, if the path has a fill, the fill color is already there and looks like cheating, so use fill:none first and fade the fill in separately after drawing. [Dependencies] None.

gooey-effect.logic: Apply an SVG filter to a group of elements: first feGaussianBlur blurs heavily, then feColorMatrix boosts the alpha channel's contrast to threshold it, so the blurred edges of neighboring elements 'stick' together into a liquid merge (metaball). The filter is attached to the parent container; often used for sticky menus and liquid loading dots.
gooey-effect.prompt: Implement "Gooey Effect" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A group of moving elements merge into sticky, liquid shapes (metaballs) via an SVG filter, commonly used for sticky menus and liquid loading animations. [When it triggers] While elements move interactively, and in hover state. [Implementation] Chain two layers in an SVG filter: feGaussianBlur with a heavy blur (sigma=8-15), then feColorMatrix boosting the alpha channel's contrast (type=saturate, value 2-3), thresholding the blurred edges so neighboring elements stick together. Attach the filter to the parent container so all children get it automatically. [Key parameters] feGaussianBlur stdDeviation=10-15, feColorMatrix saturate=2.5, spacing between elements 5-20px (too far apart and they won't merge). [Pitfalls] A high blur amount (>20) makes the performance cost explode and drops frames; an alpha threshold that's too high stops the merge from working, too low makes everything transparent; Safari's support for some filter parameters is poor and needs separate testing. [Dependencies] None.

confetti-effect.logic: Generate hundreds or thousands of particles on a canvas with random colors, angles and initial velocities; each frame update their positions and rotations under gravity and air drag and redraw, destroying them once they leave the screen. Typically triggered with a one-line confetti() from canvas-confetti, or tsParticles for celebratory bursts.
confetti-effect.prompt: Implement "Confetti Effect" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] At the moment a key action succeeds, a burst of colored paper bits explodes across the screen, drifts down for two or three seconds and disappears naturally, giving the user clear celebratory feedback. [When it triggers] Fire once, only at moments truly worth celebrating: payment success, all tasks completed, onboarding finished; never loop it, and don't fire it on every ordinary submit. [Implementation] canvas-confetti is the fastest: import it and call confetti({ particleCount: 120, spread: 70, origin: { x: 0.5, y: 0.6 } }); to burst from a button's position, convert the center of the button's getBoundingClientRect into a 0-1 origin and pass it in. To write it yourself, on a full-screen canvas that is position: fixed, pointer-events: none and on the top layer, generate a particle array where each particle has a position, velocity, rotation angle and color; in rAF apply gravity and drag to the velocity, clearRect and redraw the whole screen, remove particles from the array once they leave the viewport, and when the array is empty stop the loop and remove the canvas. [Key parameters] particleCount=120 (80-200, halve on mobile); spread=70deg; gravity=0.6; single run lasts <=2.5s. [Pitfalls] Forgetting pointer-events: none on the canvas makes the whole page unclickable for those seconds; creating a new canvas on every trigger without destroying it stacks up full-screen canvases after a few clicks; thousands of particles freeze mid-to-low-end phones; skip this effect when prefers-reduced-motion: reduce is set. [Dependencies] canvas-confetti (none if you write the particles yourself).

[Implementation] Prefer transition to cover state differences; don't reach for a library. Attach the focus ring only to :focus-visible so it isn't drawn after a mouse click. [Key parameters] hover in/out=150-200ms; press=80ms (fast in, slow out); displacement=1-2px; scale=0.97-1.03x. [Pitfalls] Making a micro-interaction a big 500ms animation means several rapid clicks queue up waiting for animations to finish, which feels sluggish; also, writing only :hover without :active leaves touch screens with no feedback at all on press. state-transition.logic: When a component switches between states such as default/hover/focus/active/disabled, CSS transition smoothly animates color, opacity and offset to avoid abrupt jumps. Material overlays a semi-transparent state layer at different opacities to express each interaction state, unifying the feedback intensity across controls.
state-transition.prompt: Implement "State Transition" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When clickable elements such as buttons switch between hover, pressed, focused and disabled, color and offset glide smoothly: responsive, not abrupt, no flicker. [When it triggers] Happens automatically on pseudo-class changes: :hover, :focus-visible, :active, [disabled] and [aria-pressed="true"]. [Implementation] Declare transition on the base state and list only the properties that actually change, e.g. background-color and transform at 150ms ease-out each. The state-layer approach is recommended: set position: relative on the element, use ::before to lay down an overlay in the foreground color with opacity 0, raise opacity to 0.08 on hover and 0.12 on active; the same values work over any background color, so you don't need to tune colors per button variant. Press feedback uses transform: scale(0.97), and release springs back with a shorter duration. Always use :focus-visible for focus so the ring shows for keyboard but not after a mouse click. [Key parameters] enter 150ms, leave 100ms; easing=ease-out; hover layer opacity=0.08, active=0.12; press scale=0.97. [Pitfalls] Writing transition: all drags layout properties along, so the whole block jitters when expanding or collapsing; doing :hover without :focus-visible leaves keyboard users unable to see where focus is; hover styles stick on touch screens, so wrap them in @media (hover: hover). [Dependencies] None.

gesture-driven-animation.logic: Track drag displacement and velocity with Pointer/Touch events, map the finger position to the element's transform in real time, and on release finish with a spring/inertia using the recorded velocity. framer-motion's drag and the use-gesture library wrap velocity calculation and momentum flinging.
gesture-driven-animation.prompt: Implement "Gesture-Driven Animation" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The element follows the finger in real time, and after release keeps sliding at the flick velocity and settles naturally or snaps into place, like dragging a physical object with weight. [When it triggers] pointerdown records the start point and calls setPointerCapture; pointermove follows in real time; on pointerup or pointercancel, resolve the velocity and decide whether to spring back, snap or fling. [Implementation] Use Pointer events throughout so one codebase covers mouse and touch. In move, compute the displacement dx and set el.style.transform to translate3d(dx px, 0, 0), throttling the writes inside requestAnimationFrame; meanwhile keep the last few coordinate samples with timestamps to compute velocity. On release: if the displacement or velocity exceeds its threshold, snap to the next stop, otherwise spring back into place, finishing with element.animate and a cubic-bezier that has overshoot. Set touch-action: pan-y on the container to disable native horizontal scrolling during horizontal drags. [Key parameters] snap threshold=30% of container width or velocity >0.5px/ms; finishing duration=300ms; free-fling friction=0.95 (decay per frame). [Pitfalls] Without touch-action, the page scrolls along while dragging on mobile; without setPointerCapture, events cut off when the finger leaves the element and it gets stuck midway; changing left or width every frame triggers reflow, so use transform. [Dependencies] None.

page-transition.logic: On route change, run an exit animation on the outgoing old page and an enter animation on the incoming new page. In SPAs, framer-motion's AnimatePresence with a unique key, or Vue's <transition>, ensures the leaving element unmounts only after its animation finishes; MPAs can now use cross-document View Transitions.
page-transition.prompt: Implement "Page Transition" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] On route change the old page fades out first, then the new page fades in with a slight upward shift, with no white-screen hard cut, so users sense which level they went to. [When it triggers] On route change; forward and back use opposite offset directions, determined from the history direction. [Implementation] In React with framer-motion: wrap the route outlet in AnimatePresence with mode="wait", make the page component a motion.div keyed by location.pathname, with initial opacity 0 and y 8px, animate back to zero, and exit with opacity 0 and y -8px, duration 0.25s; the key must be unique and stable, otherwise the exit animation never fires. In Vue, wrap <RouterView> in <Transition mode="out-in">. For multi-page sites or native routing, wrap the navigation directly in document.startViewTransition. After the switch completes, reset scroll position to zero and move focus to the new page's heading. [Key parameters] total duration=250ms (don't exceed 400ms or it feels slow); exit=150ms, enter=200ms (leaving is faster); offset=8-16px; easing=ease-out. [Pitfalls] Running enter and exit simultaneously without positioning handling makes the two pages overlap, collapsing the height and making the scrollbar jump; out-then-in is the safest; mashing navigation during the exit stacks up multiple page instances, so disable navigation while transitioning; adding a transition without resetting scroll leaves the new page at the previous page's scroll height. [Dependencies] framer-motion (Vue uses the built-in Transition; none needed for View Transitions).

reveal-on-scroll.logic: Elements start with opacity:0 and a translateY offset downward; when scrolled into the viewport (IntersectionObserver or scroll-driven view()), the offset is removed and they fade in and float up into place. Multiple elements usually get incrementing delays so they surface one after another; this is the most common section-by-section entrance pattern on landing pages.
reveal-on-scroll.prompt: Implement "Reveal on Scroll" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] As the user scrolls down, each section fades in and floats up from a dozen or so pixels below, so content meets the reader piece by piece and the landing page is no longer a static wall of text and images. [When it triggers] Fire once when about 15% of the element is visible in the viewport; after playing, stay in the final state and never replay. [Implementation] First define the initial state in CSS: on class .reveal set opacity: 0 and transform: translateY(24px), and give each of the two properties a 600ms transition with cubic-bezier(0.16,1,0.3,1) easing; then define the final state .reveal.is-visible, setting opacity back to 1 and transform to none. In JS, create an IntersectionObserver observing all .reveal elements on the page; in the callback, if isIntersecting is true, add is-visible and unobserve the element immediately, so it plays only once. For multiple elements in the same group, write the index into a custom property --i and use transition-delay: calc(var(--i) * 80ms) so they surface in sequence. If you only target modern browsers, the whole thing can be replaced with animation-timeline: view(), which removes the need for JS. [Key parameters] offset=16-32px (over 60px is jarring); duration=500-700ms; threshold=0.15; gap within a group=80ms. [Pitfalls] Adding reveal to first-screen content makes users see blank space before it fades in, hurting first-screen impression and LCP; give above-the-fold elements their final state directly. Also, if the script fails, the whole page stays at opacity:0 and goes blank, so keep a fallback. [Dependencies] None.

scroll-pinning.logic: Once a section scrolls to a given position, fix it in the viewport with position:sticky or GSAP ScrollTrigger's pin, while its inner content does a horizontal switch or step-by-step animation driven by the continued scroll progress, and release after a set scroll distance. This implements a narrative section with a pinned shell and internals advancing with scroll.
scroll-pinning.prompt: Implement "Scroll Pinning" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A section stops in place once it scrolls into position; as the user keeps scrolling, its interior changes step by step (horizontal advance, text/image rotation), and only after a set scroll distance does the whole block continue upward and leave. [When it triggers] Pin when the top of the section reaches the top of the viewport; release once the inner progress hits 100%. [Implementation] Prefer pure CSS: give the outer wrapper a height far greater than the viewport (e.g. 300vh), and the inner element position: sticky; top: 0; height: 100vh; overflow: hidden. Compute the inner progress yourself: progress = -wrapperTop / (wrapperHeight - viewportHeight), clamped between 0 and 1, and in rAF map it to the inner layer's transform: translateX(-progress * (totalWidth - viewportWidth)); cache the measured sizes rather than reading them every frame. Only reach for GSAP ScrollTrigger's { pin: true, scrub: true, start, end } when you need complex timeline orchestration. [Key parameters] wrapper height = number of content screens x 100vh (300-400vh for 3 screens); start='top top'; scrub=0.5s; progress clamped to 0-1. [Pitfalls] When sticky doesn't work, nine times out of ten an ancestor has overflow: hidden or auto, or the parent container isn't tall enough; check that chain top-down instead of touching sticky itself; a wrapper that's too tall makes users scroll a long time to get past this screen; on mobile use dvh for heights, otherwise the block jumps when the address bar collapses. [Dependencies] None (GSAP's ScrollTrigger for complex orchestration).

text-scramble.prompt: Implement "Text Scramble" at the place mentioned above. loading-spinner.logic: Several ways to show 'in progress': a single ring uses a border with one side transparent and rotates infinitely; an SVG ring uses stroke-dasharray + dashoffset to stretch and shrink while spinning for a 'chasing tail' ring; three dots pulse out of phase. At their core all are infinite linear loops expressing a wait of unknown length.
loading-spinner.prompt: Implement "Loading Spinner" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] While waiting, show an indicator that keeps spinning or bouncing so the user knows the program is working and not dead; use it when the duration is unknown, and switch to a progress bar when the duration is known. [When it triggers] Show it about 200ms after the request is sent (if the response comes back faster, skip the flash), and remove it immediately when the data arrives or an error occurs. [Implementation] Pick one of three. Ring: a square div with border: 3px solid rgba(0,0,0,.1), border-top-color set to the primary color, border-radius: 50%, plus animation: spin 0.8s linear infinite, with the keyframes rotating transform to rotate(360deg). SVG chasing ring: set the circle's stroke-dasharray to a quarter of the circumference, rotate the whole thing while animating stroke-dashoffset. Bouncing dots: three dots share the same bounce animation, with animation-delay of 0, 0.15s and 0.3s respectively. Add role=status and an aria-label to the container. [Key parameters] rotation period=0.8-1.2s; timing-function=linear (required, otherwise a hitch is visible every turn); size=16px (inside a button) or 32px (block level); appearance delay=200ms. [Pitfalls] Putting a spinner in a button without locking its width makes the button width jump on load; also, a single ring spinning alone on a whole page for several seconds is bad, and waits over about 1s should switch to a skeleton screen. [Dependencies] None.

progress-animation.logic: Determinate progress smoothly transitions a linear bar's fill by percentage using transform:scaleX or width; circular progress maps the percentage to arc length with an SVG circle's stroke-dashoffset; indeterminate progress uses endlessly translating diagonal stripes to say 'working'. scaleX is cheaper than width and doesn't trigger reflow.
progress-animation.prompt: Implement "Progress Animation" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The progress bar advances smoothly with real progress instead of jumping in steps, so users can see how much remains and that the system hasn't hung. [When it triggers] Transition to the new value when the progress value updates; use an endlessly looping indeterminate state when progress is unknown; stop at 100% and give a completion feedback. [Implementation] Linear bar: put a fill block in the track with transform: scaleX(var(--p)), transform-origin: left and transition: transform 200ms linear; JS only changes --p (0 to 1), one fewer layout than changing width. Circular progress: draw an SVG circle, set stroke-dasharray to the circumference 2πr, stroke-dashoffset = circumference x (1 - percentage) with a transition, and rotate the whole svg by -90deg so the start point returns to the top. For the indeterminate state, loop a fill block about 30% wide with an infinite translateX. For accessibility, use the native <progress> or add role="progressbar" with aria-valuenow. [Key parameters] transition=200ms linear (progress must be linear; easing makes people misjudge speed); indeterminate loop=1.2s; ring stroke-width=8px; minimum visible progress=2%. [Pitfalls] Animating width triggers layout every frame; progress going backward makes people think something's wrong, so only increase except on retry; fake progress stuck at 99% hurts more than none; scaleX also stretches the text and rounded corners inside the fill block, so put the border-radius on the track. [Dependencies] None.

timeline-orchestration.logic: Orchestrate multiple animations' order and overlap on a single timeline: GSAP's timeline.to(...).to(..., '-=0.3') uses relative position parameters to control chaining and overlap, or the Web Animations API shares one currentTime to sync several segments. This lets a complex multi-act sequence be paused, reversed and speed-changed as a whole.
timeline-orchestration.prompt: Apply "Timeline Orchestration" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Multiple animations play in a designed order and overlap, so the whole thing feels like a rhythmic storyboard, and it can be paused as a whole, jumped to a given moment or played in reverse. [When it triggers] Entrance sequences, elements entering one after another inside a dialog, guided demos and other scenarios where the second segment must start while the first still has 0.3s left. [Implementation] Native approach: get an Animation object from element.animate() for each segment, order them with delay and create overlap with negative delay, put them in an array and pause(), play(), reverse() them together, or set currentTime together for sync; to wait for the previous segment to really finish before the next, await its finished. For many segments needing relative positioning and overall speed changes, use a GSAP timeline: tl.to(a,{...}).to(b,{...},'-=0.3') starts 0.3s early, the position parameter '<' starts at the same time as the previous segment, and tl.timeScale(1.5) speeds up the whole. [Key parameters] overlap between segments=-0.2 to -0.3s (no overlap at all feels stop-and-go); single segment duration=300-600ms; total length cap ~1.5s. [Pitfalls] Sequencing with nested setTimeout: if the user closes the dialog early you can't cancel it, and the timing drifts from the real animation durations; leave sequencing to animation objects or a timeline. Also under prefers-reduced-motion it must be able to jump to the end state in one step. [Dependencies] None; gsap for complex sequences.

magnetic-button.logic: Listen to the mouse coordinates near a button, compute the offset vector from the pointer to the button's center, and use transform:translate with a coefficient below 1 to make the button (and its inner text) shift slightly toward the mouse as if attracted; on mouseleave it springs back. Often paired with spring or GSAP quickTo for smooth following.
magnetic-button.prompt: Implement "Magnetic Button" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When the mouse approaches a button, the button drifts gently toward the pointer as if pulled, its inner text moving a bit more, and springs back into place when the pointer leaves. [When it triggers] Starts following when the pointer enters the button's expanded sensing area, springs back on mouseleave; disabled entirely on touch screens and under prefers-reduced-motion. [Implementation] Wrap the button in a larger wrapper as the sensing area; on mouseenter, measure once with getBoundingClientRect and cache the center point, don't measure every frame; in mousemove only record dx = e.clientX - cx and dy = e.clientY - cy, and put the actual style writes in rAF: target offset = offset * coefficient, current offset does a lerp with cur += (target - cur) * 0.15, then write it into transform: translate. Give the inner text layer a larger coefficient for parallax. On mouseleave set the target to zero so the same lerp loop springs back naturally, and stop the loop when the offset is near 0. [Key parameters] sensing area expansion=20-40px; attraction coefficient=0.3 (text layer 0.5, any more and it leaves the frame); lerp=0.15; max displacement=15px. [Pitfalls] Reading getBoundingClientRect while writing transform in mousemove alternates reads and writes and forces synchronous layout, so the whole page stutters as soon as the mouse moves; attaching the listener to document without distance filtering makes dozens of buttons compute at once; if not disabled on mobile, the first tap only triggers the hover state, creating the illusion that it takes a tap to work. [Dependencies] None (for smoother following use gsap's quickTo).

cursor-follow.logic: Replace or overlay the native cursor with a custom DOM element; after mousemove records the target coordinates, each frame a lerp makes the follower catch up to the pointer smoothly with damping (instead of teleporting), scaling up or snapping when hovering interactive elements. Often paired with mix-blend-mode:difference for an inverted-color cursor.
cursor-follow.prompt: Implement "Custom Cursor Follow" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A custom dot or ring trails the pointer with damping, growing or snapping when passing over interactive elements, making the page feel more refined. [When it triggers] On mousemove only update the target coordinates, and requestAnimationFrame interpolates to catch up each frame; switch to an enlarged state when hovering links and buttons; not enabled at all on (pointer: coarse) touch devices. [Implementation] Put a position:fixed, pointer-events:none, very high z-index div on the page. In the mousemove callback only store e.clientX and e.clientY in variables, never change styles there; in the rAF loop interpolate cur += (target - cur) * ease, then set el.style.transform to translate3d(cur.x px, cur.y px, 0) together with translate(-50%,-50%) so the center aligns with the pointer. The hover state changes scale by toggling a class. For an inverted-color cursor, add mix-blend-mode: difference and set the color to white, and set cursor: none on body. [Key parameters] interpolation factor ease=0.15 (0.1-0.2, smaller is laggier); ring diameter=32px; hover enlargement=scale(1.6); z-index=9999. [Pitfalls] Writing styles directly in mousemove stutters as soon as the mouse moves fast; you must store the value and use rAF; positioning with left/top instead of transform reflows every frame; hiding the native cursor while it also applies in touch or keyboard scenarios leaves users with no pointer at all. [Dependencies] None.

scrollytelling.logic: Split a long page into several steps, use scrollama or IntersectionObserver to detect the currently active step and trigger the matching chart/graphic/text state change. A typical structure is two columns: a sticky pinned graphic layer plus a text step layer that flows with scrolling, used for data-journalism-style narratives.
scrollytelling.prompt: Implement "Scrollytelling" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Split a long page into several steps; as the user scrolls to each step, the corresponding text, chart and graphic states switch, for data-journalism-style narratives. fade-through.logic: A Material pattern: the old content first fades out and shrinks slightly (e.g. scale 0.92 to 1), then the new content fades in from the shrunken state, with the two phases not overlapping. Used for switching between screens without a strong relationship (such as bottom-navigation page switches); it differs from a crossfade in that the two phases are staggered rather than simultaneous.

[When it triggers] When switching where old and new content have no correspondence, such as bottom-navigation page switches, tab switches and route changes. [Implementation] The key is that the two phases don't overlap. Exit: opacity from 1 to 0 and transform from scale(1) to scale(0.92), about 90ms, ease-in. In React, set the container's key to the current page identifier to trigger a remount, or use framer-motion's AnimatePresence with mode set to wait. Don't use it for switches with a parent-child relationship (list to detail); use a shared-element transition for those. [Key parameters] exit=90ms; enter=210ms with delay=90ms; scale start=0.92 (no lower than 0.9, or the shrink looks like a popup). [When it triggers] Fire once when the element enters the viewport, when a card is clicked to expand, or when the theme switches; it can also be used on the old and new layers of View Transitions. [Key parameters] Layers = 3; blur steps = 4px/10px/24px; alpha = 0.8/0.5/0.3; transition = 200ms ease-out. [Pitfalls] A glow on a light background is darker than the base, so it looks like a dirty edge rather than a glow; glow only works on dark backgrounds. Also, stacking seven or eight large-blur shadows at once drops frames noticeably, so keep it to 4 layers or fewer. [Dependencies] None.

vignette.logic: Darkens the edges of the frame and keeps the center bright, guiding the eye to focus and strengthening the atmosphere. Overlay a pseudo-element with radial-gradient(ellipse, transparent 60%, rgba(0,0,0,.6)) on the image, or use a large-spread inset box-shadow that darkens inward from the edges.
vignette.prompt: Implement "Vignette" (Vignette) at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Darken the edges and keep the center bright, guiding the eye to focus and strengthening the atmosphere. [When it triggers] Always on, or when the center content needs emphasis. [Implementation] Overlay a ::before pseudo-element with radial-gradient(ellipse at center, transparent 40%, rgba(0,0,0,0.6) 100%); or use an inset box-shadow such as box-shadow: inset 0 0 60px 30px rgba(0,0,0,0.5) to darken inward from the edges; filter: brightness() can fine-tune overall brightness. [Key parameters] radial-gradient transparent-center stop = 30-50%, edge darkness rgba(0,0,0,0.4-0.8); inset box-shadow blur-radius = 40-80px, spread-radius = 20-40px; z-index = 1 to cover the content, but pointer-events: none so it does not block interaction. [Pitfalls] A transparent-center stop that is too close to the edge lets the vignette intrude on the subject; too much darkness feels oppressive; forgetting pointer-events makes buttons unclickable. [Dependencies] None.

inner-shadow.logic: Uses the inset keyword of box-shadow to cast the shadow inside the element along its top edge, creating a recessed or pressed texture; commonly used for inputs, progress tracks, and the pressed state of buttons. The typical form is box-shadow: inset 0 2px 4px rgba(0,0,0,.15), and adding a bottom inset highlight makes it more three-dimensional.
inner-shadow.prompt: Implement "Inner Shadow" (Inner Shadow) at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The element looks recessed inward, with a soft dark shadow along the top edge, like a groove or a pressed-down button rather than something floating on the page. [When it triggers] Always on for inputs and progress tracks; for buttons, switch to it in :active for the pressed state. [Implementation] Use the inset keyword of box-shadow: box-shadow: inset 0 2px 4px rgba(0,0,0,0.15). A positive y offset with blur no more than twice the offset gives the most realistic recess. For more depth, add a bottom highlight: box-shadow: inset 0 2px 4px rgba(0,0,0,0.15), inset 0 -1px 0 rgba(255,255,255,0.6), with the two comma-separated and the earlier one on top. For the button pressed state, swap the outer shadow for an inner shadow and add transform: translateY(1px) so it visually looks pressed down. Inset shadows follow border-radius automatically, so rounded elements need no extra handling. [Key parameters] y offset = 2px (3px for deep grooves); blur = 4px; shadow alpha = 0.12 to 0.20 (in dark themes use a darker base color rather than just adding more black); highlight alpha = 0.6. [Pitfalls] Trying to add an inner shadow directly to an img: box-shadow is painted above the background but below the content, so the bitmap covers it completely; wrap it in a container and draw the shadow on a pseudo-element above the image. Also, inset shadows take no layout space, so do not use them as a border. [Dependencies] None.

long-shadow.logic: In flat design, an icon drags a solid-color long shadow along 45° that extends to the edge. In CSS, stack dozens of same-color text-shadow/box-shadow layers with per-pixel offsets (0 0, 1px 1px, 2px 2px...) that accumulate into a continuous cast shadow, usually generated with a Sass loop or pre-generated, and the end can fade to transparent.
long-shadow.prompt: Implement "Long Shadow" (Long Shadow) at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Drag a solid-color long cast shadow along 45° to the edge, adding depth to flat design. [When it triggers] To make an icon or heading stand out. [Implementation] Stack dozens of per-pixel offset text-shadows (1px 1px, 2px 2px...), usually with a Sass loop or pre-generated; the end fades to transparent. [Key parameters] @for $i from 1 to 50 text-shadow: #{$i}px #{$i}px rgba(color, calc(1-$i/50)); use the brand color for the shadow, with opacity from 100% to 0%. [Pitfalls] Too many shadows hurt performance; the color must be consistent; the opacity gradient at the end must be symmetric. [Dependencies] Sass (optional).

drop-shadow.logic: Adds a cast shadow that separates the element from the background. box-shadow casts along the box's rectangular boundary, whereas filter: drop-shadow() casts along the element's actual opaque outline (including transparent PNGs, rounded corners, and SVG shapes), so for irregular icons or images you must use drop-shadow rather than box-shadow.
drop-shadow.prompt: Implement "Drop Shadow" (Drop Shadow) at the place mentioned above. [Goal] For transparent PNG icons, SVG graphics, and irregularly shaped elements, the shadow follows the element's own shape instead of throwing out a rectangular dark box around it. [When it triggers] Always on; on hover, enlarge the shadow to convey lifting. [Implementation] Use filter: drop-shadow(offsetX offsetY blur color) instead of box-shadow. box-shadow only recognizes the rectangular boundary of the box model, while drop-shadow casts along the outline of the element's actual opaque pixels, so transparent PNGs, SVG graphics, and shapes cut by clip-path all get correct shadows. For multiple shadows, chain several drop-shadow() calls, which apply in sequence. Note that it does not accept a spread value; for a thicker shadow you can only increase blur or stack layers. For a group of icons, put the filter on the parent container to apply to all at once. [Key parameters] offset = 0 4px; blur = 8px (about 2x the offset); color = rgba(0,0,0,.25); on hover raise to offset 0 8px, blur 16px. [Pitfalls] Do not use drop-shadow on ordinary rectangular cards with a solid background: it is far more expensive than box-shadow and creates a new stacking context, so use box-shadow for regular rectangles. Also, overflow: hidden on the parent will clip the shadow. [Dependencies] None.

bevel.logic: Creates an angled 3D facet on the edges. Visually, fake a lit bevel with light and dark border colors on adjacent sides (light on top-left, dark on bottom-right) to make a raised or recessed 3D edge; for geometric chamfers, use clip-path: polygon() to cut off the rectangle's corners into solid bevels.
bevel.prompt: Implement "Bevel" (Bevel) at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Create angled 3D facets on the edges, giving a raised or recessed 3D feel. [When it triggers] Always on for UI elements such as buttons and cards. [Implementation] Fake a lit bevel with a light and a dark border on adjacent sides (e.g. border-top/left as rgba(255,255,255,0.5) white light, border-bottom/right as rgba(0,0,0,0.5) dark) to give a raised look; for geometric chamfers use clip-path: polygon() to cut off the rectangle's corners into solid bevels, e.g. clip-path: polygon(20px 0, 100% 0, 100% calc(100% - 20px), calc(100% - 20px) 100%, 0 100%, 0 20px). [Key parameters] Border width = 2-4px, color pair = top-left white rgba(255,255,255,0.5) and bottom-right black rgba(0,0,0,0.5); clip-path chamfer size = 8-20px. [Pitfalls] Border colors with too little contrast give weak depth; clip-path percentages above 50% distort the shape; using border and clip-path together duplicates the effect. [Dependencies] None.

gloss-specular.logic: Overlays a semi-transparent white gradient on the upper half of the element to simulate the specular highlight of a glossy surface (the signature of Web 2.0 glass buttons). Use a pseudo-element with linear-gradient(rgba(255,255,255,.5), transparent) covering only the upper half, with large rounded corners and a slightly curved border-radius so the highlight looks like a reflection on a curved surface.
gloss-specular.prompt: Implement "Gloss / Specular Highlight" (Gloss / Specular Highlight) at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A white gradient over the upper half simulates a glossy reflection, the signature of Web 2.0 buttons. [When it triggers] Buttons or cards that need a glossy feel. [Implementation] Absolutely position a ::before pseudo-element over the upper half with linear-gradient(rgba(255,255,255,.5), transparent); mix-blend-mode: overlay; pointer-events: none so it does not block the text. [Key parameters] linear-gradient(to bottom, rgba(255,255,255,.5), transparent 60%); height: 50%; pointer-events: none. [Pitfalls] Too bright and it obscures text; overdoing overlay looks cheap, so control opacity; the edge can cut into Chinese font glyphs. [Dependencies] None.

alpha-compositing.logic: Uses transparency to blend multiple layers of pixels according to the alpha channel. The basics rely on opacity or the alpha component of rgba()/hsla() for semi-transparent layering; more advanced use applies mix-blend-mode/background-blend-mode with multiply, screen, overlay and other blend algorithms to decide how upper and lower colors are computed and composited.
alpha-compositing.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Alpha Compositing" (Alpha Compositing) requirements. [Goal] Transparency is computed and layered by the alpha channel, so multiple layers of pixels composite into the expected blended result. [When it triggers] When stacking multiple layers or specifying a blend mode. [Implementation] For the basics, use opacity or the alpha component of rgba()/hsla() for semi-transparent layers; for advanced use, specify algorithms with mix-blend-mode or background-blend-mode: multiply (multiplies, darkens), screen (inverse multiply, lightens), overlay (strengthens overall contrast), color-dodge (highlights), etc.; the browser composites automatically by the formula (C_result = C_top * alpha + C_bottom * (1-alpha)). [Key parameters] opacity = 0-1 or alpha = 0-255; blend-mode choice (multiply for darkening, screen for lightening, overlay for balancing contrast); stacked opacity compounds multiplicatively, roughly x0.7 per layer. [Pitfalls] Blend modes interact with the base color and give unexpected results, especially on solid backgrounds; multiplied opacity across layers makes the bottom layers so faint they are almost invisible; omitting background-color lets the transparency show through to what is behind. [Dependencies] None.

flexbox.logic: After setting display: flex on a container, its children are laid out one-dimensionally along the main axis (flex-direction), with justify-content controlling main-axis distribution and align-items controlling cross-axis alignment. Children share the remaining space via the three flex values grow, shrink, and basis, and flex-wrap controls whether they wrap.
flexbox.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Flexbox" (Flexbox) requirements. [Goal] Elements in a row or column align as expected with even spacing, the remaining space is taken up by designated items, and nothing gets crammed together or overflows when the window narrows. [When it triggers] Always-on layout; it reflows automatically when the container width or the number of children changes. [Implementation] Write display: flex on the container, set the main axis with flex-direction, use justify-content for main-axis distribution (flex-start/center/space-between), and align-items for cross-axis alignment (default stretch; use center for vertical centering). Always use gap for spacing between children, instead of writing margin-right on each child and then clearing the last one. To have one item take the remaining space, give it flex: 1 (equivalent to 1 1 0%); to keep it from being compressed, write flex: 0 0 auto. To allow wrapping, add flex-wrap: wrap, with children set to flex: 1 1 240px for an auto-wrapping card row. To push a single item to the edge, use margin-left: auto, which is cleaner than adding another wrapper. [Key parameters] gap = 8px/16px/24px (pick from the 8px grid); flex-basis = 0% (equal split) or 240px (minimum card width); flex-shrink = 0 (icons and avatars must not be squashed). [Pitfalls] Text children blow out the container: flex items default to min-width: auto and refuse to shrink, so for ellipsis or wrapping you must give them min-width: 0 (min-height: 0 in the column direction); also, align-items: center cancels stretch, which breaks equal-height cards. [Dependencies] None.

css-grid.logic: display: grid establishes a two-dimensional grid, and grid-template-columns/rows define the tracks (often with the fr flexible unit, minmax(), repeat(), auto-fill/auto-fit). Children are positioned across rows and columns with grid-column/row or grid-area, and gap sets the spacing between tracks.
css-grid.prompt: Implement "CSS Grid" (CSS Grid) at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The page aligns into a tidy two-dimensional grid of rows and columns, column widths stretch with the container, elements can span rows and columns, and there is no need for layers of nested divs and floats. [When it triggers] Always-on layout; switch the number of columns when breakpoints change. [Implementation] Write display: grid on the container and define column tracks with grid-template-columns: use repeat(3, 1fr) for equal split, or repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)) for responsive columns whose count grows and shrinks with width; leave row heights to grid-auto-rows: minmax(120px, auto). Children span columns with grid-column: 1 / 3 or grid-column: span 2; for complex fixed layouts, use grid-template-areas to draw an ASCII map and name children with grid-area. Always use gap for track spacing and place-items for alignment. [Key parameters] columns = repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px,1fr)); gap = 16px; min-track = 240px (narrowest readable card width); minimum row height 120px. [Pitfalls] Hard-coding percentage widths on children together with gap adds up to more than 100% and overflows; in a grid, leave widths to the tracks. Also, the minimum of 1fr is auto, so long words or long URLs will blow out the track; write minmax(0,1fr) or give the child min-width: 0. Also, auto-fill keeps empty tracks while auto-fit collapses them so existing items stretch to fill; do not mix the two. [Dependencies] None.

subgrid.logic: Write subgrid on grid-template-columns or rows of a nested grid so the child grid inherits the parent grid's track lines directly instead of creating its own tracks. This lets the title, body, and button inside cards align to the same baseline across multiple cards. It is now widely available (Baseline; Chrome 117+/Firefox 71+/Safari 16+).
subgrid.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Subgrid" (Subgrid) requirements. [Goal] The child grid inherits the parent grid's track lines, so content of nested elements aligns to a baseline across multiple items. [When it triggers] When grid items nest children with the same structure, such as a card list whose interiors need vertical alignment. [Implementation] Set grid-template-columns: subgrid or rows: subgrid on the grid item instead of creating its own tracks; the item's content then lays out along the parent grid automatically; use grid-column to specify the span. [Key parameters] grid-template-columns: subgrid; grid-template-rows: subgrid; grid-column: span N. [Pitfalls] Works only on direct children, not on grandchildren; unsupported browsers need an @supports fallback. [Dependencies] None.

svg.卡片内部对齐到父网格同一基线: Card interiors align to parent baseline

masonry-layout.logic: Stacks items of unequal height tightly in columns (Pinterest style), eliminating gaps in the grid. The spec is still contested: Firefox/Safari extend Grid with grid-template-rows: masonry, Chrome once argued for a standalone display: masonry, and in 2025 the CSSWG leaned toward a grid-lanes approach. For now every browser requires an experimental flag.
masonry-layout.prompt: Implement "Masonry Layout" (Masonry Layout) at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Cards of varying height stack tightly in columns, each one filling into the currently shortest column, with no large gaps between columns, like a Pinterest image wall. [When it triggers] Relayout on first render of the list, when the next page of data is appended, and when the window width crosses a breakpoint and changes the number of columns. [Implementation] Native masonry is still being contested in standards and needs experimental flags in every browser, so do not depend on it in production. Two safe paths: first, pure CSS multi-column: on the container write columns: 4 240px; column-gap: 16px, and on children add break-inside: avoid and margin-bottom: 16px; the cost is that reading order runs down each column rather than left to right. Second, compute positions yourself: use ResizeObserver to get the container width and compute the column count, maintain an array of current column heights, put each card into the shortest column, position it with position: absolute plus transform: translate(), and set the container height to the tallest column. Images must first reserve space with aspect-ratio to fix their height. [Key parameters] Column width = 240px to 320px; column gap = 16px; columns per breakpoint = 2 on phone / 3 on tablet / 4 to 5 on desktop. [Pitfalls] If you measure height only after image onload, users will see cards jump around; reserve space in advance using the aspect ratio. Also, relaying out the whole list when appending data flickers; only continue the column-height computation for the new cards. [Dependencies] None.

gap.logic: On flex, grid, and multicol containers, use gap (or row-gap/column-gap) to declare the gutter between children in one go, replacing the old approach of adding margin to every child and then removing it from the first or last. gap only applies between items and creates no outer-edge spacing.
gap.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Gap" (Gap) requirements. [Goal] Adjacent children in lists and grids have an even gutter, the container's outermost edge gets no extra ring of whitespace, and spacing does not break when an item is removed. [When it triggers] Always on; switch to a smaller spacing tier at responsive breakpoints. [Implementation] Delete all the margins on children that were used to space them out, and write gap on the flex, grid, or multicol container instead. For different horizontal and vertical values write gap: 12px 24px (row then column) or write row-gap / column-gap separately. gap only creates gutters between items and no outer-edge spacing, so keep using the container's padding for outer whitespace. Take values uniformly from spacing variables (e.g. var(--space-3)) instead of scattering literals in components; old tail-clearing rules such as :last-child { margin-right: 0 } can be removed too. [Key parameters] gap = 16px (card grids); gap = 8px (button groups, tag groups); drop one tier to 12px on mobile; for different row and column values write gap: 24px 16px. [Pitfalls] Writing gap on an ordinary display: block container has no effect at all and the cause is hard to find; the parent must first be flex / grid / multicol. Also, under flex-wrap a child with 33.33% width gets pushed to the next row by the gap; use calc((100% - 2*gap)/3) instead or switch to grid. [Dependencies] None.

svg.gap 只在项与项之间(无外缘): gap: between items only, no outer edge

place-items.logic: place-items is shorthand for align-items and justify-items, and place-content is shorthand for align-content and justify-content, setting alignment on both axes in one line. Writing place-items: center on a grid centers all children in both directions, the shortest way to achieve perfect centering.
place-items.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Place Items / Content" (Place Items / Content) requirements. [Goal] One line of code sets alignment on both axes (align and justify) of flex or grid, the shortest way to achieve perfect centering. [When it triggers] At layout time. [Implementation] place-items is shorthand for align-items and justify-items, and place-content is shorthand for align-content and justify-content; writing place-items: center on a grid container centers all children in both directions; on a flex container, place-items: center is equivalent to justify-content: center plus align-items: center; values can be start, end, center, stretch, space-between, etc. [Key parameters] place-items value = center (most common) or start/end/stretch; applies to flex/grid containers; needs a height (height or min-height) for the vertical effect to be visible. [Pitfalls] Using place-items on flex without setting a height means vertical centering is not visible; forgetting gap leaves children stuck to the edges; it has no effect on non-flex/grid elements; mixing with margin: auto causes conflicts. [Dependencies] None.

inset.logic: inset is shorthand for top/right/bottom/left and follows the same four-value order as margin. With position: absolute, writing inset: 0 makes the element fill its positioned parent, commonly used for overlays and absolute-positioned centering.
inset.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Inset" (Inset) requirements. [Goal] Replace top/right/bottom/left with a single property, simplifying absolute positioning and filling the container. [When it triggers] When absolute positioning needs specified offsets or to fill the parent. [Implementation] inset is a four-property shorthand that follows margin's four-value order; inset: 0 equals 0 in all four directions (fill); inset: 10px equals 10px top, right, bottom, left; inset: 10px 20px equals 10 vertical and 20 horizontal. [Key parameters] inset: 0; inset: 10px; inset: 10px 20px; inset: T R B L. [Pitfalls] Must be paired with position: absolute/fixed; it only changes position, not size; it conflicts with width/height. [Dependencies] None.

position-sticky.logic: position: sticky makes an element behave as relative until scrolling reaches a given threshold (such as top: 0), then behave as fixed within its scroll container. An offset in one direction is required for it to take effect, and it is affected by the nearest scrollable ancestor and overflow clipping.
position-sticky.prompt: Implement "Position Sticky" (Position Sticky) at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The element scrolls normally with the page, stops and sticks once it reaches a given position, and is only pushed away when the section it lives in has fully scrolled past. [When it triggers] Sticking begins when scrolling carries the element past the set threshold (e.g. 0px from the container top), and it returns to its original position when scrolled back past the threshold. [Implementation] Write position: sticky, and you must give an offset in one direction, such as top: 0 to stick to the top or bottom: 0 to stick to the bottom; writing position without an offset is the most common reason it fails. The sticking reference is the nearest scrollable ancestor, not the viewport. For sticky table headers, put the styles on th and give it an opaque background color, otherwise content below shows through. When multiple sticky elements stack, order them with z-index. To change styles the moment it sticks (such as adding a shadow), place a 1px sentinel element above it and detect with IntersectionObserver instead of listening to scroll and computing coordinates. [Key parameters] top = 0px (when the page has a fixed nav, use the nav height, e.g. 56px); z-index = 10 (raise to 20 if a filter bar sits above); stuck-state shadow = 0 1px 3px rgba(0,0,0,0.12). [Pitfalls] If any ancestor has overflow: hidden/auto/scroll, sticky switches to that container as its reference or fails entirely; when debugging, check overflow level by level going up. Also, when the parent container's height is exactly the element's own height there is no scroll room, which looks like it is not sticking. [Dependencies] None.

aspect-ratio.logic: aspect-ratio: 16/9 declares the element's aspect ratio directly, and the browser computes the other dimension from the known one (usually width), replacing the old hack of padding-top percentages to prop up height. Commonly used as a placeholder for images, videos, and cards to avoid layout shift (CLS) during loading.
aspect-ratio.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Aspect Ratio" (Aspect Ratio) requirements. [Goal] Images, videos, and card placeholders reserve space with the correct ratio before content finishes loading, so the page does not suddenly jump down when an image loads. [When it triggers] Always on; when the element width changes with its container, the height is computed automatically. [Implementation] Write aspect-ratio: 16 / 9 directly on the element; the browser derives the other dimension from the determined one, usually with width given by layout and height solved automatically. For images, also add width: 100%, height: auto, and object-fit: cover so originals of different sizes are cropped to fill without distortion; also add width and height attributes on the img tag so the browser reserves space by intrinsic ratio before CSS is parsed. The old padding-top: 56.25% plus absolutely positioned child hack can be removed entirely. [Key parameters] 16/9 (video); 1/1 (avatars, square images); 4/3 (content images); 3/4 or 2/3 (portrait posters). [Pitfalls] If a fixed height is also written on the element, aspect-ratio is ignored; keep only one of the two. Also, when child content is taller or has a min-height, the ratio is broken; in that case give the container overflow: hidden and use object-fit on the child. [Dependencies] None.

svg.aspect-ratio 声明比例,浏览器算另一维防抖动: aspect-ratio: browser derives other side, no shift

object-fit.logic: object-fit determines how the content of replaced elements such as img/video fills its own box: cover crops proportionally to fill, contain scales proportionally so everything is visible, and fill stretches and distorts. Together with object-position to adjust the crop focus, it is equivalent to background-size/position for background images.
object-fit.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Object Fit" (Object Fit) requirements. [Goal] Images or videos fill a fixed-size frame without distortion: what should fill does so and the excess is cropped, and what should show in full is shown in full with margins. [When it triggers] Always-on styling; recomputed automatically after an image finishes loading and when the container size changes. [Implementation] Fix the container's size or aspect ratio (aspect-ratio: 16/9), and on the img write width: 100%; height: 100%; object-fit: cover for proportional crop-to-fill, or contain for fully visible with margins; the default fill stretches and distorts and should basically not be used. Adjust the crop focus with object-position; portrait lists often use object-position: center 20% to keep faces inside the frame. For avatars, use aspect-ratio: 1 with border-radius: 50%. Decorative background images can still use background-size: cover, but for content images use img with object-fit, which is friendlier to accessibility and lazy loading. [Key parameters] object-fit = cover (list thumbnails) / contain (white-background product images, logos); object-position = center (center 20% for portraits); container aspect ratio = 16/9, 4/3, or 1/1. [Pitfalls] If only object-fit is written and the img has no height, the image still stretches the container by its original ratio and cover has no visible effect; give both width and height. Also, contain leaves blank bars in the frame, so give the container a background color and do not let transparent areas reveal content underneath. [Dependencies] None.

multi-column.logic: Use columns (shorthand for column-width and column-count) to make content flow automatically into multiple columns like a newspaper, with the browser deciding the number of columns from the available width. column-gap sets the gutter, column-rule draws dividers, and break-inside: avoid prevents elements from being split across columns.
multi-column.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Multi-column Layout" (Multi-column Layout) requirements. [Goal] Content flows automatically into multiple columns like a newspaper, with the browser deciding the number of columns from the available width. [When it triggers] At layout time. [Implementation] Use columns (shorthand for column-width and column-count) to set the column count or width; set column-gap for the gutter, 24px recommended; column-rule: 1px solid #ddd draws dividers; break-inside: avoid prevents children from being split across columns; set break-inside: avoid individually on elements you do not want split (such as cards). [Key parameters] column-width = 250-300px (recommended, responsive column width) or column-count = 2-4 (fixed column count); column-gap = 16-32px; column-rule = 1px solid rgba(0,0,0,0.1). [Pitfalls] A fixed column-count causes content to be cut off on narrow screens; applying break-inside: avoid to all children makes column heights unbalanced; forgetting to set the container width prevents columns from adapting; too small a line-height makes text stick to the column edges. [Dependencies] None.

writing-mode.logic: writing-mode switches the direction in which text lines progress: horizontal-tb is the default horizontal layout, and vertical-rl/vertical-lr set text vertically (traditional CJK typesetting, side labels). It redefines the directions of the block and inline axes, and works with text-orientation to control the rotation of individual characters.
writing-mode.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Writing Mode" (Writing Mode) requirements. [Goal] Change the direction text runs, switching from horizontal to vertical, supporting traditional CJK typesetting. [When it triggers] When vertical text or a side navigation is needed. [Implementation] writing-mode: horizontal-tb (horizontal) / vertical-rl (vertical right-to-left, traditional Chinese) / vertical-lr (vertical left-to-right); text-orientation: mixed / upright; block and inline axes swap. [Key parameters] writing-mode: vertical-rl | vertical-lr; text-orientation: mixed | upright; width/height/margin/padding swap. [Pitfalls] In vertical mode width becomes the vertical dimension; kana glyph shapes; grid/flex main axes swap; line-height direction changes. [Dependencies] None.

logical-properties.logic: Use inline (flow direction) and block (block direction) in place of physical left/right/top/bottom, as in margin-inline, padding-block, inset-inline-start. Styles then flip automatically with writing-mode and direction (RTL), so one codebase fits the typesetting directions of many languages.
logical-properties.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Logical Properties" (Logical Properties) requirements. [Goal] Use inline (flow direction) and block (block direction) in place of physical left/right/top/bottom, so styles flip automatically with writing-mode and direction and one codebase fits multilingual typesetting. [When it triggers] When internationalized typesetting must be supported. [Implementation] margin-inline replaces margin-left/right, padding-block replaces padding-top/bottom, inset-inline-start replaces left, border-inline replaces border-left/right, inline-size replaces width, block-size replaces height, and so on; they flip automatically when writing-mode: vertical-rl or direction: rtl is set on html or body. [Key parameters] margin-inline = horizontal spacing, padding-block = vertical spacing, inset-inline-start = logical left, border-inline-width/color = logical left and right borders. [Pitfalls] Mixing physical and logical properties confuses direction; old browsers lack support and need a fallback; when writing-mode becomes vertical, text-align behavior changes and needs adapting. [Dependencies] None.
