container-query.logic: First set container-type: inline-size on the parent (optionally with container-name) to make it a query container, then use @container (min-width: 400px) to switch child component styles based on the container's own size rather than the viewport. It comes with container-relative units such as cqw/cqi/cqh. Widely available in Chrome 105+/Firefox 110+/Safari 16+.
container-query.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Container Query" (Container Query) requirements. [Goal] The same component is laid out horizontally with an image in a wide sidebar, and automatically becomes vertical and compact in a narrow card slot, based on the width of its container rather than the browser window width. [When it triggers] Recomputed live when the container size changes, including cases where the window does not change but the container does, such as dragging a split pane or expanding a drawer. [Implementation] First write container-type: inline-size on the component's outer wrapper element, and to target across levels also add container-name: card; then in the component styles use @container card (min-width: 400px){...} for the wide-state styles, keeping the default styles as the narrow state (mobile first). Sizes inside the component can use container-relative units cqw / cqi, e.g. font-size: clamp(14px, 4cqi, 20px). Note that the query container itself must not have its width changed by rules inside it, otherwise it loops. [Key parameters] container-type = inline-size (query only the horizontal axis, avoiding layout loops); breakpoints = 400px / 600px; font size = 4cqi. [Pitfalls] Putting container-type on the queried component itself and then querying itself never takes effect; the query targets an ancestor container, so add one more wrapper. Also, an element with container-type gets size containment and can no longer be sized by its content. [Dependencies] None; native support in Chrome 105+ / Safari 16+ / Firefox 110+.

has-selector.logic: :has() is a relational pseudo-class: parent:has(child) matches the parent element when it contains a matching descendant or sibling, providing the long-missing "parent selector" and reverse selection. It supports the >, +, ~ combinators, as in label:has(+ input:checked). It cannot be nested within itself. Widely available as Baseline (Chrome 105/Safari 15.4/Firefox 121).
has-selector.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the ":has() Relational Selector" (:has() Relational Selector) requirements. [Goal] A parent element can change its style based on what is inside it, for example switching layout when a card contains an image, or highlighting a whole row when an input is selected, with no need for JS to add class names. [When it triggers] The browser recomputes automatically when the DOM structure or child state changes, with no event listeners needed. [Implementation] Write it as parent:has(selector); the selector in the parentheses is evaluated relative to the parent: .card:has(img) matches cards that contain an image; .field:has(input:invalid) turns the whole form row red; label:has(+ input:checked) uses the adjacent sibling combinator to match the label of a checked item; :has(> .badge) looks only at direct children. It can be combined with :not() for inverse checks. Page-level switches also work, such as body:has(dialog[open]) { overflow: hidden }, replacing the JS scroll-locking approach when a dialog opens. It cannot nest another :has() inside, and it cannot act on pseudo-elements. [Key parameters] Combinators = > for direct children, + for adjacent siblings, ~ for following siblings; narrow the scope to a specific class name and do not write :has(*). [Pitfalls] Hanging :has() on a broad selector like body or * and stuffing in complex conditions makes the style-recalculation scope the whole tree, causing visible jank in long lists; also, it matches the parent element itself, so do not expect .a:has(.b) to style .b. [Dependencies] None.

anchor-positioning.logic: Set anchor-name: --foo on the anchor element and position-anchor: --foo on the positioned element, then place it relative to the anchor with the anchor() function or the position-area grid (tooltips, dropdowns, popovers). @position-try provides flip fallbacks when space is insufficient. Supported in Chrome 125+/Firefox 147+; Safari 18 lacks @position-try.
anchor-positioning.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Anchor Positioning" (Anchor Positioning) requirements. [Goal] Precisely position floating layers (tooltip, dropdown, popover) relative to a named anchor. [When it triggers] When a floating layer needs to be positioned relative to a specific element. [Implementation] Set anchor-name: --foo on the anchor element; set position-anchor: --foo on the positioned element; use the anchor() function to reference edges or position-area for quick positioning; @position-try provides flip fallbacks. [Key parameters] anchor-name: --foo; position-anchor: --foo; top: anchor(bottom); position-area: top-center. [Pitfalls] Supported in Chrome 125+ / Firefox 147+; it does not refresh automatically on size changes, so use ResizeObserver; Safari lacks @position-try. [Dependencies] None.

cascade-layers.logic: @layer explicitly orders cascade priority with named layers: earlier-declared layers are, as a whole, weaker than later-declared ones, decoupled from selector specificity. You can predefine the order with @layer reset, base, components; to make the override relationship among third-party libraries, resets, and app styles controllable, reducing overuse of !important.
cascade-layers.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Cascade Layers" (Cascade Layers) requirements. [Goal] Use @layer to explicitly order style priority: earlier-declared layers are as a whole weaker than later-declared ones, decoupled from selector specificity, reducing overuse of !important. [When it triggers] When managing global style priority. [Implementation] Write @layer reset, base, components; to predefine the layer order; put reset styles in the reset layer, global basics in the base layer, app components in the components layer, and third-party library styles can go in their own @layer third-party; priority is determined only by layer declaration order, not selector specificity, and inline styles still take precedence over everything. [Key parameters] Layer order (reset -> base -> components -> unlayered); selector specificity applies only within a layer; !important reverses priority. [Pitfalls] Inline styles and !important still beat layers, making layers useless; third-party library styles that are not in a layer cannot be overridden; writing the layer order backwards reverses priority; forgetting that unlayered styles have the highest priority. [Dependencies] None.

custom-properties.logic: Declare custom properties with --name: value and read them with var(--name, fallback); they follow the cascade and inheritance, and can be rewritten at runtime with JS or a :root theme class to achieve dynamic theming. With @property you can register a type so they can take part in animated transitions.
custom-properties.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "Custom Properties (CSS Variables)" (Custom Properties (CSS Variables)) requirements. [Goal] Values such as colors, spacing, and radii are defined in one place and changing one line takes effect site-wide; at runtime you can also re-theme and override per component locally, with no recompiling. [When it triggers] Always on; takes effect immediately when switching theme, switching density, or when JS changes a value. [Implementation] Declare global values on :root with --token-name: value and read them with var(--token-name, fallback), where the second argument is the fallback when undefined. They follow the cascade and inheritance, so redeclaring a variable of the same name on a container overrides it locally, and theme switching is swapping in a set of variables under [data-theme] on html. On the JS side, write with el.style.setProperty('--x', v) and read with getComputedStyle. To let a variable take part in transition animations, first register syntax, initial-value, and inherits with @property, otherwise it is treated as a string and cannot be interpolated. [Key parameters] Two naming layers: raw values --blue-500, semantic values --color-primary, with components referencing only semantic values; always write the var() fallback; @property syntax is '<color>' or '<length>'. [Pitfalls] Declaring a variable inside a child component but referencing it elsewhere yields an empty value and invalidates the whole declaration; variables are looked up along the inheritance chain and only work on ancestors. Also, you cannot write var(--n)px; write calc(var(--n) * 1px). [Dependencies] None.

color-mix.logic: color-mix(in oklch, blue 30%, white) mixes two colors by percentage in the specified color space, natively implementing tint/shade/alpha derivation. It is often combined with custom properties to generate derived colors such as hover, border, and light background in bulk from a single brand color. Supported in Chrome, Firefox, and Safari.
color-mix.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "color-mix()" (color-mix()) requirements. [Goal] Maintain only one brand color site-wide, and derived colors such as hover state, light background, outline, and disabled state are computed by the browser, so the whole set follows when the main color changes. [When it triggers] Evaluated continuously; recomputed automatically when a theme switch or a user customization rewrites the main color variable. [Implementation] The syntax is color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand) 85%, black): the first argument is the interpolation color space, followed by two colors each with a percentage. Mix with black to darken, with white to lighten, with transparent for translucency. Write the hover background as color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand) 88%, black), the light background as color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand) 12%, white), and the outline as color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand) 40%, transparent), which is easier than handwriting rgba and follows the variable. Prefer oklch or oklab as the color space, since the mixed intermediate colors have even lightness; srgb often comes out gray and muddy. [Key parameters] Color space = in oklch; hover darkening = mix with 12% to 15% black; light background = 10% to 15% brand mixed with white; outline = 30% to 40% brand mixed with transparent. [Pitfalls] Writing the mix expression separately at every place a color is used spreads a dozen derived variants from one brand color, which is no easier to change than hard-coding; derive --brand-hover and --brand-soft once in :root and reference them. Also, old browsers that do not recognize it invalidate the whole declaration, so write a static color first as a base at critical spots. [Dependencies] None.

oklch.logic: oklch(L C H) describes color with three perceptually uniform components: lightness, chroma, and hue. The same L value gives consistent perceived brightness across hues, making palettes more harmonious, and it can express the P3 wide gamut beyond sRGB. Compared with HSL, it avoids distortions such as dark blues and overly bright yellows. Available in all major browsers.
oklch.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "OKLCH Color" (OKLCH Color) requirements. [Goal] Hues at the same lightness level look equally bright, so the palette is tidy and does not jump; light-to-dark steps transition evenly, with no dark blues or glaring yellows, and you can also use more vivid P3 wide-gamut colors. [When it triggers] When defining palettes and design variables; when deriving state colors such as hover and disabled. [Implementation] Write colors as oklch(L C H): L is perceptual lightness 0~1, C is chroma (generally not above 0.37 within sRGB), H is the hue angle 0~360, and with alpha write oklch(0.7 0.15 250 / 0.5). When building a color ramp, fix C and H and vary only L; for different hues at the same level, fix L and the palette will be naturally harmonious. Derive state colors with native color-mix(in oklch, var(--accent), black 12%) instead of hand-tuning hex values. For old-browser compatibility, wrap it in @supports (color: oklch(0 0 0)) and leave a hex fallback outside. [Key parameters] Body text L≈0.25, page background L≈0.98; brand color C=0.12~0.18; hover ΔL=-0.05; C beyond sRGB is gamut-mapped automatically. [Pitfalls] Copying HSL numbers straight into oklch gives a wash of dead gray, because the ranges and meanings are completely different; re-pick the color or convert with a tool. Also, pushing C too high gets clipped on ordinary sRGB screens, so different devices show different colors. [Dependencies] None.

text-wrap-balance.logic: text-wrap: balance makes the browser distribute characters evenly across lines, avoiding a lone word on the last line of a heading (suited to headings with few lines); pretty optimizes orphans and word breaks in long paragraphs. balance is fairly widely supported, while pretty is currently mainly in Chromium/WebKit.
text-wrap-balance.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "text-wrap: balance / pretty" (text-wrap: balance / pretty) requirements. [Goal] Headings no longer end with an awkward last line of just one or two words, lines are close in length and the outline is tidy; long paragraphs also do not end with an orphan word. [When it triggers] Takes effect automatically at browser layout time; rebalances when the container width changes and after web fonts finish loading. [Implementation] Write text-wrap: balance on heading elements, and the browser will spread characters across lines as evenly as possible, suited to short text of two to four lines. For body paragraphs use text-wrap: pretty instead, which only optimizes end-of-line orphans and word breaks without reflowing the whole paragraph, at much lower cost. Split by element: h1, h2, card titles, and button labels use balance; p and caption text use pretty. Pair it with max-width to constrain line width so the effect is visible; on single-line text it does nothing. Browsers that do not support it ignore the declaration and fall back to default wrapping, so no fallback is needed. [Key parameters] balance applies to up to 4 lines (beyond 6 lines the browser gives up balancing); heading max-width = 20ch to 30ch; body max-width = 65ch; always use pretty rather than balance for body text. [Pitfalls] Applying balance to every p site-wide makes the browser try layouts multiple times on long paragraphs, noticeably slowing layout on long-form pages, and lines all stretched to equal length actually look unnatural; also, it only controls line-break positions, and long English words or URLs that overflow still need overflow-wrap: anywhere. [Dependencies] None.

clamp-fluid-typography.logic: clamp(min, preferred, max) gives a variable value constrained by lower and upper bounds; the preferred value often uses vw or an expression containing vw, so font size and spacing scale smoothly with the viewport without running out of control. Use it in place of many media queries that change font-size step by step at breakpoints, achieving truly continuous responsive typography.
clamp-fluid-typography.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "clamp() Fluid Typography" (clamp() Fluid Typography) requirements. [Goal] Headings and spacing scale continuously and smoothly with the window width: never too small to read on phones, never too large on ultrawide screens, and without the jump of a breakpoint step in between. [When it triggers] Always on; follows live as the window resizes, no media queries needed. [Implementation] Write font-size: clamp(min, preferred, max); the preferred value in the middle must contain vw to be fluid, and a form like clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 2vw, 3rem) is recommended: the fixed rem part ensures it still works when users enlarge the default font size, and the vw part follows the viewport. Convert the whole type scale to clamp, with a steep gradient for headings and a gentle or even non-fluid gradient for body text. The same pattern can be used on padding, gap, and border-radius so the page's rhythm scales together; store these expressions in --step-1 through --step-5 and use them consistently. [Key parameters] Body clamp(1rem, 0.95rem + 0.25vw, 1.125rem); H1 clamp(2rem, 1.2rem + 3vw, 4rem); unitless line-height 1.2~1.5; minimum no lower than 14px. [Pitfalls] Writing the preferred value as pure vw (e.g. clamp(1rem, 4vw, 3rem)) makes it completely unresponsive when users increase the default font size in the browser, failing accessibility; always mix rem and vw. Also, do not forget the cap, otherwise body text is too large on big screens. [Dependencies] None.

scrollbar-gutter.logic: scrollbar-gutter: stable reserves the gutter width occupied by the scrollbar, so content does not shift horizontally when the scrollbar appears or disappears. both-edges reserves a symmetric gutter on both sides to keep visual balance, commonly used for dialogs and scrollable panels.
scrollbar-gutter.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "scrollbar-gutter" (scrollbar-gutter) requirements. [Goal] Reserve the scrollbar gutter so there is no horizontal jitter when the scrollbar appears or disappears. [When it triggers] Scrollable containers, dialogs, and sidebars that need a stable layout. [Implementation] Set scrollbar-gutter: stable on elements that can produce a scrollbar (html, body, or overflow: auto), and the browser reserves the standard width; scrollbar-gutter: stable both-edges reserves a symmetric gutter on both sides. [Key parameters] scrollbar-gutter: stable; scrollbar-gutter: stable both-edges. [Pitfalls] Width differs across browsers (usually 15-17px); a customized width does not adapt after it changes; both-edges wastes space when only one direction scrolls. [Dependencies] None.

scroll-behavior.logic: scroll-behavior: smooth makes anchor jumps and scripted scrollTo scroll smoothly with animation instead of teleporting. Combine it with scroll-padding (to leave a stop offset for sticky headers) and scroll-margin (to adjust the alignment margin of the target element) to fix positioning. It should respect prefers-reduced-motion and turn animation off.
scroll-behavior.prompt: Implement "scroll-behavior" (scroll-behavior) at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When a table-of-contents anchor is clicked or back-to-top is used, the page slides smoothly there so users can see where they were taken, instead of the view jumping instantly. [When it triggers] When an anchor link is clicked, or a script calls scrollTo or scrollIntoView; the same applies when form validation fails and scrolls to the first error. [Implementation] Write scroll-behavior: smooth on html, which covers both anchor jumps and scripted scrolling; to make only one scroll container smooth, write it on that container. When the page has a fixed sticky nav, add scroll-padding-top: 64px on html, or scroll-margin-top: 64px on each anchor target, otherwise the heading is covered by the nav bar. The more controllable form in script is el.scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth', block: 'start' }) or window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: 'smooth' }). You must respect the system preference: inside @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) set scroll-behavior back to auto. [Key parameters] scroll-padding-top = actual nav height (commonly 64px); block = 'start' (use 'center' to center); for scroll distances over 3 screens, prefer auto, since a long slide is disorienting. [Pitfalls] Writing it on body when html is what actually scrolls has no effect at all; also, triggering a new scroll during a smooth scroll interrupts the previous one, so rapid clicks on the TOC look laggy; add a short throttle on click. [Dependencies] None.

overscroll-behavior.logic: overscroll-behavior: contain breaks scroll chaining: once the inner element scrolls to the end it no longer passes scrolling to the page, commonly used for dialogs, sidebars, and chat lists. The value none also disables the browser's default pull-to-refresh and rubber-band bounce effects.
overscroll-behavior.prompt: Handle the code mentioned above according to the "overscroll-behavior" (overscroll-behavior) requirements. [Goal] In dialogs, side drawers, and chat lists, when you keep scrolling after reaching the end, the page behind does not move at all, and there is no more jumpiness where the outer container keeps scrolling after the inner one is done. [When it triggers] When the inner scroll container reaches its top or bottom boundary and the user keeps scrolling or swiping in the same direction. [Implementation] Add overscroll-behavior: contain to this inner scroll container (it must itself have overflow: auto or scroll), and the scroll chain breaks there; to handle only vertical, write overscroll-behavior-y: contain. The value none, on top of contain, also turns off the browser's default pull-to-refresh and rubber-band bounce, suited to full-screen pages with an app-like feel, and can be written on html. It replaces the old hacks of preventDefault on touchmove or adding position: fixed to body, which lose the scroll position and can be removed. [Key parameters] contain (breaks scroll chain, keeps own bounce); none (additionally disables pull-to-refresh and bounce); auto (default); write it on the scroll container itself, not on its parent. [Pitfalls] Writing it on the outermost overlay of a dialog has no effect; the property must be on the element that actually scrolls. Also, it is equally ineffective when the container's content does not overflow and cannot scroll at all. [Dependencies] None.

feature-queries.logic: @supports (property:value) tests in the stylesheet whether the browser supports a given CSS feature, and applies the enclosed rules only if it does, enabling progressive enhancement and graceful degradation. Combine conditions with not, and, or; it can also test selectors via @supports selector(:has()).
feature-queries.prompt: Apply "Feature Queries (@supports)" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Detect in the stylesheet whether the browser supports a CSS feature, and apply rules only when it does, giving progressive enhancement and graceful degradation. [When it triggers] When the stylesheet loads (parse time, not runtime). [Implementation] Use @supports(property:value){…} or @supports(selector(:has())){…}; combine conditions with not, and, or; when unsupported the block is skipped automatically and the fallback styles render. [Key parameters] Property tests (e.g. aspect-ratio, gap), selector tests (:has() / :is() etc.), logical combinations and/or/not. [Pitfalls] Syntax inside @supports must match exactly, including whitespace (color: red vs color:red differ); selector tests are error-prone, especially pseudo-classes; results can change after browser updates and cause sudden style shifts; without a fallback, unsupported browsers may not render at all. [Dependencies] None.

css-containment.logic: contain promises the browser that a subtree's layout/paint/size will not leak outside (layout, paint, size, style, or the shorthands content and strict), so reflow and repaint stay local and performance improves. paint and layout also create their own stacking context and containing block.
css-containment.prompt: Apply "CSS Containment (contain)" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Limit how far a subtree's layout, paint and size can affect the rest of the page, localizing reflow and repaint to improve performance. [When it triggers] Large lists or repeated card components that need performance tuning. [Implementation] contain: paint (own layer) / layout (does not affect outside) / content (layout+paint+style) / strict (all); most effective together with fixed width and height. [Key parameters] contain: paint; contain: layout; contain: content; contain: strict; explicit width/height. [Pitfalls] size containment needs explicit fixed dimensions; paint creates a stacking context, which changes z-index behavior; replacing overflow: hidden with contain performs better but does not clip the content. [Dependencies] None.

clip-path.logic: clip-path cuts out an element's visible region with geometry functions: circle(), ellipse(), inset(), or a polygon() vertex list; it can also reference an SVG <clipPath>. Anything outside is clipped away and stops receiving events. Common for slanted cuts, hexagonal avatars and irregular cards; with percentage vertices it can be animated in transitions.
clip-path.prompt: Implement "clip-path" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Clip an element into a non-rectangular shape, such as a slanted section divider, a hexagonal avatar, or a card with a notch; the clipped-off part is neither visible nor clickable. [When it triggers] Always-on style; changing vertex coordinates on hover or scroll gives a shape transition. [Implementation] Four common functions: inset(10px round 8px) insets all four edges with rounded corners, circle(50% at 50% 50%) makes a circle, ellipse(40% 30% at center) an ellipse, and polygon() lists vertices clockwise, e.g. polygon(0 0, 100% 0, 100% 85%, 0 100%) gives a banner with a slanted bottom edge. For complex shapes reference SVG instead: clip-path: url(#myClip), and set clipPathUnits="objectBoundingBox" on the clipPath so vertices use 0 to 1 ratios. To animate, the two polygons must have the same number of vertices to interpolate; when a shape has fewer corners, repeat a coordinate to pad. [Key parameters] Use percentages for all vertex units (so it scales with the container); slant drop = 10% to 15% of the bottom edge; inset radius = round 8px; transition duration = 300ms. [Pitfalls] Clipping also cuts off box-shadow and outline; for a shadow, wrap the element in a parent and use filter: drop-shadow() instead; also, clipped-off areas no longer receive mouse events, so if a button's clickable area is clipped smaller, users will miss it. [Dependencies] None.

mask.logic: mask-image uses the alpha or luminance of an image or gradient as a mask that decides how visible each part of the element is, enabling fading edges, cut-out icons and texture reveals. Multiple mask layers can be combined with mask-composite (intersect/add/subtract). For Safari compatibility the -webkit-mask prefix is usually needed.
mask.prompt: Implement "CSS Mask" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Fade an element's edges to transparent, punch an icon out so the background shows through, or reveal a texture only within a given shape, all without pre-slicing images. [When it triggers] Always-on; you can also transition mask-position or mask-size for wipe or shine-sweep animations. [Implementation] Specify the mask source with mask-image: for a fade, write mask-image: linear-gradient(to bottom, black 60%, transparent); where the mask is opaque the element is visible, where it is transparent it is erased. For single-color icons prefer mask over img: give the element a background color, then mask-image: url(icon.svg) with mask-size: contain and mask-repeat: no-repeat, so one SVG works in any color. Separate multiple masks with commas and combine them with mask-composite for intersection or cut-out. For Safari, also write the -webkit-mask- prefixed properties. [Key parameters] mask-image=linear-gradient(...); mask-size=contain or 100% 100%; mask-repeat=no-repeat; mask-composite=intersect. [Pitfalls] With only the standard properties and no -webkit-mask, the whole content may disappear or the mask may not work in Safari; masks use the alpha channel by default, so if a grayscale image has no effect add mask-mode: luminance; also, a mask only changes visibility, not the hit area, so erased parts remain clickable; to clip those too, combine with clip-path. [Dependencies] None.

shape-outside.logic: On a floated element, shape-outside: circle()/polygon() or an image's alpha outline makes adjacent inline text flow around that geometric shape instead of the rectangular box. shape-margin adds extra breathing room around the shape, giving magazine-style text wrap.
shape-outside.prompt: Apply "shape-outside" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Make inline text around a floated element flow along a specified geometric shape instead of the rectangular box, for magazine-style layouts. [When it triggers] When applied to a floated element. [Implementation] On a float:left/right element set shape-outside: circle(100px), polygon(0 0, 100% 0, 100% 100%) or url(image.png); circle() takes a radius, polygon() a coordinate list, url() uses the image's alpha outline; shape-margin adds extra spacing around the shape. [Key parameters] The shape-outside value (circle radius, polygon percentage coordinates, url image path), shape-margin = 8-20px recommended, float direction matching the side. [Pitfalls] A circle() radius larger than the float's size makes the wrap behave oddly; polygon() coordinates outside the box give irregular shapes; the url() image must have an alpha channel or it falls back to a rectangular wrap; too large a shape-margin makes the gap too wide. [Dependencies] None.

mix-blend-mode.logic: mix-blend-mode defines how an element's pixels blend with the content beneath it using Photoshop-style algorithms: multiply darkens, screen lightens, overlay/difference and more. Commonly used for text that inverts against the background and colored overprint effects. background-blend-mode blends multiple background layers of the same element. Blending causes the browser to create a new stacking context.
mix-blend-mode.prompt: Implement "mix-blend-mode" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Blend the top element's pixels with the content beneath it algorithmically, e.g. text that automatically inverts over any background to stay readable, or color blocks that overlap with a print-like overprint texture. [When it triggers] Always-on style; you can also switch modes on hover or when scrolling past dark sections. [Implementation] Set mix-blend-mode on the top element; four common modes: multiply darkens (white becomes transparent, good for laying textures over a base color), screen lightens (black becomes transparent, good for light effects), overlay boosts contrast, difference inverts (text flips automatically with the background brightness). To blend multiple backgrounds within one element use background-blend-mode instead. Blending applies to the content beneath within the same stacking context; to confine the effect inside a container, add isolation: isolate to it, otherwise it blends all the way down to the page's root background. [Key parameters] Mode = multiply / screen / overlay / difference (try all four before deciding); top element opacity = 1 (changing opacity creates another stacking context and alters the result); container isolation = isolate. [Pitfalls] Using difference on body text makes the color uncontrollable once the background changes, and contrast can drop too low to read; use it only on decorative large headings; also, blending forces the element onto its own layer, and large-area blending is GPU-heavy on mobile, so keep the area small. [Dependencies] None.

backdrop-filter.logic: backdrop-filter applies filters such as blur(), saturate() and brightness() to the content behind the element (not the element itself), and is the core technique for real-time blur behind translucent panels. The element itself needs some transparency to let the processed backdrop show through; Safari needs the -webkit- prefix.
backdrop-filter.prompt: Implement "backdrop-filter" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The page content behind a translucent nav bar, modal or card is blurred in real time; when scrolling, the content underneath blurs as it moves, like frosted glass. [When it triggers] Always-on; you can also transition the blur from 0 to the target value when a modal opens. [Implementation] Write backdrop-filter: blur(20px) saturate(180%) on the panel, and its own background must be translucent, e.g. background: rgba(255,255,255,.6) — an opaque background covers the whole result and defeats the effect. Filter functions can be chained; a bit of saturate recovers color lost by blurring. Safari also needs -webkit-backdrop-filter. For dark themes use a dark translucent color like rgba(20,20,22,.6) plus a 1px light inner stroke (inset box-shadow) to outline the glass edge. [Key parameters] blur = 16~24px (nav bar 12px, large modal 30px); background alpha = 0.5~0.7; saturate = 180%; stroke = 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.18). [Pitfalls] When a parent or the element has overflow:hidden with rounded corners, the blur can spill past the corners in some browsers — give the panel its own border-radius and isolation:isolate; also, keeping large areas on permanently is GPU-heavy and drops frames on low-end devices; use @supports to degrade to a plain translucent background if needed. [Dependencies] None.

filter.logic: filter applies graphical filter functions to the element's own pixels, chainable: blur(), brightness()/contrast(), saturate()/hue-rotate(), grayscale()/sepia(), and drop-shadow() which casts a shadow that follows the opaque outline. Most functions animate smoothly in transitions.
filter.prompt: Implement "filter" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Make the element look image-processed: blurred, brightened or darkened, desaturated, hue-shifted, or casting a shadow that follows its opaque outline, all without changing the image asset. [When it triggers] Always-on, or toggled on the underlying element on hover, disabled state, or when a modal opens. [Implementation] filter takes a list of functions applied in written order: grayscale(1) for an inactive gray state; brightness(0.6) saturate(1.2) for a dimmed background layer; blur(4px) for out-of-focus; drop-shadow(0 4px 8px rgba(0,0,0,0.3)) to cast a shadow on transparent PNGs or clip-path-clipped elements, following the real outline rather than the rectangular box. For a hover color reveal write transition: filter 200ms, going from grayscale(1) to grayscale(0). Note that when filter is not none, the element creates a new stacking context and becomes the containing block for descendants with fixed positioning. [Key parameters] blur = 4px to 8px (8px for background defocus); brightness = 0.6 (dim the underlying layer); saturate = 1.1 to 1.3 (slight saturation boost); transition duration = 200ms. [Pitfalls] Adding filter to a container that holds a position:fixed child makes that child scroll along with the container, because the containing block changed; move the filter elsewhere; also, large-area blur is recomputed every frame and is GPU-heavy, so don't use it on elements that scroll or reflow frequently. [Dependencies] None.

isolation.logic: isolation:isolate forces the creation of a new stacking context with no side effects, locking the influence of children's z-index and mix-blend-mode inside it so they don't bleed out to blend unexpectedly or overlap sibling layers. It is a clean way to control blend modes and stacking boundaries.
isolation.prompt: Apply "isolation" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Create a stacking context without side effects, locking child z-index and mix-blend-mode inside so they cannot leak out. [When it triggers] When blend modes or z-index stacking need to be isolated. [Implementation] isolation: isolate forces a stacking context without changing position/opacity/transform; it prevents mix-blend-mode or high z-index children from reaching the outer layer. [Key parameters] isolation: isolate; combine with mix-blend-mode (screen, multiply, overlay) or multiple z-indexes. [Pitfalls] It isolates only direct children, and grandchildren can still leak through; mix-blend-mode looks different on different backgrounds (screen is too bright on dark); it is not a substitute for position: relative. [Dependencies] None.

safe-area-inset.logic: Use env(safe-area-inset-top/bottom/left/right) to read the margins taken up by notches, rounded corners and the bottom home indicator, and add them to padding to avoid being covered. This requires the viewport meta to set viewport-fit=cover so the page extends to the screen edges; often combined with max() to keep regular spacing.
safe-area-inset.prompt: Apply "Safe Area Inset" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] On notched phones and phones with a bottom indicator bar, the top title is not blocked by the cutout, bottom buttons do not sit on the home indicator, and in landscape the left and right content does not touch the rounded edges. [When it triggers] Always-on; recomputed automatically when the safe area changes, e.g. on device rotation or entering fullscreen. [Implementation] First add viewport-fit=cover to the HTML viewport meta so the page extends to the physical screen edges; otherwise env() always returns 0. Then on elements that need to avoid the insets use env(safe-area-inset-top/bottom/left/right), usually with max() to keep regular spacing: padding-bottom: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-bottom)). The bottom-fixed action bar and the top immersive nav are the two must-change places. The background color should extend to the edge and only the content should avoid it, so add the inset to padding rather than to margin or container height. [Key parameters] viewport-fit=cover (prerequisite; without it all values are 0); base spacing = 16px (with max() as a floor); bottom indicator about 34px; top notch 44~59px; never hardcode them. [Pitfalls] env() without a fallback value invalidates the whole declaration in unsupporting browsers — write env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px); also, do not hardcode 34px per device model, since it misaligns on other devices; always let env() compute it. [Dependencies] None.

line-clamp.logic: The classic recipe is display:-webkit-box; -webkit-box-orient:vertical; -webkit-line-clamp:3; overflow:hidden, which limits text to a set number of lines and ends with an ellipsis. The new standard line-clamp shorthand is landing, removing the need for the -webkit-box combination.
line-clamp.prompt: Implement "Line Clamp" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Summaries in a list all show a fixed number of lines, with overflow ending in an ellipsis, so card heights stay uniform and are not blown out by long text. [When it triggers] Always-on style; when the text or container width changes, the browser recomputes the truncation point automatically. [Implementation] The reliable recipe is to set all four together: display: -webkit-box; -webkit-box-orient: vertical; -webkit-line-clamp: 3; overflow: hidden. Despite the -webkit- prefix, all major browsers support it and it is production-ready; the unprefixed line-clamp shorthand is landing and can be added in the same rule as progressive enhancement, but do not write only that for now. For single-line truncation don't use this; use white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis, which is more robust. To fix the card height, compute it as line count times line-height. [Key parameters] Lines = 3 (list summary) / 2 (card title); line-height = 1.5; container height = lines times 1.5em; use text-overflow: ellipsis for single-line truncation. [Pitfalls] Adding margin or padding to children of the -webkit-box throws off the line-height calculation and the number of visible lines, so put the text directly in this element; also, this recipe changes the layout behavior of children, so don't put complex structures with buttons or tags inside; plain text only. [Dependencies] None.

stacking-context.logic: z-index is only compared within the same stacking context. A positioned (non-static) element with z-index, opacity<1, transform, filter, will-change and so on creates a new stacking context, and its descendants are sealed inside the parent's level. Understanding this explains why an element with a huge z-index still can't beat another one.
stacking-context.prompt: Apply "Stacking Context (z-index)" to the code mentioned above. [Goal] Modals, dropdown menus and sticky navs sit above exactly what they should, and there are no more cases where z-index is already 9999 yet the element is still covered by something else. [When it triggers] When debugging overlap issues; before adding a new overlay component or adding animation or opacity to a container, first confirm which layer it is in. [Implementation] Remember that z-index is only compared inside the same stacking context: once an ancestor creates a new stacking context, no z-index on a child, however large, can escape that ancestor's level. Common properties that create a new context: position non-static with z-index not auto, opacity less than 1, transform, filter, backdrop-filter, will-change, isolation:isolate, contain:paint, and fixed/sticky positioning. When debugging, walk up from the problem element and check each ancestor for these properties. The real fix is to move the overlay under body with a Portal, or use native dialog and popover, which render in the top layer, instead of increasing the number. [Key parameters] z-index scale: content 0, sticky 100, drawer 200, modal 300, tooltip 400; use isolation:isolate to isolate deliberately; 9999 is not allowed. [Pitfalls] Adding transform for animation or an opacity transition to a parent container makes the dropdown menu inside get covered by sibling cards — clear the transform after the animation ends, or move the menu out of that container. [Dependencies] None.

[Goal] On a long page, once the user has scrolled down more than one screen, a round button fades in at the bottom right; clicking it smooth-scrolls the page back to the top, and the button then fades out. [Dependencies] None.

sticky-footer.prompt: Implement "Sticky Footer" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] On pages with little content (404, empty states) the footer also sits at the bottom of the viewport instead of hanging mid-air; when content is long the footer naturally follows the content and never covers the body. [When it triggers] Pure layout, no interaction; recalculated automatically when the viewport height changes. [Implementation] Give the outermost container min-height: 100dvh, display: grid, and grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto for header, main, and footer; the 1fr on the main row absorbs the extra space. **Use dvh, not vh**: when a mobile browser's address bar collapses, vh doesn't change and the footer gets pushed off screen. For older browsers, write min-height: 100vh before it as a fallback. [Key parameters] min-height=100dvh (fallback 100vh); row template=auto 1fr auto; main min-height 0 (prevents inner overflow from blowing out the layout). [Pitfalls] Pinning the footer to the bottom with position: fixed: that is "always floating", not "sticky to the bottom", and on long pages it keeps covering content; and giving main min-height: calc(100vh - footer height), which breaks the moment the footer height changes (and it does change responsively). [Goal] In a corner of the footer there is a "Subscribe for updates" line with an email field and button below it; on invalid input a line of red text appears right under the field, and after a successful submit the whole block is replaced in place by "Subscribed, confirmation email sent", with no page navigation. [When it triggers] Validate the first time on blur (don't report errors while typing); validate again on submit; success and failure are both reported in place. [Implementation] Wrap it in a real
, with the input type="email", autocomplete="email", required, letting the browser act as a fallback. Submit with fetch; while pending, the button goes into loading and disabled to prevent duplicate submits. Put the error message in a

and add aria-describedby="err" and aria-invalid on the input so screen readers announce it. On success, replace the whole form with the confirmation text and give the container role="status" so the change is announced. [Key parameters] Validation timing = blur + submit; request timeout 8s; loading state shown for at least 300ms (if it flashes too fast it looks like nothing happened); error copy must be specific ("This email address looks invalid" rather than "Invalid input"). [Pitfalls] Reporting errors while typing, so users see a wall of red after two letters; and on success only changing the button text to "Subscribed" while the input is still there and clickable, leaving users unsure whether it worked. [Dependencies] None.

sitemap-footer.logic: The footer serves as the site-wide navigation fallback: it lists main sections and second-level pages in a hierarchy, using a nav landmark and group headings so screen readers and search engines can both understand the structure.
sitemap-footer.prompt: Implement "Sitemap Footer" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The footer is not just a few links but a readable site structure: main sections are the first level, each with three to eight second-level pages beneath it, so readers can see at a glance what the site contains. [When it triggers] Static; with many sections it can be combined with collapsible groups. [Implementation] Wrap the whole block in <nav aria-label="Sitemap">, with one <section> per section containing an <h3> group heading and a <ul> of second-level links. **Group headings must be real heading tags** so screen-reader users can jump by heading. Link text should use the page's real title, never "click here". The link for the current page gets aria-current="page" and no underline. [Key parameters] 3~8 items per group (more than 8 means the section should be split); first-level heading 13px/600, second-level 13px/400; group spacing 32px, item line-height 1.9. [Pitfalls] Stuffing every link into the footer, ending up with hundreds: the weight is diluted and nobody can read it, so list only the main paths; and omitting the nav landmark and aria-label, so screen-reader users hear a pile of context-free links, and since the page usually already has other navs, without a label they can't tell which is which. [Dependencies] None.

sticky-table-header.logic: The table header stays pinned to the top of the container while the table scrolls vertically. position:sticky goes on th, not thead (most browsers don't honor it on thead), and the scroll container must be an ancestor of the table.
sticky-table-header.prompt: Implement "Sticky Table Header" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When the table scrolls down, the header stays pinned at the top so you still know what each column is at row 200; a divider line or shadow under the header separates it from the content scrolling past. [When it triggers] Takes effect automatically when the table content exceeds the scroll container's height; no interaction needed. [Implementation] Put position: sticky; top: 0 on **th, not thead**: many browsers don't honor sticky on thead/tr. The th must have an opaque background color, otherwise rows underneath show through. The scroll container is a div wrapping the table with overflow: auto and a fixed max-height. The header z-index must be higher than the cells; if there are also frozen columns, the intersection cell needs one more level. [Key parameters] th top=0 (use the height of the sticky nav instead if the page has one); th z-index=2, frozen column 1, intersection cell 3; shadow under header 0 1px 0 rgba(0,0,0,.14); container max-height computed from screen height, not hard-coded. [Pitfalls] Setting sticky on thead and then searching everywhere for why it doesn't work; and using a semi-transparent background on th, so text visibly overlaps while scrolling, which looks very dirty. [Dependencies] None.

frozen-columns.logic: When a wide table scrolls horizontally, the first column (usually name/ID) stays pinned on the left. Again use position:sticky with a left offset; when freezing multiple columns, each left value must accumulate the widths of the preceding columns.
frozen-columns.prompt: Implement "Frozen Columns" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When a table with many columns scrolls horizontally, the leftmost name column stays visible while the data columns on the right slide underneath it; a shadow between the frozen area and the scrolling area makes the boundary obvious at a glance. [When it triggers] Takes effect automatically as horizontal scrolling when the table is wider than its container. [Implementation] Give the cells to freeze position: sticky; left: 0; if a second column is frozen, its left must equal the first column's width (store column widths in CSS variables, don't hard-code). Frozen columns must have an opaque background. The divider shadow **shows only when actually scrolled**: listen for the container's scrollLeft > 0 and add a class to the container that toggles the box-shadow on the right side of the frozen column; showing it all the time leaves a needless line even when not scrolled. The cell where the header and frozen column intersect must set both top and left, with z-index one higher than the larger of the two. [Key parameters] Frozen column width should be fixed (e.g. 200px), since fluid widths make the accumulated left inaccurate; divider shadow inset -1px 0 0 border color plus a 4px outward spread; shadow fade-in 150ms. [Pitfalls] Using percentage widths for frozen columns, so the left offsets are all misaligned once multiple columns are frozen; and forgetting to give frozen columns a background, so during horizontal scrolling two layers of text just overlap. [Dependencies] None.

table-sort.logic: Clicking a header cycles through ascending / descending / none; the currently sorted column is marked with aria-sort and shows a direction arrow. Sort state should be reflected in the URL so it survives a refresh.
table-sort.prompt: Implement "Sortable Columns" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Clicking a header cycles through ascending -> descending -> unsorted; the currently sorted column shows an arrow in a brighter color, while other columns' arrows appear faintly only on hover, hinting that "this column is clickable too". [When it triggers] Clicking the header, or pressing Enter/Space on it; after a sort change, sync it into the URL query parameters. [Implementation] Put a real <button> in the header to carry the click (if the whole th is clickable, keyboard users can't focus it), and add aria-sort="ascending|descending|none" on the th so screen readers announce the sort state. Do the sorting itself in the data layer; don't reorder the DOM. Don't enable multi-column sort by default; if really needed, add columns with shift+click and show sequence numbers in the headers. After sorting, **keep the scroll position**; don't jump back to the top. [Key parameters] Cycle order = asc -> desc -> none; arrow opacity .35 on hover, 1 when active; click target at least 44px high; URL parameters such as ?sort=name&dir=asc. [Pitfalls] Sorting already-paginated data on the frontend: that only reorders the current page, while users think they are seeing the global top item; and sorting numbers with string comparison, so "10" lands before "9". [Dependencies] None.

column-resize.logic: Drag a header's right edge to change the column width. table-layout:fixed with widths on col elements is the most robust; while dragging only change a CSS variable and persist only on release, avoiding a whole-table reflow every frame.
column-resize.prompt: Implement "Column Resize" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Moving the cursor to the boundary between two header columns turns it into a left-right arrow; press and drag to change the column width, with a vertical line following along while dragging; on release the width is fixed and remembered. [When it triggers] Starts on press inside a 6px hot zone on the header's right edge; live preview while moving; ends on release or Esc (Esc restores). [Implementation] Set table-layout: fixed on the table and use <colgroup><col> to hold each column's width; changing width only changes the col's width, so the browser doesn't need to re-measure content. The drag handle is a narrow absolutely-positioned strip inside the header; call setPointerCapture on pointerdown, and in pointermove only update the position of an indicator line driven by a CSS variable, **don't change the real column width every frame** (wide tables will drop frames); write the col width and persist only on pointerup. Add cursor: col-resize and user-select: none to body to prevent selecting text while dragging. [Key parameters] Hot zone width 6px; minimum column width 48px; indicator line 1px primary color; persist to localStorage keyed by table id. [Pitfalls] Without table-layout: fixed, changing one column's width reflows the other columns too, and dragging feels like jelly; and forgetting pointer capture, so if you drag a bit fast the cursor leaves the handle and the drag breaks. [Dependencies] None.

row-selection.logic: A checkbox on each row and a select-all checkbox in the header. The select-all box must set indeterminate when partially selected (a JS property, not an HTML attribute). Once rows are selected, a bulk-action bar floats up.
row-selection.prompt: Implement "Row Selection" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A checkbox at the left of each row, and the header one selects the whole current page; when only some rows are selected the header box shows a "half-selected" dash instead of a check; as soon as anything is selected, an action bar floats up at the bottom showing "N selected" and bulk-action buttons. [When it triggers] Clicking a checkbox toggles a single row; clicking the header box selects all / none; shift+click selects a range. [Implementation] The header checkbox's indeterminate state can only be set in JS: el.indeterminate = selectedCount > 0 && selectedCount < total; **there is no such HTML attribute**, and in JSX you need a ref or a controlled assignment. Store the selection as a Set of ids, not indexes (indexes get scrambled after pagination/sorting). Be clear about the scope of select-all: when it selects only the current page, add a "Select all N items" link in the action bar. Stick the bulk-action bar to the bottom of the table with position: sticky; bottom: 0; don't use fixed, which would cover other content. [Key parameters] Action bar appears with a 180ms slide-up fade-in; checkbox click target 44px; shift range selection anchors on the last click. [Pitfalls] Storing selection by row index, so one sort selects the wrong people; and select-all covering only the current page without saying so, leading users to think everything is selected and then bulk-delete: this is a real incident. [Dependencies] None.

table-density.logic: One toggle switches row height between comfortable / standard / compact by changing a single CSS variable. It is for people who want more data on one screen, and the preference should be remembered.
table-density.prompt: Implement "Table Density" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A small control at the top right of the table switches between "Comfortable / Standard / Compact"; in compact mode one screen shows about half again as many rows, with the font size unchanged and only row height and padding reduced. [When it triggers] Takes effect immediately on click; the choice is remembered and the next visit uses the last setting. [Implementation] Drive it with a single CSS variable: --row-py, with the three levels at 14px / 10px / 6px, and cell padding-block reads it. **Don't change the font size**: changing it makes text rewrap, cancelling the row-height gain, and narrow columns suddenly wrap. Add a short transition to the table on switching (padding 120ms) so the change between levels isn't abrupt. Store the preference in localStorage and read it before first paint to avoid a flash of the default. [Key parameters] Three levels padding-block = 14/10/6px; transition 120ms ease; font size constant at 13px; the control itself is a segmented control with the current level highlighted. [Pitfalls] Compact mode squeezing tap targets below 44px makes in-row buttons and links hard to hit; in compact mode turn row actions into icon buttons and preserve the hit area; and reading the preference only after rendering, so the page first paints at standard density and then jumps to compact, causing a flash. [Dependencies] None.

responsive-table.logic: A wide table doesn't fit on a narrow screen. Two routes: scroll the whole table horizontally (keeps the table mental model) or collapse each row into a card (more readable). Which to choose depends on the column count and whether horizontal comparison is needed.
responsive-table.prompt: Implement "Responsive Table" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] On phones a wide table no longer gets crammed together: either the whole table scrolls horizontally with the first column frozen, or each row becomes a card with field names and values stacked. On desktop it remains a normal table. [When it triggers] The layout switches when the viewport crosses the breakpoint. [Implementation] First decide which route: **if users need to compare multiple rows horizontally, use scrolling** (with frozen columns); **if they only view the details of a single record, use cards**. Scrolling approach: wrap in a div with overflow-x: auto and -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch, and add gradient masks on both sides of the container hinting that "there is more to swipe". Card approach: under a media query set table/tr/td to display: block, use td::before { content: attr(data-label) } to bring the column name in front of each cell, and give every td a data-label. **After cardifying, add role="list" to the container**, because display:block breaks the table semantics and screen readers no longer announce "table". [Key parameters] Breakpoint 768px; scrolling approach gradient mask width 24px; card approach field name takes 40% width, value 60%; card spacing 12px. [Pitfalls] When cardifying, forgetting that display:block has broken the table semantics, so screen-reader users hear a pile of unstructured text; and horizontal scrolling with no visual hint, so users have no idea there are more columns on the right. [Dependencies] None.

cell-truncate.logic: Long text is truncated to an ellipsis inside the cell, and hover or focus shows the full text in an overlay. Truncation requires table-layout:fixed and definite column widths; otherwise the cell is stretched by its content instead of truncating.
cell-truncate.prompt: Implement "Cell Truncation" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Very long fields (URLs, descriptions, paths) are cut to a single line with an ellipsis inside the cell without widening the column; on mouse hover or keyboard focus the full content floats up. [When it triggers] Text is truncated automatically when it exceeds the column width; hover or focus shows the full-text overlay. [Implementation] The truncation trio: overflow: hidden, text-overflow: ellipsis, white-space: nowrap, **and the table must be table-layout: fixed**: the default auto layout computes column widths from content, so the cell gets stretched and truncation never triggers. Don't use the native title attribute for the full-text tooltip (it appears after a one-second delay, can't be styled, and doesn't exist on touch); use your own overlay. **Attach the tooltip only when the text is actually truncated**: check el.scrollWidth > el.clientWidth; attaching tooltips to non-truncated cells is noise. For multi-line truncation use -webkit-line-clamp with display: -webkit-box. [Key parameters] Single-line truncation white-space: nowrap; multi-line uses line-clamp: 2; overlay appears after 300ms and disappears immediately; overlay max width 420px and allowed to wrap. [Pitfalls] Forgetting table-layout: fixed and then searching everywhere for why ellipsis doesn't work: this is the most common pitfall; and adding a title to every cell, so native tooltips pop up everywhere as the mouse sweeps across the table, which is very noisy. [Dependencies] None.

collapsible-sidebar.logic: The sidebar toggles between expanded and collapsed states, and the main content area widens accordingly. Transitioning the grid column width is the most robust; don't shift the main content with margin-left.
collapsible-sidebar.prompt: Implement "Collapsible Sidebar" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The left navigation can collapse into a narrow strip while the main content area smoothly widens to fill the space; click again to expand back. The collapsed state persists across refreshes. [When it triggers] Toggled by clicking the collapse button; a keyboard shortcut (e.g. Cmd/Ctrl + B) is also supported. [Implementation] Use grid for layout: container grid-template-columns: var(--side-w) 1fr; when collapsing, change --side-w from 240px to 56px, and **put the transition on grid-template-columns**. Don't push the main content with margin-left: that leaves the main content's width unchanged, so its inner responsive layout and ResizeObserver never recompute. The collapse button needs aria-expanded and aria-controls. Save the collapsed state to localStorage and read it before the first frame, otherwise you will see the sidebar expanded first and then snap shut. [Key parameters] Expanded width 240px, collapsed width 56px; transition 200ms cubic-bezier(.4,0,.2,1); shortcut Cmd+B; collapsed by default on narrow screens (<1024px). [Pitfalls] During the transition, charts/canvases in the main content don't recompute their size and jump only after the animation ends: send a resize notification once in transitionend; and a collapse button with only an icon and no aria-label is read out by screen readers as an empty button. [Dependencies] None.

sidebar-icon-mode.logic: When the sidebar collapses, only icons remain, and hover shows the name in an overlay. Icons must have aria-label; the overlay is only a visual supplement and can't replace the accessible name.
sidebar-icon-mode.prompt: Implement "Icon Rail" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When the sidebar is collapsed it is a column of icons; when the mouse rests on an icon, its name floats out to the right; the icon of the current item has a clear highlight (a vertical bar or a filled background). [When it triggers] Active while the sidebar is collapsed; the tooltip overlay appears 300ms after hover or keyboard focus. [Implementation] The icon button itself must carry aria-label (in the collapsed state the text is hidden, and **screen readers rely on this, not the overlay**). Don't remove the text with display:none; transition its width to 0 with overflow:hidden so the expand animation stays smooth. Build the overlay with popover or absolute positioning, placed to the right of the icon, vertically centered, with an arrow pointing to the icon. Highlight the current item with a 3px vertical bar on the left plus a light background; don't rely on color alone (people with color-vision deficiency can't tell). [Key parameters] Rail width 56px; icon 20px, tap target 44x44; overlay appears after 300ms and disappears after 80ms; current-item bar 3px. [Pitfalls] Putting the name only in the title attribute, so touch users never see it and screen readers read it late and messily; and removing the text with display:none when collapsing, so on expand the text pops in abruptly with no sense of transition. [Dependencies] None.

sidebar-resize.logic: A draggable divider on the sidebar's right edge changes its width when dragged. Use pointer capture so fast drags aren't lost, write the width to a CSS variable, and persist only on release.
sidebar-resize.prompt: Implement "Sidebar Resize Handle" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The sidebar's right edge has an almost invisible divider; the cursor turns into a left-right arrow and it lights up on hover; press and drag to change the width, within lower and upper limits; on release the width is remembered. [When it triggers] Starts on press inside the 6px hot zone of the divider; the width changes live while moving; ends on release or Esc (Esc restores the width from before the press). [Implementation] Give the divider role="separator", aria-orientation="vertical", aria-valuenow/min/max, and **make it keyboard-operable**: once focused, the left/right arrow keys adjust by 16px each. Dragging calls setPointerCapture in pointerdown, and pointermove only changes the CSS variable that drives the layout (--side-w); don't setState every frame. During the drag add cursor: col-resize and user-select: none to body. On release write to localStorage. [Key parameters] Hot zone 6px; minimum 180px, maximum 480px; keyboard step 16px (64px with shift); apply damping when out of bounds (the overshoot follows at only half) to give a feeling of hitting the limit. [Pitfalls] Building only mouse support and no keyboard support: for keyboard users the divider effectively doesn't exist; and changing React state directly while dragging, so wide tables/long lists re-render every frame and dragging feels like being stuck in mud. [Dependencies] None.

nested-nav.logic: Sidebar navigation has second and third levels, and parent items can expand and collapse. Use nested ul with aria-expanded, animate expansion with grid-template-rows 0fr->1fr, and auto-expand the ancestor chain when entering a child page.
nested-nav.prompt: Implement "Nested Navigation" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] Groups in the sidebar can be opened to reveal child items, with the arrow rotating along; when entering a child page, all its ancestors expand automatically and scroll it into view, and the current item is highlighted. [When it triggers] Clicking a parent item toggles expansion; on route change, the current item's ancestor chain is expanded automatically. [Implementation] Structure with nested <ul>; a parent item is a <button aria-expanded aria-controls> and the child list is a <ul id>. Animate expansion with an outer grid-template-rows: 0fr -> 1fr and an inner overflow: hidden; **this is the only clean way to transition to "auto height"** (height:auto can't be transitioned, and the measure-the-height approach breaks when content changes). Mark the current item with aria-current="page". After a route change, bring the current item into view with scrollIntoView({ block: "nearest" }): use nearest rather than center, so nothing scrolls needlessly when it is already visible. [Key parameters] Expand 200ms ease; arrow rotates 90deg; 16px indent per level; allow multiple siblings to be expanded at once (accordion-style exclusivity is actually harder to use). [Pitfalls] Using height: auto in a transition, which doesn't move at all; and resetting the whole tree to collapsed on every route change, so after the user clicks into a third-level page the sidebar "forgets" where they are. [Dependencies] None.

active-nav-indicator.logic: Marks "you are here" in the navigation. Route-based navs use aria-current="page"; in-page anchor navs use IntersectionObserver to follow scrolling; don't compute offsetTop in a scroll handler.
active-nav-indicator.prompt: Implement "Active Nav Indicator" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] The current item in the navigation has a clear marker: a vertical bar or background color, with heavier text; in-page anchor navigation also switches the highlight automatically as you scroll, lighting up whichever section you are reading. [When it triggers] Updates immediately on route change; for in-page anchors it switches when the corresponding section enters the viewport. [Implementation] **Semantically you must use aria-current="page"** (aria-current="location" for in-page anchors); with only a class, screen-reader users have no idea where they are. For scroll following, observe each section with IntersectionObserver and set rootMargin to "-40% 0px -55% 0px" to create a detection band in the middle of the viewport; the section that enters this band is the current one. This is far cheaper and more stable than computing offsetTop in a scroll callback. **Don't rely on color alone** for the highlight; add a vertical bar or bold. Moving the indicator between items can use a transform transition to give a sliding feel. [Key parameters] Detection band rootMargin="-40% 0px -55% 0px"; indicator 3px, move transition 200ms; the highlight also changes font weight 500 -> 600. [Pitfalls] Iterating over all sections in a scroll event to compute positions: on long documents that reads layout every frame and drops frames outright; and when clicking an anchor to jump, the observer fires for several intermediate sections in a row and the indicator "sweeps" all the way down, so disable the observer temporarily during programmatic scrolling. [Dependencies] None.

sidebar-to-drawer.logic: On narrow screens a permanent sidebar doesn't fit, so it degrades into a drawer sliding out from the left: with a scrim, background scroll lock, a focus trap, and Esc to close. On desktop it becomes permanent again.
sidebar-to-drawer.prompt: Implement "Sidebar to Drawer" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] On desktop the sidebar stays on the left; on narrow screens it collapses, and tapping the hamburger button slides it out from the left over the content with a semi-transparent scrim behind it; clicking the scrim or pressing Esc closes it. [When it triggers] The form switches when the viewport crosses the breakpoint; in drawer mode, the button opens it, and clicking the scrim / Esc / selecting an item closes it. [Implementation] When the drawer is open, none of three things can be skipped: **lock background scroll** (set overflow:hidden on body and compensate for the scrollbar width, otherwise the page jumps sideways), **a focus trap** (Tab cycles only within the drawer), and **after closing, return focus to the hamburger button**. Slide out with transform: translateX(-100%) -> 0, which saves a reflow compared with changing left. The scrim is a separate layer with an opacity transition. When the viewport widens back to desktop, actively close the drawer and unlock body, otherwise you leave behind a locked page. [Key parameters] Breakpoint 1024px; drawer width min(300px, 85vw); slide-out 240ms cubic-bezier(.32,.72,0,1); scrim rgba(0,0,0,.4); with prefers-reduced-motion, fade in directly instead. [Pitfalls] Forgetting to unlock body's overflow on breakpoint switch, so after the user widens the window the whole page can never scroll again; and no focus trap, so Tab moves to the content behind the drawer and keyboard users get completely lost. [Dependencies] None.

bottom-tab-bar.logic: A row of primary navigation fixed to the bottom on mobile, 3~5 items, icon plus text. It must handle the safe-area inset and must not exceed 5 items.
bottom-tab-bar.prompt: Implement "Bottom Tab Bar" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] On phones a row of 3~5 entries is fixed at the bottom, each an icon plus a line of small text; the current item's icon is filled and its text takes the primary color; the bar itself has a frosted-glass or opaque background so content scrolling underneath doesn't show through. [When it triggers] Always visible; tapping switches the main area, preserving each tab's own scroll position when switching. [Implementation] Container position: fixed; bottom: 0, and **padding-bottom must be env(safe-area-inset-bottom)**, otherwise on devices with a gesture bar the last row gets partly eaten. Also give the page body padding-bottom of the same height so the last line of content isn't permanently covered. Each item is an <a> or <button>, and the current item gets aria-current="page". Use two icon sets (outline/filled) rather than only changing the color. [Key parameters] Bar height 49px plus the safe area; 3~5 items (beyond 5 switch to "More" or a drawer); icon 24px; text 10px; the whole item is the tap target, at least 44px high. [Pitfalls] Forgetting env(safe-area-inset-bottom), so text is pressed by the gesture bar on iPhone; and not reserving an equal bottom padding on the page body, so the last item of a long list can never be fully seen. [Dependencies] None.

tab-badge.logic: An unread count or red dot on a tab. Numbers need a cap (99+), and the meaning must be put into the accessible name; a bare red dot reads as nothing to screen readers.
tab-badge.prompt: Implement "Tab Badge" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A small red dot or number bubble hangs at the top right of the tab icon to indicate unread items; numbers above 99 show 99+; when there are no unread items the whole badge takes no space and leaves no gap. [When it triggers] Updates when the unread count changes; fades out and disappears when going from some to none. [Implementation] The badge is absolutely positioned at the top right of the icon container, which needs position: relative and enough padding to leave room for the overflow (don't let the badge be clipped by overflow). **The accessible name must carry the meaning**: write the tab's aria-label as "Messages, 3 unread", or use a visually-hidden span to carry the text; a bare red dot doesn't exist for a screen reader. Use tabular-nums for numbers to prevent jitter. When the number changes you can do one slight scale pop (1 -> 1.15 -> 1), but don't do looping animation. [Key parameters] Red dot diameter 8px; number bubble min width 16px, height 16px, font size 10px, horizontal padding 4px; cap 99+; appear/disappear 150ms; pop scale 1.15, 220ms spring. [Pitfalls] A badge that is only visual with no readable text, so screen-reader users never know there is anything unread; and a badge clipped at a corner by the parent's overflow: hidden, which looks like a notch. [Dependencies] None.

auto-hide-bar.logic: Scrolling down hides the top or bottom bar to free up screen space, and scrolling up brings it back immediately. Needs a threshold and direction debouncing, otherwise it flickers wildly at the tipping point.
auto-hide-bar.prompt: Implement "Auto-hide Bar" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] While scrolling down to read, the top bar (or bottom tab bar) smoothly retracts and the whole screen goes to content; scrolling up even a little slides it right back. It is always shown when scrolled to the top of the page. [When it triggers] Toggles when the scroll direction changes and cumulative displacement exceeds the threshold; forced visible when scrollY is less than the bar height. [Implementation] Record the previous scrollY and toggle the state only when **cumulative displacement in the same direction exceeds a threshold** (e.g. 12px); without a threshold, small finger jitters make the bar flicker wildly. Hide with transform: translateY(-100%); don't change height or top. Attach the scroll listener with { passive: true }, and throttle state computation with requestAnimationFrame, at most once per frame. **Force it visible at the top and bottom of the page**: at the top the user hasn't started reading, and at the bottom rubber-band bounce misjudges the direction. Never hide it while focus is inside the bar (a keyboard user has tabbed into the navigation). [Key parameters] Direction threshold 12px; forced-visible zone at top = bar height; transition 200ms cubic-bezier(.4,0,.2,1); listener passive: true. [Pitfalls] Without direction debouncing, the bar flickers at high frequency at the critical scroll position, which feels terrible; and hiding while focus is still inside the bar, so a keyboard user pressing Tab sends focus to something invisible. [Dependencies] None.

center-fab.logic: A larger, taller round primary-action button in the middle of the bottom tab bar, visually protruding above the bar. It carries the single most frequent global action and doesn't take part in tab selection state.
center-fab.prompt: Implement "Center FAB" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] In the middle of the bottom tab bar sits a round button larger than the other items, with a primary-color fill and a shadow, visually protruding above the bar's top edge, so it reads at a glance as "the most important action" (post / create / scan). [When it triggers] Clicking directly performs the primary action or opens an action menu; it is **not a tab**, and clicking it doesn't change the tab selection state. [Implementation] Offset the button upward relative to the tab bar (transform: translateY(-30%)); the tab bar itself must not have overflow: hidden or it will be clipped. The protruding part covers content, so the bottom padding reserved on the page should be computed as "bar height + protrusion height". Use a two-layer shadow (one tight layer to define the shape, one diffuse layer to give height). Since it isn't a tab, **semantically don't put it in the tablist**; make it a standalone <button aria-label>. On click you can add a slight press-and-rebound. [Key parameters] Diameter 56px; raised by 30% (about 17px); shadow 0 4px 12px rgba(primary, .35) plus 0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,.2); press scale .94, 120ms. [Pitfalls] Stuffing it into the tablist as a third tab, so screen readers announce "tab 3 of 5" though it never switches pages; and setting overflow: hidden on the tab bar, so the protruding part is cut flat and the effort is wasted. [Dependencies] None.

tab-switch-transition.logic: When switching tabs, content slides left or right according to the tabs' relative positions, giving a sense of direction. Switching to a tab on the right pushes content left, and vice versa; the indicator bar moves at the same time.
tab-switch-transition.prompt: Implement "Tab Switch Transition" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When switching from the 1st tab to the 3rd, content slides in from the right and the old content slides out to the left; switching from the 3rd back to the 1st is the reverse. The indicator bar translates under the new tab at the same time. The direction matches the tab arrangement, so users can feel "I moved two steps to the right". [When it triggers] When the selected tab changes; swiping left/right in the content area also switches. [Implementation] Remember the previous tab's index and compare old and new indexes to get the direction (+1 or -1); pass it to the container as a CSS variable or data attribute, and use it to decide the sign of the enter/exit displacement. The old content fades out with translateX(+-100%) while the new content fades in from the opposite direction with translateX(-+100%), both at the same time (shared axis transition). **Don't use the full width for the displacement**; 24~32px plus an opacity change is enough: a full-width sweep quickly becomes annoying in a high-frequency action like tab switching. With prefers-reduced-motion keep only the cross-fade. [Key parameters] Displacement 28px; duration 220ms cubic-bezier(.2,0,0,1); fade in/out synchronized with the displacement; indicator movement also 220ms. [Pitfalls] Hard-coding the direction as "always enter from the right", so switching back and forth feels like always moving in one direction and the spatial sense is lost; and during the transition both panels are in the DOM and both focusable, so Tab jumps into the one that is leaving. [Dependencies] None.

entry-grid.logic: A block of icon entries below the hero, arranged with equal width and equal spacing. Column count sets the character: 4 columns are big and steady, 5 are dense and complete. More than two rows means you should consider paging or collapsing.
entry-grid.prompt: Implement "Entry Grid" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A tidy block of icon entries, each cell an icon plus a short title, with equal widths horizontally and equal spacing vertically, at most two rows overall; icons have consistent visual weight, with none looking heavier or lighter than the others. [When it triggers] Static; clicking enters the corresponding feature. [Implementation] Use grid-template-columns: repeat(var(--cols), 1fr) rather than flex with percentage widths: grid gaps don't participate in width calculation, so the classic problem of the last column being squeezed out doesn't occur.
