Inside each cell use a vertical flex, center-aligned, with the icon in a fixed-size square container (don't let different icons' actual sizes decide row height). Keep the title on one line with an ellipsis for overflow, **and don't wrap**: if some wrap and some don't, the row heights become uneven. Control the column count with a CSS variable so it's easy to change per breakpoint. [Key parameters] Columns = 4 (large icons) or 5 (compact); icon container 44~48px; title 11~12px, single-line truncation; row spacing 16px, column spacing from grid gap; block vertical padding 16px. [Pitfalls] Forcing more than two rows: the icon grid then turns into a second-level menu that users can't scan, so beyond that switch to paging or fold into "More"; and letting titles wrap, so in a row some have two lines and some one, and the whole block instantly looks unfinished. [Dependencies] None.

grid-paging.logic: When there are too many entries, page horizontally with 8~10 per page, swipe to switch pages, and show page dots below. Build it with scroll-snap instead of hand-written gestures.
grid-paging.prompt: Implement "Grid Paging" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When entries exceed one screen they are split horizontally into two or three pages; a swipe flips a whole page and it settles firmly, with a row of small dots below showing which page is current. [When it triggers] Switches by horizontal swipe or by tapping a page dot; each page snaps into alignment and never stops between two pages. [Implementation] The container is display: flex, overflow-x: auto, scroll-snap-type: x mandatory; each page is a width: 100% flex child with scroll-snap-align: start. **This way the browser handles page snapping**, with no hand-written gesture recognition or inertia. Determine the current page by observing each page with IntersectionObserver; don't compute scrollLeft/pageWidth in a scroll handler (it comes out wrong under zoom and fractional widths). The page dots are **an indicator, not the primary control**, but should still be clickable, and clicking smooth-scrolls there via scrollIntoView. Hide the scrollbar (scrollbar-width: none). [Key parameters] 8 or 10 per page (two rows x 4/5 columns); snap-type: x mandatory; dot diameter 6px, current dot stretched into a 12px capsule; switch transition 200ms. [Pitfalls] Implementing paging yourself with transform, then having to add inertia, edge bounce, and mouse wheel support, and still ending up less smooth than native snap; and showing page dots when there is only 1 page: a lonely dot looks odd, so hide them entirely for a single page. [Dependencies] None.

grid-edit-sort.logic: A long press enters edit mode, icons jiggle slightly to signal "draggable", dragging reorders them, and delete badges appear at the top right. This mental model comes from phone home screens, so users know it instinctively.
grid-edit-sort.prompt: Implement "Long-press Edit & Sort" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] After long-pressing any entry for about half a second, the whole grid enters edit mode: each icon starts jiggling slightly and a delete badge appears at its top right; now icons can be dragged to reorder, with the others making way in real time; tapping blank space or "Done" exits. [When it triggers] Enter with a 500ms long press; reorder live during dragging; exit by tapping Done / blank space / pressing Esc. [Implementation] Long-press detection must **allow a little movement tolerance** (within 8px doesn't count as movement), otherwise a slight finger shake cancels it; as soon as the long press is confirmed, give haptic feedback immediately (navigator.vibrate or a native bridge). Build the jiggle with keyframes of a small +-1.2deg rotation, **and give each icon a different animation delay**: a perfectly uniform jiggle looks broken. Use FLIP for the reorder animation: record each cell's position first, then after changing the order use transform to animate them from the old position to the new one. In edit mode, block the original click navigation. [Key parameters] Long press 500ms, movement tolerance 8px; jiggle +-1.2deg, 300ms period, random per-item delay 0~200ms; make-way animation 200ms ease-out; on exit the jiggle stops immediately, no fade-out. [Pitfalls] A long press with no movement tolerance: a user who wants to scroll the list accidentally enters edit mode (or, conversely, wants to long-press but fails because the finger moved slightly); and all icons sharing the same animation phase, so it looks like the whole thing is vibrating rather than each icon jiggling. [Dependencies] None.

more-entry.logic: The icon grid shows only the most-used one or two rows, with a "More" in the last slot; tapping it expands the rest in place or pulls up a panel. Expansion needs a height transition; don't let it pop in instantly.
more-entry.prompt: Implement "More Entry" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] By default the icon grid shows only the 8~10 most-used entries, and the last cell is "More"; tapping it expands the remaining entries downward in place (or pulls up a panel from the bottom), and tapping "Collapse" returns to the original state. [When it triggers] Tap "More" to expand; tap "Collapse", tap outside the panel, or press Esc to close. [Implementation] For in-place expansion, use an outer grid-template-rows: 0fr -> 1fr with an inner overflow: hidden for the height transition: this is the clean way to transition to auto height. The "More" button gets aria-expanded and aria-controls. The entries newly revealed after expansion use a **very light staggered fade-in** (20ms delay each); showing all at once feels stiff, but keep the delay under 30ms, otherwise the last one waits ages. If the remaining items exceed two screens, don't expand in place; pull up a scrollable panel instead. On collapse, bring the scroll position back to what it was before expanding so the page doesn't jump. [Key parameters] Show 8~10 by default; expand 240ms ease; stagger 20ms per item, total delay capped at 200ms; with more than 20 remaining items use a panel. [Pitfalls] After expansion the sudden change in page height pushes the content below away, so what the user was looking at disappears: smoothly grow the added height and make sure the "More" button itself stays in the viewport; and not returning to the original scroll position after collapsing, so the page feels like it "caved in" for a moment. [Dependencies] None.

icon-micro-motion.logic: When an icon entry is tapped, a very short scale or bounce confirms "you hit it". The key is short and light: beyond 200ms it slows down the feel of the whole action.
icon-micro-motion.prompt: Implement "Icon Micro-motion" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When an icon entry is tapped it first shrinks slightly and then springs back to its original size, as if pressed in; navigation happens during the animation rather than after it, so it doesn't feel slow at all. Some entries can do a one-time light pop-in when they first appear. [When it triggers] Shrink immediately on pointerdown (don't wait for click), spring back on pointerup or when the pointer leaves; a staggered pop-in can play once when the page is first entered. [Implementation] Press uses transform: scale(.92), **triggered on pointerdown** rather than click: waiting for click adds a delay of more than 100ms on touch screens, and the feedback feels "late". The rebound uses a curve with a slight overshoot (cubic-bezier(.34,1.56,.64,1)) or a short spring. Animate only transform and opacity; don't touch width/margin. **Don't make navigation wait for the animation to end**; run the two in parallel. With prefers-reduced-motion, replace the scale with one very short opacity change. [Key parameters] Press scale .92, 80ms; rebound 220ms with overshoot curve; first pop-in scale .8 -> 1, stagger 30ms per item; keep total duration within 250ms. [Pitfalls] Waiting for the animation to finish before navigating, so every click wastes 200ms: one of the most common sources of "this app is laggy"; and animating the width/height of the icon container, which triggers a reflow every frame. [Dependencies] None.

mega-menu.logic: Hovering or clicking a nav item expands a full multi-column panel. The keys are hover-intent detection and tolerance for diagonal mouse movement, otherwise moving the mouse diagonally downward closes the menu.
mega-menu.prompt: Implement "Mega Menu" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] When the mouse rests on an item in the top navigation, a whole panel expands below it, listing links grouped by section and possibly with images and featured slots; when the mouse moves diagonally into the panel the menu doesn't vanish midway. [When it triggers] Opens after hovering 120ms (not instantly), closes 200ms after leaving both the panel and the trigger; for keyboard, Enter/Down arrow opens it, Esc closes it and returns focus to the trigger. [Implementation] **Hover intent is the entire difficulty of this component**: add a short delay to opening so it doesn't pop up when the mouse merely passes by; add a longer delay to closing, and **fill the gap between the trigger and the panel with a transparent "safe triangle" area** (or just make the panel abut the trigger with no gap), otherwise when the mouse moves diagonally from the nav item toward the panel's bottom-right corner it passes through the gap and triggers a close. The panel fades in with opacity + translateY(-6px); don't use a height expansion (height animation is janky when there is a lot of content). Keyboard access must work: after the panel opens, the Tab order naturally enters the panel. Only one panel may be open at a time, and when switching don't replay the enter animation (just swap the content). [Key parameters] Open delay 120ms, close delay 200ms; enter 180ms, 6px displacement; panel max width aligned to the content container; z-index above the sticky nav. [Pitfalls] No close delay or safe area, so the menu closes as soon as the mouse moves diagonally and is nearly unusable; and a panel that responds only to the mouse, so keyboard users cannot open it at all. [Dependencies] None.

breadcrumb.logic: Shows the current page's path in the site hierarchy, with each level clickable to go back. Use nav + ol semantics; the last level is not a link and is marked aria-current="page". When the hierarchy is too deep, collapse the middle.
breadcrumb.prompt: Implement "Breadcrumb" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] A line at the top of the page reading "Home / Products / Details", where every preceding level can be clicked to go back, and the last level is the current page, not clickable, in a lighter color; when the hierarchy is very deep or the screen very narrow, the middle collapses into "...", and clicking it reveals the omitted levels. [When it triggers] Static; clicking "..." expands the middle levels. [Implementation] The structure must be <nav aria-label="Breadcrumb"><ol><li>, using an ordered list to express hierarchy order so screen readers announce "item 2 of 4". **Don't wrap the last level in <a>**: it points at the current page, and making it a link creates a pointless clickable element; give it aria-current="page". Generate the separators with CSS ::before content, **don't write them into the HTML**: if you do, screen readers read out the slashes. When collapsing, keep the first level and the last two, and fold the middle into one button. Another approach on narrow screens is to show only the parent level plus a back arrow. [Key parameters] Collapse threshold = more than 4 levels or insufficient container width; separator "/" or ">" in a lighter color than the text; font size 12~13px; tap target at least 32px high. [Pitfalls] Writing the separator as text inside the tags, so screen readers read "Home slash Products slash"; and making the last level a link too, so the user clicks it and finds nothing changes. [Dependencies] None.

nav-search-expand.logic: In the nav bar, search is normally an icon; clicking it expands horizontally into an input and auto-focuses, and it collapses back on blur when nothing is typed. The expansion needs a width transition and focus management.
nav-search-expand.prompt: Implement "Nav Search Expand" at the place mentioned above. [Goal] On the right side of the nav bar there is normally only a magnifier icon; clicking it expands horizontally into an input field that is immediately ready for typing; when the input loses focus and is empty it automatically collapses back into an icon, and if there is content it stays expanded. [When it triggers] Click the icon or press Cmd/Ctrl+K to expand and focus; Esc clears and collapses; collapse on blur when empty. [Implementation] Expand by transitioning width from 0 (or the icon width) to the target width; the input is always in the DOM, just at width 0 with overflow: hidden, **so focus() can be called in the same frame as the expansion**: if the input is inserted into the DOM only after expanding, focus fails because the element hasn't been laid out yet, or causes a scroll jump. Blur before collapsing. The shortcut must be ignored inside inputs (otherwise typing K in another input would trigger it): check whether e.target is an editable element. After expansion, the other items on the right of the nav should yield smoothly, using flex shrinking rather than absolute-position overlap. [Key parameters] Expanded width min(320px, 40vw); transition 200ms cubic-bezier(.4,0,.2,1); shortcut Cmd+K / Ctrl+K; collapse delay 0 (collapse on blur, don't add a delay, it feels sticky). [Pitfalls] Mounting the input into the DOM only after expanding and then calling focus: on iOS the keyboard doesn't appear (you must focus an existing element within the same event loop as the user gesture); and covering the other nav items with absolute positioning on expand, so when it collapses they "flash" back. [Dependencies] None.

nav-shrink-on-scroll.logic: After the page scrolls, the nav bar goes from tall to short, the logo shrinks, and the background turns from transparent to solid. Use a sentinel element with IntersectionObserver to toggle a class; don't compute it inside a scroll handler.
nav-shrink-on-scroll.prompt:
Implement "Nav Shrink on Scroll" at the place mentioned above.
[Goal] At the top of the page the nav bar is tall, transparent, with a large logo. After scrolling down a little it becomes shorter, gains an opaque (or frosted-glass) background and a thin divider line, the logo shrinks, and the whole transition is smooth.
[When it triggers] Switch to the condensed state once scrolling passes a threshold; restore when back at the top.
[Implementation] **Do not check in a scroll event**: put a sentinel div at the very top of the page whose height equals the threshold, observe it with IntersectionObserver, and add an .is-condensed class to the nav when it leaves the viewport. Put every change on that class (height, background, logo size, shadow) so one toggle drives them all. A height transition shifts the content below, so the nav must be position: fixed and the page body must reserve a fixed top padding (based on the expanded height) so content doesn't jump when condensing. Scale the logo with transform: scale rather than changing width/height. When going from transparent to frosted glass, transition backdrop-filter at the same time, otherwise it pops in abruptly.
[Key parameters] Threshold 64px; height 72px -> 56px; logo scale 1 -> .82; transition 220ms ease; the divider only appears in the condensed state, with an opacity transition.
[Pitfalls] Reading offsetHeight inside a scroll callback to decide forces a synchronous layout every frame and drops frames on long pages; also, if the nav is sticky instead of fixed and its height changes, the content below jumps up as a whole at the moment of condensing.
[Dependencies] None.

idempotency-key.logic: The client generates a unique key for every write operation and sends it with the request. The server uses it to deduplicate: when the same key arrives again, it returns the result of the first execution instead of running the operation again.
idempotency-key.prompt:
Implement "Idempotency Key" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] After a network timeout the client retries, or the user double-clicks submit, and the same operation runs twice: two charges, two messages sent. Such bugs almost never show up in test environments; in production they appear sporadically and are hard to reproduce.
[Approach] The client generates a UUID for every write operation and puts it in the Idempotency-Key request header; on retry it **reuses the same key** (this is the crux: regenerating it means no protection at all). On receipt, the server first does an atomic reservation write with that key (e.g. Redis SETNX or a database unique index); only if the reservation succeeds does it actually run the business logic, and after completion it stores the response body and status code together. If the key already exists, return the stored response directly without re-executing. A crash mid-execution must be re-entrant: the reservation record carries a state (processing / completed), and a duplicate request that arrives while processing returns 409 so the client retries later.
[Which layer] Middleware at the gateway or service entry point; business code should not be aware of it.
[Key parameters] Key TTL 24h (just cover the client's longest retry window; storing longer wastes space); lock timeout for the processing state 30s; the key's scope must include the user id to prevent cross-user collisions.
[How to verify] Send two create requests with the same key back to back: the second must return a response body **byte-for-byte identical** to the first, and the database must contain only one record. Then interrupt the first request midway through execution and confirm the second re-enters correctly instead of getting 409 forever.
[Pitfalls] Storing the key only in a cache and not in the database, so idempotency vanishes on a cache restart; also setting the key TTL shorter than the client's retry window so it expires exactly when the retry arrives, which is the same as having none.

svg.同一个键第二次到达：不再执行，直接返回上次结果: Same key again: skip, return prior result

cursor-pagination-api.logic: Continue the query using "the sort value of the last item on the previous page" as a cursor instead of OFFSET. Deep pages don't get slower, and new rows inserted while paging cause neither duplicates nor gaps.
cursor-pagination-api.prompt:
Implement "Cursor Pagination API" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] OFFSET pagination has two ailments: on page 5000 the database must first scan and discard all the preceding rows, so it gets slower the deeper you go; and if new rows are inserted at the front while paging, later pages repeat or miss records.
[Approach] Use keyset pagination: encode the sort field values (e.g. a composite cursor of created_at plus id) into an opaque string returned to the client, and have the next-page query use WHERE (created_at, id) < (:t, :id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT n. **The sort key must be unique**, so add id as the final tie-breaker; otherwise records with the same timestamp get skipped or duplicated. The cursor should be base64-encoded and **make no format promises**, so changing the implementation later is not a breaking change. Return next_cursor in the response; when there is no next page return null, not an empty string.
[Which layer] The query layer; the index must match the sort key exactly (see "Composite Index Column Order").
[Key parameters] Default page size 20, cap 100 (no cap is effectively a data-dump endpoint); cursor encoding base64url; sort key (created_at, id).
[How to verify] Generate 100k rows and compare query time for page 1 vs page 5000: keyset should be roughly flat while OFFSET degrades linearly. Then insert a batch of new records midway through paging, fetch all pages, and assert the set of ids obtained has no duplicates and nothing missing.
[Pitfalls] Putting only the timestamp in the cursor and not the id, so multiple records in the same millisecond are lost; also allowing the client to pass an arbitrarily large page_size, so a single request can knock the service over.

svg.拿上一页最后一条的位置往下取，不数 OFFSET: Resume after last item, no OFFSET

api-versioning.logic: When an API must change in an incompatible way, use versions to separate old from new so old clients keep working. The key is not which versioning scheme you pick, but first defining exactly what counts as a "breaking change".
api-versioning.prompt:
Implement "API Versioning" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] A field type is changed or a field is removed, old app versions are still running on users' phones, and the release triggers widespread errors; old mobile versions can stay alive for years.
[Approach] First fix the list: **adding optional fields, adding new endpoints, and adding enum values (when clients already fall back on unknown values) are not breaking**; changing a field type, removing a field, changing a field's meaning, making an optional field required, or narrowing the allowed value range **are all breaking**. Only breaking changes bump the version. Putting the version in the path (/v1/, /v2/) is the most intuitive and easiest to debug; putting it in a header is more "elegant" but makes caching and logs hard to split by version. **Keep one copy of the business logic and handle version differences only in the outermost serialization layer**; do not duplicate the whole codebase, since two copies will inevitably drift. Old versions need an explicit sunset schedule, and you should count real call volume per version from logs; only shut one down when the traffic is gone.
[Which layer] Routing plus the serialization layer.
[Key parameters] Maintain no more than 2 versions at once; give at least 6 months and an advance announcement before sunset; during the rollout watch old-version traffic and only shut it down once it drops to single digits per day.
[How to verify] Replay request samples from the old version against the new service; responses must be compatible field by field. Also check that logs can aggregate call volume by version, otherwise you will never dare to retire the old version.
[Pitfalls] Quietly changing a field's meaning inside the v1 endpoint to save effort (e.g. amount from yuan to fen) is worse than removing a field: no error, just all the numbers wrong; also never counting per-version traffic, so v1 can never be turned off and you end up maintaining five versions at once.

svg.破坏性改动才升版本，两版共存到老客户端退完: Bump only if breaking; 2 versions coexist

error-code-layers.logic: The HTTP status code says "which side owns this kind of problem", while the business code in the response body says "which specific thing happened"; each layer has its own job. The client uses them to decide whether to retry, redirect to login, or show a message to the user.
error-code-layers.prompt:
Implement "Layered Error Codes" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Every error returns 200 plus {"code": -1, "msg": "failed"}; the client can't tell whether to retry, redirect to login, or prompt the user, and monitoring can't alert by error type either.
[Approach] Two layers. **The HTTP status code answers "who owns it"**: 4xx is the caller's problem (400 bad params, 401 not logged in, 403 no permission, 404 not found, 409 state conflict, 422 semantically invalid, 429 rate limited), 5xx is the server's problem, and **only 5xx is worth retrying**. **The business code in the body answers "which specific thing"**: use a stable string enum (e.g. ORDER_ALREADY_PAID) rather than numbers, since numbers turn into magic values nobody recognizes over time. Use one uniform body shape: { code, message, details?, trace_id }. message is English for developers; **user-facing copy is decided by the client from the code**, because the server shouldn't assume the client's language or tone. trace_id is always included; it is the only thing that lets you join logs on both sides when debugging.
[Which layer] A unified exception-handling middleware; business code only throws domain exceptions carrying a code.
[Key parameters] Business codes are upper-snake-case enums; details is only given for 4xx, and 5xx must not leak internal stack traces; trace_id is written to both the response header and the logs.
[How to verify] List a table of "status code x business code x what the client should do", where every row has a clear action; then deliberately trigger each class of error and confirm the client can branch on code alone without parsing message.
[Pitfalls] Wrapping every error in HTTP 200, so gateways, CDNs, and monitoring all think everything is fine; also stuffing internal exception text directly into message and returning it to the client, when stack traces often carry table names, SQL, or even connection strings.

svg.状态码分「归谁管」，业务码说「具体哪件事」: Status = who owns it; code = which issue

partial-failure.logic: When some items in a batch endpoint succeed and others fail, return a result per item rather than failing or succeeding as a whole. That way the client knows exactly which items to retry.
partial-failure.prompt:
Implement "Partial Failure in Batch" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] A batch of 100 is submitted and 3 are invalid: rolling back everything wastes the 97 valid ones; returning overall success silently drops the 3. Both are wrong.
[Approach] First define the semantics and write them in the docs: is this batch endpoint **all-or-nothing** or **best-effort**? For best-effort, return an array of per-item results, each carrying the index in the request or a client-supplied temporary id, success or not, and a failure reason code, with HTTP 200 (or 207 Multi-Status). **Result order must match request order, or carry an explicit id**; relying on implicit ordering easily misaligns once a gateway layer is inserted in between. Failure reason codes should use the same business codes as the single-item endpoint so the client can reuse the same handling logic. Retryable and non-retryable failures must be distinguishable, otherwise the client can only retry everything. All-or-nothing semantics must really run in one transaction, with the batch limit stated in the docs.
[Which layer] The API layer; the transaction boundary is in the service layer.
[Key parameters] Batch limit 100~500 (over the limit returns 400 rather than slowly processing); each result contains index / id / ok / code; the overall timeout should scale with item count but be capped.
[How to verify] Build a request of "first 3 succeed, the 4th is invalid, the rest succeed", and assert the response shows the first 3 and the rest as successes and only the 4th as a failure, with 99 records actually written to the database; then retrying that 1 item should succeed.
[Pitfalls] Not documenting whether it is all-or-nothing or best-effort, so clients have to guess and a wrong guess means inconsistent data; also giving failed items only a message string and no code, so the client can't automatically tell "bad params, don't retry" from "temporary fault, retry".

svg.逐条返回结果，客户端才知道该重试哪几条: Per-item results show what to retry

async-job-202.logic: A time-consuming operation returns 202 and a job id immediately; the client polls status by id or waits for a webhook. Waiting synchronously runs into gateway timeouts.
async-job-202.prompt:
Implement "Async Long Job" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Operations like exporting reports or batch processing take tens of seconds to minutes; waiting synchronously hits gateway and load balancer timeouts (typically 30~60s), and once the connection drops the server often keeps running while the client assumes failure.
[Approach] The endpoint returns 202 Accepted immediately, with a job_id in the body and the status URL in the Location header. The task is queued and run in the background, with a state machine pending -> running -> succeeded/failed, and **every state change is persisted** (after a process restart it must still be able to report status). The client polls GET /jobs/{id}, and the response carries status, progress (only when meaningful; an inaccurate progress bar is worse than none), and the result URL or error code. **The job-creation endpoint itself must be idempotent** (pair it with an idempotency key), otherwise a double click starts two heavy jobs. Where possible, offer a webhook callback as an alternative to polling, but **a callback can't replace the query endpoint**, since callbacks get lost.
[Which layer] The API layer returns 202, execution happens in a separate worker, and state lives in the database, not in memory.
[Key parameters] Tell the client the polling interval via the Retry-After response header (start at 2s, back off gradually to 10s); keep task results for 7 days; after a task timeout, actively mark it failed; it must never stay running forever.
[How to verify] After starting a task, disconnect immediately: the task should still run to completion; polling should show state advancing; kill and restart the worker process, and the task state must be neither lost nor stuck in running.
[Pitfalls] Keeping job state only in memory, so a single deploy wipes it all and the client polls forever without a result; also having no timeout fallback, so one hung task stays in running forever and the client polls forever.

svg.立刻返回任务号，客户端轮询状态，不占着连接干等: Return job id at once; client polls status

webhook-retry.logic: A callback you send out may never reach the receiver, so retry with backoff and include a signature. The receiver must be idempotent, because the semantics are "at least once", not "exactly once".
webhook-retry.prompt:
Implement "Webhook Retry" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] When a callback is sent just as the other service is restarting or the network blips, that event is lost permanently and the other side's data is out of sync with yours from then on.
[Approach] On delivery failure (connection failure, timeout, non-2xx), retry with exponential backoff, with a schedule such as 10s / 1min / 5min / 30min / 2h / 6h, **with jitter on every attempt** so that all callbacks don't come back at the same moment and knock the receiver over. Every request carries a unique event_id and a timestamp, and an HMAC signature over "timestamp + request body" using a shared secret is placed in a header; the receiver must verify the signature and **reject requests with overly old timestamps** (replay protection). The semantics are **at-least-once**, so the docs must tell receivers explicitly: process idempotently by event_id. After retries are exhausted, move the event to a dead-letter queue, and provide an admin entry for "manual redelivery" and a list of failed events; without them, you can do nothing when the other side discovers missing data.
[Which layer] A separate delivery worker, decoupled from business writes (business code only writes events into an outbox).
[Key parameters] Timeout 10s; at most 6 attempts; backoff with +/-20% jitter; sign with HMAC-SHA256; timestamp tolerance 5 minutes; keep dead letters 30 days.
[How to verify] Make the receiver return 500 continuously and check that retry intervals follow the backoff schedule and carry jitter; then have it receive the same event_id twice and confirm it handles them idempotently with no duplicate data; finally verify that signature validation fails after the request body is tampered with.
[Pitfalls] Retrying without jitter, so the moment the receiver recovers it is hit by the backlog all at once, fails again, and enters a death loop; also sending callbacks synchronously inside the business transaction, so when the receiver is slow it stretches your own transaction until it times out.

rate-limit-headers.logic: Rate limiting shouldn't only reject; it should also tell the caller how much quota is left and when it resets. Without these headers, clients can only retry blindly, turning rate limiting into an avalanche.
rate-limit-headers.prompt:
Implement "Rate Limit Headers" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] A rate-limited client doesn't know how much quota remains or when it can try again, so it can only retry immediately; rate limiting then generates even more requests and pushes the service toward an avalanche.
[Approach] Every response (**not just the rejected one**) carries quota information: RateLimit-Limit (total quota in the window), RateLimit-Remaining (what's left), RateLimit-Reset (seconds until reset). On rejection return 429 with an additional Retry-After whose value **includes jitter**, otherwise all rejected clients come back in the same second. Use a sliding window or token bucket for the limiting window; a fixed window lets through double the traffic at the boundary. State clearly whether the limit dimension is per IP, per token, or per user, and give the quota for each dimension in the docs. **Calls between internal services get their own quota tier**; don't share one bucket with public traffic.
[Which layer] The gateway or entry middleware; keep counters in shared storage such as Redis, since per-process in-memory counting with multiple replicas means quota multiplied by replica count.
[Key parameters] Retry-After with +/-20% jitter; token bucket capacity leaves burst headroom of 2x the steady-state rate; counter keys include a dimension prefix; quota headers are also returned on 2xx.
[How to verify] Push past the limit and check that the 429 response carries Retry-After and that different clients get different values (jitter); then confirm Remaining decreases in normal responses; finally scale the service to two replicas, and the total quota must not double.
[Pitfalls] Keeping counters in process memory, so after scaling out the quota multiplies by the replica count and rate limiting is effectively void; also giving Retry-After a fixed value, so all clients return simultaneously and create regular spikes.

svg.拒绝时要告诉对方「还剩多少、多久能再来」: On reject: quota left + retry time

sparse-fieldsets.logic: Let the caller declare which fields it wants, and the server queries and returns only those. It saves bandwidth and database work, but you must prevent it from turning into a query interface that can be combined arbitrarily.
sparse-fieldsets.prompt:
Implement "Sparse Fieldsets" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] A list endpoint returns dozens of fields to serve every caller, while mobile uses only three of them, paying for bandwidth and database reads in vain; and creating a separate endpoint per page leads to endpoint explosion.
[Approach] Support ?fields=id,name,status so the caller declares the fields it needs. **Field names must go through a whitelist**; never concatenate the parameter into the SQL SELECT, since that is injection and also permanently exposes internal column names as a public contract. In the whitelist, distinguish "light fields" from "heavy fields": heavy fields (those needing extra queries or computation, such as joined statistics) are **not returned by default and must be requested explicitly**, which is far more effective than optimizing after the fact. When no fields parameter is given, return a conservative default set rather than everything. The response cache key must include fields, otherwise results of different projections pollute each other.
[Which layer] The serialization layer parses the whitelist, and the query layer selects only the columns actually needed and skips unneeded join queries; **trimming only at serialization while the database still queries everything is the same as doing nothing**.
[Key parameters] At most 30 fields; an unknown field name returns 400 rather than being silently ignored (silent ignoring means the client's typos are never discovered); write the default field set in the docs.
[How to verify] Compare the actual SQL with and without fields to confirm the query itself shrank and not just the response; then pass a nonexistent field name, which should return 400.
[Pitfalls] Concatenating fields directly into SELECT is both an injection surface and makes internal column names an external contract, so renaming a column later becomes a breaking change; also trimming only in the serialization layer, so the database does all the same work and you saved bandwidth but not the real cost.

contract-test.logic: The consumer declares "which fields and shapes of yours I depend on", and the provider runs that declaration in CI. If something breaks, it goes red before merge instead of being discovered by the other side after release.
contract-test.prompt:
Implement "Contract Testing" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] When changing an API, nobody knows who depends on which field, and full end-to-end tests are slow and brittle. The result is either not daring to change anything, or having downstream discover the breakage in production for you.
[Approach] The consumer records its expectations of the provider in its own tests: what the request looks like and which fields and types the response must contain. This contract is published to a shared location, and the provider runs it in CI against its own real implementation (not a mock); if it isn't satisfied, CI goes red. **The contract asserts only the fields the consumer actually uses**; don't assert the whole response body, because if you do the provider goes red even for adding an optional field and soon nobody takes it seriously. One provider has multiple contracts (one per consumer), and it counts as compatible only if all pass. Contracts should also cover the shape of error responses, which is often where breakage goes unnoticed.
[Which layer] The CI pipeline, run before every provider merge.
[Key parameters] Contracts contain only required fields; provider CI takes the full set of contracts from all active consumers; tag contract versions together with consumer versions.
[How to verify] Deliberately remove a depended-on field, and the provider's CI should immediately go red and point to which consumer's which contract failed; then add a new optional field, and CI should stay green as usual.
[Pitfalls] Contracts asserting byte-for-byte equality of the whole response body, so any added field fails and the team soon learns to blindly regenerate contracts, which kills the tests; also the provider running contracts against a mock, which only proves the mock matches the contract, not the real implementation.

svg.消费方声明依赖，提供方 CI 里跑，改坏了合并前就红: Consumer declares; provider CI runs; red pre-merge

composite-index-order.logic: A composite index can only be used starting from its leftmost column. The column order decides which queries it can serve; pick wrong and you've built an index that never gets used, and this raises no error, it is just slow.
composite-index-order.prompt:
Implement "Composite Index Order" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] You built an index and the query is still slow. Most likely the column order is wrong: a composite index is a tree sorted by column order that **can only be used contiguously from the leftmost column**; skip any column in the middle and the columns after it degrade into filtering rather than locating.
[Approach] Order as "equality columns first, range columns after, and the sort column in the range column's position". Concretely: put all columns used for equality matching first (WHERE a = ?), then the range column (WHERE b > ?); if the sort column is not the same as the range column, the sort can't use the index and degrades into an external sort. The order among equality columns doesn't affect whether it is hit, but putting the higher-selectivity ones first makes the tree shallower. When all columns a query touches are in the index (a covering index), no table lookup is needed at all, a huge gain on wide tables. **Every additional index has a write cost**, so don't build one per query.
[Which layer] The database schema; work with the query layer to keep the shape of the WHERE clause stable.
[Key parameters] Keep a table to at most 5 indexes; composite indexes generally have no more than 4 columns; look at the execution plan before building, not by gut feeling.
[How to verify] Use EXPLAIN to check whether the target index is used, focusing on rows scanned rather than merely "index used or not": using it but scanning 800k rows is as good as not using it. Then deliberately drop the leftmost column from the query conditions; rows scanned should grow noticeably, which conversely proves the index really is working.
[Pitfalls] Assuming that building (a,b,c) also gives you indexes on (b) and (c), when a query on b alone can't use it at all; also building a standalone index on a low-selectivity column (such as gender, or a status with three values), which the optimizer will never pick, leaving only write overhead.

svg.等值列在前、范围列在后 —— 跳过一列，后面全废: Equality, then range; skip one, rest wasted

soft-delete-cost.logic: Adding a deleted_at flag instead of truly deleting looks safe, but the cost is that every query must remember to filter, unique constraints stop working, and the table keeps growing.
soft-delete-cost.prompt:
Implement "Soft Delete Trade-offs" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Soft delete is easily treated as the default option, but its costs are hidden: every query must remember to include deleted_at IS NULL, **and missing one means a data leak or doubled statistics**, with no error raised.
[Approach] First ask what the real requirement is. Need undo? Build a 30-day recycle bin and hard-delete on expiry. Need an audit trail? Write the delete event into an audit table and hard-delete from the business table as usual. Need to keep historical associations? Archive into a separate history table. All three are more targeted than "soft delete on every table". When soft delete is truly needed: put the filter in a database view or the ORM's global scope, **and don't rely on everyone remembering to write it**; change unique constraints into partial indexes that include the delete marker (e.g. PostgreSQL's WHERE deleted_at IS NULL), otherwise after deleting a username no one can ever register that name again; periodically move soft-deleted data into an archive table so the main table doesn't grow without bound.
[Which layer] The ORM's global filter plus the database's partial unique index; you need both layers.
[Key parameters] Recycle bin retention 30 days; run the archive job once a day; partial unique indexes cover every originally unique column combination.
[How to verify] Write a test that walks all query paths and asserts each includes the delete filter (or inspect the generated SQL directly); then, after deleting a record, create a new one with the same unique value, which must succeed.
[Pitfalls] Not converting unique constraints into partial indexes, so the "delete then recreate" scenario throws a duplicate-key error and the user sees an inexplicable failure; also reports and business logic using different query paths, with the report side forgetting to filter, so the numbers don't match and are hard to trace.

svg.标记删除：漏一个过滤就是数据泄漏，而且不报错: Soft delete: a missed filter leaks silently

optimistic-lock.logic: On update, include the version number you read: WHERE version = :v. If the affected row count is 0, someone else changed it first. It replaces a lock with one conditional write.
optimistic-lock.prompt:
Implement "Optimistic Locking" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Two people open the same record to edit at the same time, and whoever saves later overwrites the earlier save entirely, and the user has no idea they lost anything. This is the lost update, the most common and quietest bug in concurrent scenarios.
[Approach] Add an integer version column to the table (or use updated_at, though insufficient timestamp precision causes false judgments). When reading, return the version to the client along with the data; when updating, run UPDATE ... SET version = version + 1 WHERE id = :id AND version = :v. **The deciding signal is the affected row count**: 0 means the record was modified by someone else after you read it, so return 409 and tell the client "data has changed". On receiving 409 the client should re-fetch and show the difference, **not retry automatically**; an automatic retry is just another overwrite and defeats the optimistic lock. Only for hot rows with frequent conflicts consider switching to pessimistic locking or splitting the field out more finely (e.g. put a counter in its own row).
[Which layer] Encapsulate uniformly in the data access layer; business code handles only the single outcome "conflict".
[Key parameters] Use bigint for version; a conflict returns 409 along with the current latest version; no server-side automatic retry.
[How to verify] Two concurrent requests read the same record and then update one after the other; the second must fail with 409, and the first person's change must still be in the database. This test must really run concurrently; running serially won't reveal it.
[Pitfalls] Treating "affected rows = 0" as "record not found" and returning 404, which confuses people; also the server catching the conflict and automatically retrying the update, which implements exactly the overwrite you set out to avoid.

svg.更新带上读到的版本号，对不上就是别人先改了: Update with version; mismatch = lost race

deep-pagination.logic: OFFSET 100000 makes the database scan and discard a hundred thousand rows first. Use cursor pagination for list endpoints and primary-key range slicing for full exports; neither uses OFFSET.
deep-pagination.prompt:
Implement "Deep Pagination" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] The cost of LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000 is scanning and discarding a hundred thousand rows first, so it gets slower the deeper you page; a crawler or export job paging all the way to the end can drag the database down, while the first few pages looked perfectly normal in testing.
[Approach] Two scenarios. **User paging** uses cursor (keyset) pagination: continue from the sort key of the last item on the previous page, at a cost independent of page number. **Full export / migration** uses primary-key range slicing: WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 1000, advancing in a loop, which is simpler than a cursor and naturally stable. When jumping to a page truly must be supported (e.g. "jump to page 50"), hard-limit the jumpable range (e.g. only the first 100 pages), and beyond that require the user to add filters to narrow down; nobody really pages to page 5000 to look at data, that's only ever a crawler. Also be wary of the total count on list endpoints: COUNT(*) is equally expensive on big tables, so replace the exact total with "has more" wherever you can.
[Which layer] The query layer; the API layer limits page size and maximum page number.
[Key parameters] Page size cap 100; maximum page number 100 (or don't support jumping at all); export slice 1000 rows per batch; when the total exceeds 10000 return "10000+".
[How to verify] On a million-row table, time page 1 and page 500 separately; the cursor approach should be roughly flat. Then run a full export and observe that the database's total rows scanned is close to the table's row count rather than its square.
[Pitfalls] Optimizing only the API while forgetting the background export job still uses OFFSET, which drags down the primary database during the overnight batch run; also running COUNT(*) every time just to display page numbers, when that one query is often more expensive than fetching the data itself.

svg.OFFSET 越翻越慢；游标翻页与页码无关: OFFSET slows with depth; cursor doesn't

replica-lag.logic: Writes go to the primary and reads go to replicas, and replicas lag by milliseconds to seconds. A user who submits and immediately refreshes sees stale data; this class of bug only shows up under production load.
replica-lag.prompt:
Implement "Replica Lag" handling in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Writing to the primary and reading from replicas can carry read-heavy traffic, but replicas always lag. The symptom: a user edits their profile and refreshes right away, still sees the old value, assumes the save failed, and edits again. In development the lag is near 0, so this bug is almost only hit in production.
[Approach] First separate out which reads **must see their own just-written data** (read-your-writes): the detail page after submit, the order status after payment, the profile page after editing. These go to the primary. The way to do it is to set a short-lived marker in the session or token after a write (e.g. for 60 seconds that user's reads go to the primary), or record the log position at write time and require a replica to catch up to that position before serving the read. Other reads (lists, search, statistics) tolerate lag and go to replicas. **The default should be replicas, with the primary an explicitly specified exception**; the other way round, soon all queries are back on the primary. Also monitor replica lag, and when it exceeds a threshold automatically switch reads back to the primary and alert.
[Which layer] The data source routing layer; business code only declares "does this read require the latest data".
[Key parameters] read-your-writes window 60s; replica lag alert threshold 1s, automatic switch-to-primary threshold 5s; reads inside a transaction always go to the primary.
[How to verify] Artificially inject 2 seconds of lag into a replica and run the "view immediately after submit" flow, which must show the new value; then run lists and statistics, which should still go to replicas (check the connection distribution).
[Pitfalls] Writing to the primary then reading from a replica inside one transaction reads the pre-write state and scrambles the logic; also having no fallback when a replica is down or its lag spikes, so read requests all time out instead of falling back to the primary.

transaction-boundary.logic: A transaction should wrap only the writes that must be atomic. Stuffing HTTP calls, file uploads, or message sends into it holds connections and locks for a long time and eventually drags down the whole pool.
transaction-boundary.prompt:
Implement "Transaction Boundary" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] The transaction is opened too wide: it has third-party API calls, email sending, and object-storage writes sandwiched inside. These operations are slow and uncontrollable, so the transaction holds database connections and row locks for a long time, the connection pool fills up as soon as concurrency rises, and the symptom is the entire service waiting on the database, while the root cause is often an HTTP call unrelated to the database.
[Approach] The principle is **only database writes inside a transaction**, and keep it as short as possible. Move external calls outside the transaction: for the scenario "send a message after the DB write succeeds", use a transactional outbox (write the message as a row into an outbox table in the same transaction as the business write, and have a separate worker read the outbox and deliver), so you neither put an MQ call inside the transaction nor get "DB written but message not sent". Don't open a transaction for reads that don't need one. **No sleep, retries, or user interaction inside a transaction.** Lock acquisition order must be consistent across all code paths, otherwise deadlocks are inevitable under concurrency.
[Which layer] The service layer declares transaction boundaries explicitly; don't let the ORM's implicit transactions decide for you.
[Key parameters] Target < 100ms per transaction, alert when over 1s; no network calls are allowed inside a transaction (enforce with static checks or runtime assertions); choose the isolation level as needed, and don't default to serializable.
[How to verify] During load testing observe average transaction duration and connection pool wait time; then deliberately set a third-party API to a 5-second timeout, and the service's overall throughput should be unaffected.
[Pitfalls] Using the ORM's automatic transaction to wrap the entire HTTP request handling, so every slow endpoint holds a database connection; also sending MQ messages inside a transaction, so the message goes out but the transaction rolls back, and downstream receives a business event that doesn't exist.

svg.事务里只放数据库写；外部调用挪出去: Tx: DB writes only; move calls out

unique-constraint.logic: "Check whether it exists, then insert if not" inevitably produces duplicates under concurrency. A unique constraint is the last and only reliable line of defense; the application-level check is only there to give a friendly message.
unique-constraint.prompt:
Implement "Unique Constraint as Backstop" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] A registration endpoint first checks whether the username exists and inserts if not. Two requests pass the check at the same time and both insert, producing two accounts with the same name; the window is only a few milliseconds, so tests never hit it, but once traffic grows it is bound to happen.
[Approach] **A database unique index is the only reliable defense**; the application-level pre-check is merely to give the user a friendly message and can't be treated as a guarantee. On insert, catch the unique-key violation exception and translate it into a business error code (e.g. USERNAME_TAKEN); don't let it bubble up as a 500. When you need "update if exists, insert if not", use the database's atomic form (UPSERT / INSERT ... ON CONFLICT / INSERT IGNORE) rather than reading first and writing after. When uniqueness spans multiple columns, build a composite unique index; when soft delete is involved, switch to a partial unique index (see "Soft Delete Trade-offs"). Case-insensitive uniqueness (email, username) must be handled at the index level, using a generated column or an expression index, otherwise Alice and alice will coexist.
[Which layer] The database constraint is the foundation; the service layer translates the conflict exception into plain language.
[Key parameters] Every business uniqueness rule needs a corresponding index; conflicts return 409; the email unique index is built on lower(email).
[How to verify] Fire 50 concurrent registration requests with the same name; in the end the database must contain exactly 1 record, and the other 49 must return a clear business error rather than a 500. Serial tests can't reveal this; it must be truly concurrent.
[Pitfalls] Deduplicating only at the application layer and cleaning up duplicates with a scheduled job after launch; the cleanup must also decide which to keep and what to do with associated data, at a cost far higher than adding the index up front; also letting the unique-conflict exception propagate straight out, so the user sees a 500 rather than "this username is already taken".

json-column.logic: Putting frequently changing or variably shaped fields into a JSON column avoids frequent schema changes. The cost is losing constraints, awkward queries and indexing, and it is easily abused as a catch-all dumping ground.
json-column.prompt:
Implement "JSON Column Trade-offs" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Some fields have no fixed shape (raw data returned by third parties, per-tenant custom attributes, config snapshots), and changing the table structure for them again and again is impractical; but dumping everything into JSON loses type constraints, foreign keys, and efficient queries. What you need is a decision criterion, not a mindless either-or.
[Approach] The criterion is **"will it be used as a query condition or sort key"**: if so it must be a real column; only if not is JSON appropriate. Typical good fits for JSON: archived raw third-party responses, audit snapshots, custom extension fields of a few tenants. Typical bad fits: status, type, amount, time, which sooner or later need filtering, sorting, and aggregation. When using JSON choose a type that supports indexing (jsonb in PostgreSQL, JSON with generated columns in MySQL), and build indexes on the paths you need to query (GIN, or an expression index plus a generated column). **Define a schema for the JSON at the application layer and validate on write**, otherwise half a year later it holds five different shapes of data and nobody dares touch it. JSON fields proven to be queried long-term should be promoted to real columns early.
[Which layer] Schema design; write-time validation in the service layer.
[Key parameters] Keep a single JSON column under 64KB; paths that need querying must have an index; validate before writing with JSON Schema or a type definition.
[How to verify] For queries on fields inside the JSON, check the execution plan to confirm an index is used rather than a full table scan; then write a record that doesn't conform to the agreed shape, and the write should be rejected.
[Pitfalls] Treating the JSON column as a "deal with it later" dumping ground where everything goes, ending up neither queryable nor safe to clean up; also storing counters that need transactional updates inside JSON, where two concurrent updates overwrite the whole JSON document.

svg.会被当查询条件的必须是真列，其余才放 JSON: Queried fields = real columns; the rest = JSON

archive-partition.logic: Unbounded table growth makes indexes deeper, backups slower, and DDL nearly impossible. Partition by time and archive cold data out so the hot table stays at a manageable size.
archive-partition.prompt:
Implement "Archiving & Partitioning" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Once append-only tables like logs, orders, and events reach hundreds of millions of rows: indexes get deeper, queries slow down, the backup window can't hold, and a DDL to add a column locks the table for hours. Dealing with it at that point costs an order of magnitude more than planning up front.
[Approach] First set a **data retention policy**; this is a product and compliance question, not a technical one: how long hot data is kept, how long cold data is kept, and when it can be truly deleted. Then partition by time (monthly or weekly), with new data always written to the newest partition and expired partitions **simply DROPped** (the biggest value of partitioning: dropping a partition is a metadata operation, whereas DELETEing tens of millions of rows generates a huge amount of log and drags replicas down). When cold data must be retained, first export it to object storage or a separate archive database and then DROP. The partition key must appear in the WHERE of the vast majority of queries, otherwise every query scans all partitions and is actually slower. **Partitioning isn't for speeding up queries**; it's for making maintenance feasible, so don't expect it to replace indexes.
[Which layer] Schema plus a scheduled partition maintenance job (create future partitions ahead of time; don't wait until a write discovers there is no matching partition).
[Key parameters] Monthly partitions, created 3 months ahead; hot data 3~6 months; run the archive job during off-peak hours; target < 50 million rows per partition.
[How to verify] Confirm partition pruning happens in the query plan (only relevant partitions are scanned); then rehearse a DROP of an old partition and observe that it takes seconds, not hours.
[Pitfalls] Forgetting to create next month's partition ahead of time, so writes fail right at midnight on the 1st, the classic production incident of partitioned tables; also picking a partition key that queries don't include at all, so every query scans all partitions, slower than not partitioning.

svg.按时间分区，过期整块 DROP —— 不用 DELETE 几千万行: Partition by time; DROP whole expired block, no mass DELETE

slow-query-hunt.logic: Find targets by "total time" rather than "slowest single run": a query that takes 50ms but runs a thousand times a second is more worth optimizing than one that takes 5 seconds but runs once a day.
slow-query-hunt.prompt:
Implement "Slow Query Hunting" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] The database is slow, but you don't know which query to optimize. The most eye-catching entry in the slow query log is often a report that runs once a day, while what actually crushes the database is an unremarkable query executed thousands of times per second.
[Approach] Use aggregated statistics rather than individual log lines: pg_stat_statements for PostgreSQL, performance_schema or a slow-log aggregation tool for MySQL, and **sort by "total time = average time x call count"**, which is the true ranking of what consumes the database. Once you have the target SQL, look at the execution plan; the point is not "was an index used" but **the ratio of rows scanned to rows returned**: scanning 800k rows to return 20 means the wrong index was chosen. Also check for sorts (an external sort means the sort column isn't covered by an index) and temporary tables. Optimization order: first change the query shape (remove unnecessary joins and sorts), then tune indexes, and only last consider changing the table structure or adding a cache. **Change one thing at a time and re-measure**; if you change three at once you won't know which one worked.
[Which layer] Database observability plus query instrumentation on the application side (link the SQL to the endpoint that calls it, otherwise you know a slow SQL exists but not who calls it).
[Key parameters] Slow query threshold 200ms; review the total-time Top 20 once a week; watch P99 rather than the average (averages get diluted by lots of fast queries).
[How to verify] Compare rows scanned and share of total time for the same SQL before and after optimization, and confirm the endpoint's P99 really dropped; if you look only at the average, an optimization affecting just 1% of requests looks like it did nothing.
[Pitfalls] Looking only at the slowest entry in the slow query log and endlessly optimizing an unimportant report; also verifying only on the test database after optimizing, when the test database's data volume and distribution differ completely from production and the execution plan may be entirely different.

svg.按「平均 × 次数」排，不是按单次最慢排: Rank by avg x count, not slowest run

backoff-jitter.logic: Retry intervals grow exponentially, and **random jitter must be added**. Without jitter, all clients come back at the same instant and knock down a service that has just caught its breath.
backoff-jitter.prompt:
Implement "Backoff with Jitter" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] When a downstream service wobbles, retrying immediately only worsens congestion; and retrying at a fixed interval makes all failed callers return at the same instant, creating regular spikes that knock the freshly recovered service over again. This is the thundering herd, and the typical cause of "the service dies again right after it recovers".
[Approach] Intervals grow exponentially (base x 2^n) up to a cap, and then **randomize on top of that**. Full jitter is recommended: sleep = random(0, min(cap, base x 2^n)), which disperses better than "fixed value +/- 20%". **Retry only retryable errors**: network timeouts, connection failures, 5xx, 429 (honoring Retry-After). Among 4xx, never retry anything except 429; a bad parameter is still bad after a hundred retries. **Non-idempotent writes must not be retried blindly**; pair them with an idempotency key (see "Idempotency Key"). Retries need a cap on count, and total time must not exceed the timeout budget your upstream gives you, otherwise you keep retrying after the upstream has given up, pure waste.
[Which layer] A unified HTTP/RPC client wrapper; don't let each call site write its own retry.
[Key parameters] base 100ms, cap 10s, at most 3~5 attempts; full jitter; total retry budget no more than 2/3 of the upstream timeout.
[How to verify] Make the downstream fail continuously and record the actual retry times; intervals should both grow exponentially and differ from each other (retry times of multiple concurrent clients should visibly spread out); then make the downstream return 400, and there should be zero retries.
[Pitfalls] No jitter, so every recovery is accompanied by a spike that knocks the service over again; also retrying at every layer (client 3 x gateway 3 x service 3 = 27 attempts), amplifying one fault into a flood of traffic; **retry at only one layer**.

svg.间隔翻倍并加随机抖动，否则大家同时回来再打一次: Double gaps + jitter, or all return together

circuit-breaker.logic: When a downstream keeps failing, cut the connection so calls fail fast instead of waiting for a timeout each time. After a while, let a few probe requests through, and restore once it is healthy.
circuit-breaker.prompt:
Implement "Circuit Breaker" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] When the downstream is dead, each of your requests waits the full timeout before failing. Threads and connections get tied up in bulk and you go down with it; that is how a non-critical dependency's failure becomes a site-wide outage.
[Approach] A three-state machine. **Closed** (normal): track the failure rate in a sliding window, and when it exceeds a threshold move to open. **Open**: all calls fail immediately without sending any real request, and go straight to the fallback logic. **Half-open**: after the cooldown ends, let a few probe requests through; if all succeed return to closed, and if any fail return to open and restart the timer. Base the decision on **failure rate, not failure count**, and require a minimum number of requests in the window (say at least 20), otherwise the first failed request during a cold start trips the breaker. Timeouts also count as failures: slow and dead are the same thing to the caller. **One independent breaker per downstream dependency**; share one and A's failure trips B too. The most important part is deciding **what to degrade to when open**: return cache, return a default value, or tell the user plainly that this part is temporarily unavailable. A breaker without a fallback plan is just a faster way to fail.
[Which layer] Client side (inside the caller's process), not the downstream.
[Key parameters] Window 10s; minimum requests 20; failure rate threshold 50%; open cooldown 5~30s; half-open lets through 3~5.
[How to verify] Make the downstream time out on everything, and observe the breaker opening at the threshold and subsequent calls **returning immediately** (duration near 0, not the timeout length); after restoring the downstream confirm it returns to normal automatically after the cooldown.
[Pitfalls] Tripping the breaker with no fallback logic, so the user still sees an error page, just failing faster; also sharing one breaker across all downstreams, so a flaky peripheral service trips the core path with it.

svg.连续失败就断开，调用立即失败；冷却后放少量试探: Trip on failures, fail fast, then probe

bulkhead.logic: Give different dependencies or different priorities of traffic independent resource pools, so exhausting one pool doesn't affect the others. The name comes from a ship's watertight compartments: one compartment floods, the ship doesn't sink.
bulkhead.prompt:
Implement "Bulkhead Isolation" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] All requests share one thread pool or connection pool. Once a slow dependency fills the pool, **endpoints that don't depend on it at all also become unavailable**; the failure spreads from one feature to the whole service.
[Approach] Split resource pools by dependency or by priority: calls to the payment gateway use one set of connections, product lookups another, each with its own limit. Core and non-core endpoints use different pools, so when the non-core pool is exhausted only non-core is affected. When a pool is full, **reject immediately instead of queueing** (or allow only a very short queue); unbounded queueing turns the failure from "partially unavailable" into "everything times out". Same for database connections: heavy report-style queries use a separate connection pool with limited concurrency and don't compete with online requests. Keep the granularity of the split restrained: every pool has a minimum standing cost, and splitting too finely wastes resources and is hard to tune.
[Which layer] Client connection pool / thread pool configuration; combine with circuit breaking and timeouts as a set.
[Key parameters] Core pool gets 70% of total capacity, non-core 30%; pool-full wait limit 0~50ms and then reject; report-style query concurrency limit 2~4.
[How to verify] Make one non-core dependency hang completely, load-test the core endpoints, and their success rate and latency should be unaffected; this is the only criterion for whether the bulkhead is done right.
[Pitfalls] Splitting the thread pools but sharing one database connection pool, so isolation is missing at the most critical layer; also unbounded queueing when a pool is full, so the queue grows longer and longer until every request times out, worse than rejecting outright.

svg.资源分池：一个池耗尽，别的照常 —— 故障不扩散: Separate pools: one exhausted, others fine

timeout-budget.logic: Each layer's timeout must be smaller than the time remaining at the layer above; otherwise the upstream has long given up while the downstream is still computing. The whole call chain shares one budget that decreases from the entry point.
timeout-budget.prompt:
Implement "Timeout Budget" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Gateway 30s, service 30s, database 30s: it looks like timeouts are set everywhere, but in practice one slow request makes every layer of the chain wait a dead 30 seconds and all resources get pinned; worse, the upstream gives up after 5 seconds while the downstream is still computing, and the finished result is wanted by nobody: pure waste, and it holds connections.
[Approach] Use a **budget** rather than setting a separate value at each layer: the entry point allocates a total budget (e.g. 3s), and on every downstream call passes "remaining budget minus a small margin" as the downstream's timeout (gRPC deadline, or a custom HTTP header, both work). The downstream decrements it the same way. Any layer that sees the remaining budget is no longer enough to finish the work should **give up immediately** and not start a call that is doomed to time out. Timeout values should be **derived from data**: look at the downstream's P99 latency and set the timeout to 1.5~2x P99 rather than picking 30s out of the air. Retries also consume budget: 3 retries must complete within the total budget (see "Backoff with Jitter"). When the client disconnects, the cancellation signal must propagate downward, otherwise the user has long gone and you are still running.
[Which layer] Handled uniformly by the RPC/HTTP client framework; business code only declares the total budget.
[Key parameters] Entry total budget set per endpoint (online endpoints 1~3s); each layer leaves a 50~100ms margin for network and serialization; timeout value = downstream P99 x 1.5.
[How to verify] Artificially make the lowest layer slow by 10 seconds, and assert that each layer returns at its own budget rather than waiting out its full time layer by layer; then confirm that after the client actively disconnects, server-side processing is actually cancelled (via logs or metrics).
[Pitfalls] Configuring timeouts independently at each layer with the downstream longer than the upstream, so the downstream's timeout never fires; also a timeout happening while the underlying task isn't cancelled, so connections and threads stay occupied and the pressure is never released.

dead-letter-queue.logic: Move messages that repeatedly fail processing into a dead letter queue, instead of letting them retry endlessly and block the whole queue. Dead letters need someone watching them, and must be searchable and replayable.
dead-letter-queue.prompt:
Implement "Dead Letter Queue" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] A "poison message" that is malformed or triggers a bug fails and gets redelivered repeatedly, consuming all consumption capacity and **blocking every normal message behind it**; the symptom is queue backlog growing sharply and consumer CPU busy, but nothing gets processed successfully.
[Approach] Set a maximum retry count on consumption; beyond it, push the message into the dead letter queue along with the failure reason, the original queue, and the retry count, and let the main queue move on. The dead letter queue **must have someone watching it**; configure an alert on backlog size, otherwise it is just a silent trash can, and by the time someone notices the data has been lost for months. Provide query and **replay** capability for dead letters (put messages back onto the main queue after the bug is fixed), and let people inspect the content before replaying to confirm. Distinguish **retryable failures** (downstream temporarily unavailable) from **non-retryable failures** (the message itself is bad): the latter should go to the dead letter queue immediately instead of wasting 5 retries. Consumption must be idempotent, since both redelivery and replay cause duplicate consumption.
[Which layer] Message broker configuration plus the consumer's error classification logic.
[Key parameters] Maximum 3~5 retries; keep dead letters 14~30 days; alert when the dead letter queue count is > 0 (don't set a "reasonable" threshold; dead letters should normally be 0); rate-limit replay.
[How to verify] Publish a message that is guaranteed to fail, and confirm that after N attempts it lands in the dead letter queue and the main queue keeps consuming normally; then after the fix, replay it, and the message should be processed correctly without duplicate side effects.
[Pitfalls] Configuring a dead letter queue that nobody monitors, so it becomes a black hole; also not rate-limiting replay, so tens of thousands of backlogged messages flood back into the main queue at once and knock the downstream over.

svg.重试耗尽就挪进死信，别让一条堵住整条队列: Exhausted → DLQ; one msg can't block all

delivery-semantics.logic: In a distributed setting almost only "at-least-once" is feasible; so-called "exactly-once" is an effect achieved through consumer-side idempotency, not a transport-layer guarantee.
delivery-semantics.prompt:
Implement "Delivery Semantics" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Assuming the message queue guarantees "exactly once", so the consumer doesn't do idempotency. In reality network timeouts, consumer restarts, and lost acks all cause redelivery, resulting in duplicate charges and duplicate shipments, and only during failures, while everything is normal the rest of the time.
[Approach] Recognize the three semantics: **at-most-once** (may lose, ack before processing), **at-least-once** (may duplicate, process before ack, the right choice in the vast majority of scenarios), **exactly-once** (nearly impossible at the transport layer; it is an effect presented via consumer-side idempotency). So the correct posture is: **at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumption**. Implement idempotency by giving each message a business-unique id and, before consuming, atomically recording "this id has been processed" (unique index or Redis SETNX); if it already exists, ack and skip. **The dedup record and the business write must be in the same transaction**; if separate, a crash in between still produces duplicates. The dedup table needs expiry cleanup, otherwise it grows without bound. Ordering also needs thought: with multiple partitions/consumers there is no global order; when ordering is needed, partition by business key so the same key lands in the same partition.
[Which layer] Dedup at the consumer entry point, and design the business logic itself to be idempotent where possible (e.g. "set to X" is safer than "increase by X").
[Key parameters] Use the business id as the dedup key, not the message id (the message id may change on redelivery); keep dedup records 7 days; fixed partition per business key.
[How to verify] Deliver the same message twice on purpose and assert the business side effect happens only once; then kill the consumer process after processing completes but before ack, and after restart no duplicate should occur.
[Pitfalls] Placing dedup after the business write, so a crash in between causes a duplicate; also assuming "my MQ supports exactly-once so I don't need idempotency", when that guarantee usually covers only its own reads and writes, not the third-party APIs you call.

compensating-transaction.logic: Cross-service operations can't use a database transaction, so they become a chain of local transactions, and on failure compensating actions run in reverse order. The compensation itself must be idempotent and must not fail.
compensating-transaction.prompt:
Implement "Compensating Transaction" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Placing an order requires deducting stock, deducting balance, and creating the order, spread across three services. When a middle step fails, the steps that already succeeded must be undone, and there is no database transaction available across services.
[Approach] Split the whole flow into a chain of **local transactions**, and define a **compensating action** for each step (deduct stock <-> restore stock, charge <-> refund). On failure, execute the compensations one by one in **reverse order**. Three hard requirements: (1) compensation must be **idempotent**, because compensation itself will be retried; (2) compensation **must not fail**, since if it fails there's no fallback, so compensation logic should be as simple as possible, and if it truly fails it goes to a dead-letter queue and **raises an alert for manual intervention**; (3) the state of each step and its compensation must be **persisted** so that after a process restart the flow can continue to completion (the easiest to miss: tracking state only in memory leaves a pile of half-finished orders after every deploy). Note that compensation is not rollback: intermediate states **have been externally visible**, so the business must be able to accept that (e.g. freeze the amount first rather than deducting directly, and unfreeze on failure, so the user never sees the money go down).
[Which layer] An orchestrator (an explicit flow state machine) or event-driven choreography; **orchestration is recommended**, because in choreography the flow is scattered across each service's event handlers and when something breaks nobody can say which step it has reached.
[Key parameters] Trigger compensation after each step's timeout; alert after at most 5 compensation retries; flow state persisted and queryable.
[How to verify] Inject a failure after each step and assert that all prior steps are correctly compensated and the data returns to its initial state; then kill the process halfway through compensation, and after restart it should finish the compensation.
[Pitfalls] Using "charge/refund" right away for problems that "freeze/unfreeze" would solve, so users see the intermediate state (balance dropped and came back) and file complaints; also a compensating action that isn't itself idempotent, so one retry refunds twice.

svg.跨服务没有事务：失败时按相反顺序逐步补偿: No cross-svc tx: compensate in reverse

graceful-shutdown.logic: After receiving the stop signal, first take the instance out of traffic, then finish the requests in hand, and finally exit. Skip any step and every release drops a batch of requests.
graceful-shutdown.prompt:
Implement "Graceful Shutdown" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Every rolling release produces a batch of 5xx errors or connection resets. The cause is the process exiting immediately on SIGTERM, interrupting in-flight requests; or, more subtly, the process has already begun shutting down while the load balancer is still sending it new requests.
