[Approach] The order is critical. (1) After receiving SIGTERM, **first set the readiness probe to fail**, but **keep accepting and handling requests**. (2) **Wait a while** (the key step) so the load balancer / service registry notices and removes you; this detection has a delay (probe interval + number of checks), and if you don't wait, the requests before removal are all lost. (3) Stop accepting new connections and wait for in-flight requests to finish (with an upper bound). (4) Shut down consumers, ack or return the messages in hand, close the database connection pool, and flush buffered logs and metrics. (5) Exit. The whole process must complete within the orchestrator's force-kill grace period, otherwise SIGKILL interrupts it and everything before was wasted. **Long-lived connections (WebSocket/SSE) must be actively told to reconnect**, otherwise they hang until timeout.
[Which layer] Process lifecycle management; coordinate with terminationGracePeriod in the deployment config.
[Key parameters] Traffic-drain wait = probe interval x failure threshold + 5s (commonly 10~15s); request drain limit 20s; total duration must be < the force-kill grace period (e.g. 45s).
[How to verify] Do a rolling release under sustained load; the **error rate should be 0**. This is the only meaningful way to verify; a log saying "shut down gracefully" doesn't count.
[Pitfalls] Stopping acceptance of new requests immediately on the signal without waiting for the load balancer to remove you, so new requests during those seconds all get connection refused, the most common real cause of "dropped requests during release"; also a drain time longer than the force-kill grace period, so SIGKILL interrupts it and it's as if nothing was done.

svg.先摘流量、等负载均衡感知到，再关 —— 顺序反了就掉请求: Drain, wait for LB, then stop; wrong order drops reqs

health-check-truth.logic: A health check that returns 200 without actually checking anything proves only that the process is alive. The criteria for the liveness probe and the readiness probe must be separate; mixing them causes a rolling-restart avalanche.
health-check-truth.prompt:
Implement "Meaningful Health Checks" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] The health check returns a hard-coded 200, so an instance whose database connections are all severed and which can process nothing is considered healthy, and traffic keeps flowing in. Conversely, putting downstream dependencies into the **liveness probe** causes an even worse incident: as soon as the downstream dies, all instances are judged dead and restarted simultaneously, and the service is completely unavailable.
[Approach] **Two probes, two sets of criteria, kept distinct.** The liveness probe answers only "is this process hung, does it need a restart": it checks only internal process state (event loop not blocked, no deadlock) and **must never check any external dependency**, because restarting can't fix someone else's database. The readiness probe answers "can I receive traffic right now": it checks whether required dependency connections are usable (can the DB connection pool hand out a connection, is the required cache ready); on failure the instance is merely removed from traffic, not restarted, and returns automatically once the dependency recovers. **Distinguish required from optional dependencies**: when an optional dependency is down you should degrade rather than mark the whole instance not ready. Checks need timeouts and caching (if every probe really queries the database, the probe itself becomes a source of load).
[Which layer] Separate /healthz (liveness) and /readyz (readiness) endpoints, bypassing business auth and rate limiting.
[Key parameters] Liveness probe interval 10s, restart after 3 failures; readiness probe interval 5s, remove from traffic after 2 failures; cache dependency check results 2~5s; the check's own timeout 1s.
[How to verify] Disconnect the database, and the instance should become "not ready but still alive" (removed from traffic, not restarted); after recovery it should return to ready automatically. Then simulate an event-loop block, and the liveness probe should fail.
[Pitfalls] Putting the database check into the liveness probe, so a database blip restarts all instances at once and amplifies a local fault into a site-wide one; also health checks going through the auth middleware, so an auth service outage marks all instances unhealthy.

svg.存活探针别查下游 —— 重启修不好别人家的数据库: Liveness skips downstream; restart can't fix it

canary-rollback.logic: Send a new version a small share of traffic first, and use metric comparison to decide whether to advance or roll back. **Rollback must be faster and more reliable than release**; this is the floor of the whole mechanism.
canary-rollback.prompt:
Implement "Canary & Rollback" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Problems are discovered only after the new version is fully rolled out, when the blast radius is already 100%; and if the rollback process is as slow and complex as a release, the outage stretches to tens of minutes.
[Approach] Ramp up the canary gradually by percentage (1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%), **with a long enough observation window at each step**; if it is shorter than the cache and retry cycles it depends on, problems have no time to surface. Compare the metrics (error rate, P99 latency, key business conversion) of the new and old versions **in the same time period**, not against yesterday, since yesterday's traffic mix was different. Define **automatic rollback conditions** and actually wire them up: automatically roll back when the error rate exceeds a multiple of baseline, and don't rely on people watching a dashboard. **Rollback must be faster than release**: database changes must be backward compatible (add columns before dropping, dual-write before switching reads, ship the deletion one release later), otherwise code can roll back but the data can't, which means you can't roll back. Keep releases and config changes separate so config can be rolled back independently and quickly. Leave an explicit version marker on each release so logs and metrics can be split by version; if you can't split by version you can't tell whether the new version introduced the problem.
[Which layer] Deployment orchestration + traffic routing + metric alerting, and the three must work in concert.
[Key parameters] First step 1% observed for 15~30 minutes; automatic rollback threshold = error rate above 2x baseline for 3 minutes; rollback target < 2 minutes to complete; leave at least one release between DDL and the code release.
[How to verify] Run a drill: deliberately ship a version that throws errors, and confirm automatic rollback triggers and completes within the target time. **A rollback process that has never been rehearsed is as good as none**; run for the first time during a real incident, it usually fails.
[Pitfalls] A canary observation period shorter than the cache TTL, so the new version's problem is masked by the old cache and only erupts after ramp-up; also making an incompatible database change, so code rolls back but the data structure can't, and you have no choice but to push forward and fix.

svg.小比例放量、按指标自动回滚 —— 回滚要比发布更快: Small ramp; metric auto-rollback; rollback faster

cache-stampede.logic: Three failures with similar-sounding names but different causes: querying keys that don't exist (penetration), a hot key expiring at an instant (breakdown), and a large batch of keys expiring together (avalanche). Each has a different remedy; don't force one solution onto all.
cache-stampede.prompt:
Implement protection against "Cache Penetration, Breakdown & Avalanche" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Three cache failures with different causes, whose symptom is always "the database is suddenly saturated". **Penetration**: querying a key that doesn't exist at all, so the cache never hits and every request lands on the database (especially deadly when maliciously crafted). **Breakdown**: at the instant a hot key expires, hundreds or thousands of concurrent requests all find a miss and all go to rebuild it. **Avalanche**: a large batch of keys set with the same TTL all expire at the same moment.
[Approach] Handle each separately. Penetration: **cache null values** (a short-TTL empty marker, e.g. 60s), or put a Bloom filter in front to block keys that certainly don't exist; also validate key legality so arbitrary input can't reach the database. Breakdown: **use a mutex on rebuild**, letting only one request query the database and rebuild while the others wait briefly or return the stale value; a better approach is **logical expiry**: the value carries an expiry timestamp, the physical TTL is longer, and when logical expiry is detected it returns the stale value and refreshes asynchronously, so users never wait. Avalanche: **add random jitter to the TTL** (base +/- 10%), and stagger the warm-up times of different businesses' caches.
[Which layer] Encapsulate uniformly in the cache access layer; leaving it to each call site to write, someone will inevitably miss it.
[Key parameters] Null-value TTL 30~60s; rebuild mutex lock timeout 3~5s; TTL jitter +/-10%; logical-expiry physical TTL = logical TTL x 2.
[How to verify] Send 500 concurrent requests at the same just-expired hot key, and the database should receive only 1 query; then request lots of random nonexistent ids, and the database query volume should be held down by the null-value cache.
[Pitfalls] Setting the null-value TTL as long as normal values, so once the data is actually created it takes a long time to become visible; also a mutex lock without a timeout, so when the request doing the rebuild crashes everyone waits forever.

svg.热点键一过期，成百上千个请求同时去重建: Hot key expires: all rebuild at once

multi-level-cache.logic: An in-process cache absorbs the vast majority of reads, with a distributed cache as backup. It's fast, but the cost is that each instance's local copy can become inconsistent, and invalidation gets hard.
multi-level-cache.prompt:
Implement "Multi-level Cache" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Going to Redis every time also has network overhead; extremely high-frequency small data (config, dictionaries, permissions) saturates bandwidth and QPS. Adding an in-process cache layer absorbs the vast majority, but it immediately introduces a consistency problem: after data changes, the local copies on N instances each still hold the old value.
[Approach] L1 is in-process (small capacity, short TTL), L2 is the distributed cache, and only a miss falls through to the database. **Only data meeting all three conditions belongs in L1**: read extremely often, changes very rarely, and short-lived inconsistency is acceptable. There are two ways to invalidate: **short TTL as a backstop** (simplest, accepting inconsistency up to the TTL, enough in most scenarios); **active broadcast invalidation** (notify all instances via pub/sub to delete their local copy, more timely but you must handle lost messages and still need the TTL backstop; **broadcast can't replace TTL**). L1 must have a capacity limit and an eviction policy; an unbounded local cache is a memory leak. **Never put per-user data in L1**: the number of entries equals the number of users and will inevitably eat all memory. Writes must invalidate both L1 and L2, in the order "delete cache then write DB" or "write DB then delayed double delete", depending on the business's tolerance for inconsistency.
[Which layer] The cache access layer uniformly encapsulates two-level reads, writes, and invalidation.
[Key parameters] L1 TTL 5~30s, capacity capped by entry count (e.g. 10000 entries); L2 TTL 5~30 minutes; broadcast invalidation + TTL as dual protection.
[How to verify] Change data once and observe that all instances get the new value within the TTL; then load-test to confirm the L1 hit rate (it should be above 90%, otherwise this layer isn't worth adding).
[Pitfalls] Doing only broadcast invalidation with no TTL, so if one broadcast message is lost that instance returns the old value forever; also building L1 as an unbounded Map, so memory slowly grows to OOM, and at the moment of peak traffic.

svg.本地挡住绝大部分；代价是各实例副本会不一致: Local absorbs most; copies may diverge

connection-pool-exhaustion.logic: When the connection pool is full, all requests queue up, and the symptom is the whole site slowing down. The real cause is almost always elsewhere: slow queries, long transactions, or connections leaked and never returned to the pool.
connection-pool-exhaustion.prompt:
Implement protection and diagnosis for "Connection Pool Exhaustion" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] The service suddenly slows down or times out across the board, while the database's own load isn't high. The typical cause is the connection pool being fully occupied, with requests all queueing; **and a full pool is almost never because the pool is too small, but because connections are held too long**.
[Approach] Diagnose first: monitoring must show three metrics: **pool utilization, wait queue length, and average time to acquire a connection**. Rising wait time is direct evidence of a full pool. Then find who is holding the connections; the common three: (1) slow queries (see "Slow Query Hunting"); (2) long transactions, especially those with external HTTP calls inside (see "Transaction Boundary"); (3) **connection leaks**: connections taken and never returned, usually a release missed on an exception path, with the symptom of utilization rising monotonically and never falling back, returning to normal after a restart. Protection: set an **acquisition wait timeout** (fail fast if you can't get one, don't wait forever), set a **maximum lifetime and idle eviction** on connections, and enable **leak detection** (print a stack trace when a connection is held longer than N seconds; this is the most effective way to find leaks). A bigger pool is not better: the database's concurrent processing capacity is limited, and an oversized pool merely moves the queueing from the application side to the database side and worsens the database's context switching.
[Which layer] Connection pool configuration plus metric instrumentation.
[Key parameters] Start the pool size from (CPU cores x 2 + number of disks) and tune with load tests, usually tens, not hundreds; acquisition timeout 1~3s; leak detection threshold 10s; maximum connection lifetime 30 minutes.
[How to verify] Observe pool utilization and wait time during load tests; then artificially create a code path that doesn't release its connection, and leak detection should print its stack trace.
[Pitfalls] Enlarging the pool on discovering it's full, pushing the problem onto the database, and it comes back a few days later in a worse form; also not configuring an acquisition timeout, so requests queue indefinitely and all threads end up stuck instead of failing fast.

n-plus-one.logic: After fetching N records, a related-data query is issued for each one, so 1 query becomes N+1. ORM lazy loading makes it completely unnoticeable to write; you only discover it by reading the SQL log.
n-plus-one.prompt:
Implement elimination of the "N+1 Query" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] A list endpoint fetches 100 orders, the template accesses order.user.name, and the ORM then issues another 100 SQL queries for users. Nothing looks abnormal in the code, and it's fast locally with only 3 rows, but after release the endpoint takes seconds.
[Approach] First **make it visible**: turn on SQL logging in development and count queries per request, and alert in the log (or even fail the test) when a threshold (say 20) is exceeded; **this matters more than any optimization technique**, because N+1 keeps getting reintroduced. There are two kinds of fixes: **eager loading** (the ORM's include / joinedload / with, fetching the relations back in one JOIN or one IN query); **batch loaders** (the DataLoader pattern: collect the many single-item requests of the same tick and merge them into one IN query, especially suited to GraphQL, where you can't predict which fields will be fetched). Note that eager loading also has traps: for one-to-many relations a JOIN multiplies the result rows (Cartesian blow-up), and with large fields you're better off doing two queries and stitching them in memory. **Don't blindly eager-load all relations just to eliminate N+1**; that turns into "querying a pile of unused data every time".
[Which layer] The data access layer; combine with field trimming at the API layer to decide whether to load a given relation.
[Key parameters] Per-request SQL count threshold 20; batch loader batch size 100~500; for one-to-many relations prefer two queries over a JOIN.
[How to verify] Write a test for key endpoints that asserts "this request issues no more than N SQL statements"; such tests catch regressions before code review, far cheaper than discovering them afterwards.
[Pitfalls] Eager-loading a one-to-many relation with a JOIN, so the main table's fields are returned repeatedly and data volume multiplies several times, slower than N+1; also fixing it only in the development environment, after which newly added code paths introduce new N+1s because there is no automated gatekeeper.

svg.取完列表又逐条查关联 —— 预加载或批量合并: List, then per-row lookups; preload or batch

request-coalescing.logic: Gather multiple operations of the same kind within a short time into one batch and send them out together. Throughput improves greatly, at the cost of each request waiting a bit longer, so you have to pick a point between latency and throughput.
request-coalescing.prompt:
Implement "Request Coalescing" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] High-frequency small operations (writing metrics one by one, looking up users one by one, sending messages one by one) each pay a network round trip and transaction overhead. Each looks fast on its own, but cumulatively they saturate the downstream.
[Approach] Two modes. **Batching**: use a short window (e.g. 10ms) or a count threshold (e.g. 100 items) to collect requests, and send the whole batch once either condition is met. A longer window means higher throughput and higher latency, so set it per business: metrics can be batched for 1 second, user lookups only a few milliseconds. **Single flight**: of fully identical concurrent requests, only one is actually sent, and the rest wait and share the result; this is especially effective for cache rebuilds (see the breakdown case in "Cache Penetration, Breakdown & Avalanche"). Both modes must handle **partial failure**: when some items in a batch fail, results must be returned per item (see "Partial Failure in Batch"), and the whole batch can't be counted as failed. You also need **backpressure**: the batching queue must have a cap and reject or block when full, since an unbounded queue eats all memory when the downstream slows. Before the process exits, flush whatever is left in the queue (see "Graceful Shutdown").
[Which layer] The client-side call wrapper.
[Key parameters] Window 5~20ms (online path) / 200~1000ms (async path); batch size cap 100~500; queue cap computed from memory, with a rejection policy.
[How to verify] Compare downstream QPS and your own P99 before and after enabling: QPS should drop noticeably and P99 should increase by no more than the window length. If P99 rises far beyond the window, the batch is too large or the downstream is slower at handling batches.
[Pitfalls] An unbounded batching queue, so memory grows to OOM as soon as the downstream slows; also not flushing the queue on process exit, so the last batch of data is silently lost, a loss that almost never gets noticed.

cache-warmup.logic: When a new instance comes up its cache is empty, so all requests hit the database directly. The very moment of scaling out or restarting is when the database is most likely to be knocked over.
cache-warmup.prompt:
Implement "Cache Warm-up" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] When scaling out or restarting, the new instance's local cache, connection pool, and JIT are all cold, and it immediately takes an even share of traffic, hitting the database at a rate far above steady state; **precisely when you scaled out because load was high**, the scale-out itself crushes the database.
[Approach] Three things working together. (1) **Warm up**: after the instance starts and **before** the readiness probe returns success, proactively load hot data (config, dictionaries, the Top N hot objects) and establish the connection pool's minimum connections. The hot list can be computed offline from production access statistics; don't list it by gut feeling. (2) **Slow start**: after becoming ready, don't take full traffic immediately; have the load balancer ramp up gradually by weight (many gateways support slow start), or implement a gradually loosening rate limit at the entry point yourself, giving the cache time to fill. (3) **The readiness probe must honestly reflect warm-up state**: an instance that hasn't finished warming up shouldn't claim to be ready (see "Meaningful Health Checks"). Note that warm-up itself also hits the database, so rate-limit it and stagger the warm-up times of multiple instances; otherwise warming up 10 instances scaled out at once is a self-made avalanche.
[Which layer] The startup sequence + the readiness probe + the load balancer's slow-start configuration.
[Key parameters] Warm-up timeout 30~60s (let it through even on timeout; don't block the release); slow-start window 30~60s; rate-limit warm-up queries; add random delay to stagger warm-up across instances.
[How to verify] Scale out one instance under production traffic and observe that database QPS shows no noticeable spike and the first batch of requests on the new instance has latency close to the old instances.
[Pitfalls] Warm-up without a rate limit, so several new instances pull data at full speed at the same time during scale-out and knock the database over, and the firefighting action becomes a new source of failure; also never becoming ready when warm-up fails, so the new version can never be released.

backpressure.logic: When you can't keep up, make the pressure **propagate upstream** instead of accepting without limit. An unbounded queue isn't a buffer; it postpones "denial of service" into "out of memory".
backpressure.prompt:
Implement "Backpressure" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] When traffic exceeds processing capacity, if you keep accepting, requests pile up in queues, latency grows without bound, memory keeps rising, and finally you OOM or everything times out; **every request failing is much worse than rejecting some**.
[Approach] The core is to make pressure visible and propagate it upstream. (1) **Every layer's queue must have a cap**, and fail fast when full (return 429/503 with Retry-After); no unbounded queueing. (2) **Drop work that has already become meaningless first**: when a request enters the queue, note its deadline, and on dequeue if it has already exceeded the upstream's timeout budget, drop it directly; don't spend effort computing a result nobody wants (this alone reclaims a lot of compute immediately under overload). (3) **Distinguish priorities**: under overload reject low-value traffic first (batch jobs, non-core endpoints) and protect the core path (combined with bulkhead isolation). (4) In stream processing use mechanisms that support backpressure (such as request(n) in reactive streams, or TCP windows) so that consumption speed controls production speed in reverse; when writing your own producer-consumer, a blocking write into a bounded queue is naturally backpressure. (5) Load shedding must happen **as early as possible**, rejecting at the entry point, rather than letting requests travel through most of the system and then fail.
[Which layer] Entry rate limiting + a bounded queue at every layer + deadline checks.
[Key parameters] Derive the queue cap from "cap x per-item processing time < timeout budget"; under overload reject with 503 + Retry-After (with jitter); the deadline travels with the request.
[How to verify] Load-test to 3x capacity, and the service should **steadily** handle the portion within capacity and quickly reject the rest, rather than overall latency soaring until everything times out. The shape of that curve is the criterion for whether backpressure exists.
[Pitfalls] Using an unbounded queue as "peak shaving", so when a peak arrives memory climbs linearly, finally OOM and restart, and all backlogged requests are lost; also starting to drop only under overload, but with the dropping happening at the last stage of the processing chain, so the compute upstream of it was already wasted.

svg.有界队列＋快速拒绝；无界排队只是把拒绝推迟成 OOM: Bounded queue + fast reject; unbounded = OOM later

hot-cold-split.logic: Move rarely accessed historical data to cheaper, slower storage so the hot dataset is small enough to fit in memory. It saves money and is faster, at the cost that accessing cold data takes a different path.
hot-cold-split.prompt:
Implement "Hot/Cold Data Split" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] More than 90% of total data is often historical data that is almost never accessed, but it shares the same table and the same indexes as hot data, making indexes deeper, lowering cache hit rates, slowing backups and migrations, and costing more.
[Approach] First use access logs to compute the **real hot/cold boundary** (e.g. 95% of reads concentrate in the last 30 days); don't set it by gut feeling. Then tier: the hot tier is the primary database, the warm tier can be archive tables in the same database or a separate analytics database, and the cold tier is columnar files in object storage. Moves are done in time-based batches and are **reversible**: copy first, then verify, then delete, never delete first. **The key is that query paths must be explicitly distinguished**: by default query only the hot tier, and when historical data is needed the caller declares it explicitly (e.g. an include_archived parameter or a separate history query endpoint); **don't build a transparent fallback of "query hot, and if not found automatically query cold"**, because that makes an endpoint that should be fast suddenly dozens of times slower for certain inputs, and completely unpredictably. Cold-tier queries should give a clear latency expectation (or even return via an async job, see "Async Long Job").
[Which layer] Storage tiering + query routing; combine with partitioned tables so that moving becomes DROP PARTITION (see "Archiving & Partitioning").
[Key parameters] Set the hot/cold boundary from the access distribution, commonly 30~90 days; move batch size 1000~10000 rows, run during off-peak; rate-limit cold-tier queries separately.
[How to verify] After the move, compare the hot table's row count, index size, and cache hit rate, which should improve noticeably; then verify that the history query path correctly returns the moved data and that **the default path's latency shows no long tail**.
[Pitfalls] Building a transparent fallback, so an endpoint that looks up one old record is occasionally 30x slower and can never be reproduced during troubleshooting (since it depends on which tier the data landed in); also deleting before writing during the move, so a mid-way failure loses data permanently.

load-test-baseline.logic: The value of load testing isn't in measuring a "maximum QPS" but in establishing a comparable baseline so that the performance impact of every change becomes visible.
load-test-baseline.prompt:
Implement "Load Test Baseline" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Performance problems usually degrade slowly: each change adds 5ms, and six months later an endpoint goes from 50ms to 500ms, while no single change looked wrong. Without a baseline you can't attribute the regression and can only search for a needle in a haystack after an incident.
[Approach] The goal of load testing is to be **comparable**, so three things must be fixed: a **fixed scenario** (mixed according to real traffic composition, not hammering only the fastest endpoint), a **fixed dataset** (data volume and distribution close to production; conclusions from load testing on 100 rows are meaningless, since index behavior is completely different), and a **fixed environment** (configuration and instance specs isomorphic to production, otherwise the numbers aren't comparable). The metric isn't the single number "maximum QPS" but **a curve**: as concurrency rises, how throughput, P99 latency, and error rate each change. The truly useful output is the **knee**: the concurrency at which throughput stops rising and latency starts to soar, and that is your capacity. **Watch P99, not the average**, since averages get diluted by lots of fast requests while users feel the long tail. Run this baseline in CI or on a nightly schedule, compare with the last run, and alert when a regression exceeds a threshold.
[Which layer] A dedicated load-test environment + scheduled job + archived results.
[Key parameters] Dataset at least 1/10 of production with a similar distribution; test duration >= 10 minutes (short tests can't reveal GC and cache effects); regression alert threshold P99 degrading by 20%; vary only one variable at a time.
[How to verify] Deliberately merge a change known to slow things down, and the baseline comparison should flag it. A baseline never proven to raise an alarm is as good as no baseline.
[Pitfalls] Load-testing on a small dataset, with conclusions opposite to production (on a small table a full scan is faster than using an index); also recording only a single "maximum QPS" number, which can't be compared next time because the scenario has changed.

svg.要的是一条曲线和那个拐点，不是一个「最大 QPS」: Want a curve and its knee, not one max QPS

capacity-watermark.logic: Set a "time to scale out" line for each critical resource, and alert before it is reached. If you wait until 100% to act, the time scaling itself takes is already too late.
capacity-watermark.prompt:
Implement "Capacity Watermark" in the service mentioned above.
[Problem it solves] Capacity problems always erupt at the busiest time, and that is when scaling out is slowest and most dangerous (cold caches, warm-up pressure, see "Cache Warm-up"). What's missing isn't monitoring but **lead time**: if you only alert at 90% CPU, the time left for you is already not enough.
[Approach] Set watermarks for every resource that may become a bottleneck, not just CPU: connection pool utilization, queue backlog, disk usage and growth rate, message consumption lag, license/quota limits, per-table row count. Give each line **two tiers**: a warning watermark (say 60%, triggering "time to plan a scale-out", via a ticket rather than the on-call) and a danger watermark (80%, triggering an on-call alert). **Convert watermarks to time using the growth rate**: "30% of disk left" carries no information, while "full in 9 days at the current growth rate" is actionable. Review periodically (monthly): capacity assumptions go stale as the business changes. You also need to know **per-instance capacity limits** (from the load test baseline, see "Load Test Baseline"), to work out "how many instances current traffic needs and how much headroom remains". **Factor in the lead time of scaling out as well**: if scaling out takes 20 minutes, the watermark must leave more than 20 minutes of margin.
[Which layer] Monitoring and alerting + a periodic capacity review process.
[Key parameters] Warning 60%, danger 80%; alert on disk by "days remaining < 14" rather than by percentage; review monthly; headroom must at least cover redistribution after a single availability zone failure.
[How to verify] Look back at the most recent capacity-related incident and ask: would the current watermark have alerted in advance? How far in advance? If not enough, adjust the line. This is far more useful than adding more monitoring items.
[Pitfalls] Monitoring only CPU and memory, then getting stuck on file descriptor count, connection pool, or some third-party quota; also setting the alert at 90% when going from alert to scale-out complete takes half an hour and going from 90% to 100% takes only five minutes.

svg.水位线要按增长速率折算成「还剩几天」才可行动: Watermark → days left, so it's actionable
